title: DriftOPD: Sequence-Level Reverse-KL Distillation for One-Step VLA Policies
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models increasingly rely on action experts that generate short action chunks under receding-horizon control. While chunk-level training is convenient across robot embodiments, it optimizes local action likelihood without explicitly accounting for long-horizon task success. Sequence-level reinforcement learning can address this limitation, but typically requires policy rollouts and closed-loop interaction, which are costly for real-robot manipulation. We introduce DriftOPD, a teacher-free, rollout-free framework for sequence-level on-policy distillation of continuous VLA action experts. We show that the sequence-level reverse Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence decomposes into a chunk-level reverse-KL term and a future-potential term that captures the long-horizon effect of the current action. DriftOPD optimizes these two terms using a one-step drifting objective and a Q-function critic learned from offline demonstrations, respectively, enabling sequence-level optimization with only offline data and one-step action generation. Across multiple VLA architectures in simulation and real-world manipulation, DriftOPD generally outperforms existing one-step distillation baselines while achieving task success performance comparable to multi-step teacher policies. These results demonstrate that long-horizon behavior can be effectively distilled into one-step VLA action experts without online interaction or a separate teacher.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models increasingly rely on action experts that generate short action chunks under receding-horizon control. While chunk-level training is convenient across robot embodiments, it optimizes local action likelihood without explicitly accounting for long-horizon task success. Sequence-level reinforcement learning can address this limitation, but typically requires policy rollouts and closed-loop interaction, which are costly for real-robot manipulation. We introduce DriftOPD, a teacher-free, rollout-free framework for sequence-level on-policy distillation of continuous VLA action experts. We show that the sequence-level reverse Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence decomposes into a chunk-level reverse-KL term and a future-potential term that captures the long-horizon effect of the current action. DriftOPD optimizes these two terms using a one-step drifting objective and a Q-function critic learned from offline demonstrations, respectively, enabling sequence-level optimization with only offline data and one-step action generation. Across multiple VLA architectures in simulation and real-world manipulation, DriftOPD generally outperforms existing one-step distillation baselines while achieving task success performance comparable to multi-step teacher policies. These results demonstrate that long-horizon behavior can be effectively distilled into one-step VLA action experts without online interaction or a separate teacher. Introduction sec:intro Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation~ RT2,OpenVLA,pi05 . As a robot manipulation system, a VLA leverages the reasoning and planning knowledge of Vision-Language Models (VLMs), corresponding to System 2, together with the intuitive behavior generation of a flow-based action expert, corresponding to System 1~ pi0,HiRobot . This VLA architecture is designed to reflect the state (e.g., environment and proprioception) that change according to actions, and VLAs perform tasks through closed-loop execution~ RT1,Gr00tN1 . Since replanning every low-level action at each control step is computationally inefficient, VLAs commonly adopt a receding-horizon control scheme, repeatedly predicting short action chunks from updated observations~ ACT,OpenVLA-OFT . Action chunks provide a convenient common training unit for action experts across multiple embodiments~ pi05,Gr00tN1 . However, under this chunk-level training paradigm, VLAs suffer from two problems ( a). First, because VLAs are trained on demonstration states at train time, these VLAs suffer from a test-time distribution mismatch and fail to generalize to model-generated states~ DAger,Stable-BC . Second, within an action sequence composed of action chunks, the policy na\"ively generates only locally likely action chunks at each step without considering the final task success~ ProphRL . On the other hand, while recent reinforcement learning methods improve VLA training using various forms of sequence-level feedback~ VLA-RL,SimpleVLA-RL,VLA-RFT , these approaches heavily rely on policy-generated action sequences to obtain such supervision. They must execute the current policy, evaluate the resulting sequences, and often recollect new rollouts as the policy changes. This dependence on closed-loop interaction is particularly costly for real-robot manipulation~ WMPO . To this end, we explore a scalable and simple sequence-level objective function for action-expert training ( b). Currently, due to the multi-step sampling of diffusion/flow action experts, research on the trajectory-level reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD) for continuous generative policies has remained at the level of chunk-level ODE trajectories~ DiffusionOPD,FlowOPD . In this work, we formulate sequence-level on-policy distillation (OPD) through the reverse KLD over the action sequence leading to success. Our formulated sequence-level OPD consists of a chunk-level reverse KLD term and a future-potential term for the current action chunk, similar to MiniLLM~ MiniLLM . However, unlike MiniLLM, the clean logits of continuous action chunks required for the future-potential term remain intractable. Therefore, the sequence-level OPD formulation itself still relies on rollout data, is bounded by the performance of the teacher model, and incurs multi-step sampling latency. To address these challenges, we propose DriftOPD, a teacher-free sequence-level OPD method for one-step distillation. DriftOPD calculates the chunk-level reverse KLD term as a one-step distribution-matching drifting objective~ Drifting , while estimating the future-potential term with a critic-based neural network. In this way, DriftOPD achieves one-step inference while learning directly from human demonstrations, without a separate teacher model. In practice, we adapt VGAS~ VGAS , which provides a demonstration-trained Q-function critic, to achieve fully rollout-free sequence-level OPD. Consequently, because DriftOPD uses only demonstration data, it can be readily applied across multiple embodiments, while its generated-sample-based sequence-level OPD avoids the test-time mismatch. Moreover, one-step policy generation through the drifting objective reduces robot manipulation latency. We apply DriftOPD to a diverse set of VLA models spanning different architectures, fine-tuning strategies, and action-expert parameterizations~ pi05,Gr00tN1,SmolVLA,ABot-M0 . We distill their multi-step sampling capability into one-step policy generation at the action-sequence level. Our experiments cover simulation and real-world execution across a wide range of robot manipulation tasks~ RoboCasa365,RoboTwin2,Libero,LiberoPlus . Experiments show that DriftOPD outperforms existing one-step distillation methods for the VLA action expert, achieving task success rates comparable to those of multi-step teachers. Further analysis shows that DriftOPD provides more stable training in data-scarce VLA settings, remains effective across diverse VLA configurations (e.g., architecture, fine-tuning strategy, and parameterization), and enables faster execution through one-step policy generation, with negligible loss of action diversity. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: [noitemsep, nolistsep, leftmargin=*] We formulate sequence-level on-policy-distillation for VLAs by minimizing the reverse KLD over action-sequence distributions, decomposing it into a local action-chunk reverse-KL term and a future-potential term. We propose DriftOPD to make sequence-level OPD tractable for continuous VLA action experts. It realizes the local reverse KLD term with a one-step drifting objective and approximates the future-potential term with a demonstration-trained Q-function critic, enabling teacher-free and rollout-free one-step distillation. Across diverse VLA configurations in simulation and real-world manipulation, DriftOPD generally outperforms existing one-step distillation baselines while achieving task success comparable to multi-step policies. It further provides stable training in data-scarce VLA settings and faster execution than multi-step policy generation. Related Work sec:related Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Models ssuc:related-VLA Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as general-purpose robot policies that couple vision-language representations with imitation learning from large-scale robot demonstrations~ RT2,pi0,Gr00tN1 . Early models such as RT-1~ RT1 and RT-2~ RT2 established scalable language-conditioned robot policies. Recent models such as series~ pi05,pi0 use continuous action experts for diverse robot tasks. In parallel, ACT~ ACT and Diffusion Policy~ DiffusionPolicy demonstrated the effectiveness of predicting short action sequences (i.e., chunk) rather than individual actions. Action chunking has since become a common training and execution unit in continuous-control VLAs~ pi0,OpenVLA-OFT,RLDX1 , and is adopted by recent models such as series~ pi05,pi0 , RLDX~ RLDX1 , ABot~ ABot-M0 , and GR00T series~ Gr00tN1 . However, behavior-cloned policies remain vulnerable to test-time distribution shift, where the pretrained model fail to generalize to model- generated state at the test time~ DAger,Stable-BC . Moreover, chunk-level imitation objectives provide no direct supervision for final task success~ ProphRL,WMPO . Recent reinforcement learning methods address these limitations through sequence-level feedback~ VLA-RL,SimpleVLA-RL,VLA-RFT . However, obtaining such feedback from physical rollouts requires costly closed-loop interaction on real robots~ WMPO . One-Step Distillation of Diffusion/Flow Models ssec:related-distill Diffusion and flow-based models~ NCSN,SongSDE,RectifiedFlow have been widely adopted as action experts in VLA models~ pi05,Gr00tN1 , but their iterative sampling incurs substantial inference latency~ DDIM,DPMSolver . To reduce the number of sampling steps, prior work has explored progressive and consistency distillation~ PD,CM,sCM , distribution matching~ DMD , and more recently native one-step formulations such as consistency objective~ CM,iCM,sCM , MeanFlow~ MF,iMF , and distribution drifting~ Drifting . Similar ideas have been introduced for robotic policies, including consistency- and distribution-matching-based policy distillation~ ConsistencyPolicy,SDMPolicy . For VLA models, OFPolicy employ self-distillation for one-step action generation, while MFPolicy and DriftingVLA directly introduce native one-step generation objectives into VLA action experts. Despite their efficiency, existing approaches mainly optimize action-chunk-level ODE-trajectory or distribution matching, without directly distilling supervision from task success, which can leave a gap between chunk-level training objectives and closed-loop test-time behavior. On-Policy Distillation ssec:related-OPD Prevalent action-chunking VLAs can be viewed as autoregressive (AR) sequence models at the chunk level, where each action chunk is conditioned on states induced by previously executed chunks. This perspective naturally connects VLAs to knowledge distillation in large language models (LLMs), where recent work minimizes the divergence between teacher and student distributions~ MiniLLM,GKD . In particular, a common formulation of on-policy distillation (OPD) minimizes the sequence-level reverse Kullback-Leibler divergence (KLD), thereby evaluating the student and teacher distributions at student-visited states~ MiniLLM,DecouplingKLTraj . This reverse KLD formulation alleviates the train-test distribution mismatch of supervised fine-tuning by training on student-generated sequences~ MiniLLM,GKD . Such on-policy supervision has been particularly effective for long-horizon generation and reasoning tasks, including mathematical reasoning~ DecouplingKLTraj,SelfDistilledReasoner . Recent works extend this principle to continuous generative models, where DiffusionOPD~ DiffusionOPD and FlowOPD~ FlowOPD distill teacher knowledge along student-generated ODE trajectories from noise to data. However, these ODE trajectory-level OPD still distills knowledge only within each action chunk. It does not explicitly capture the sequence of executed chunks that determines final task success. Moreover, flow-based action experts do not directly provide clean-action likelihoods ~ FlowMatching , making sequence-level OPD over action chunks difficult to apply directly. VLA-OPD~ VLA-OPD instead derives dense teacher-based distillation rewards on student rollouts, but requires closed-loop environment interaction and repeated teacher queries. This work therefore aims to overcome these challenges, thereby enabling task-success signals to be incorporated across action-chunk sequences. title: DSSR-3D: Decoupled Reasoning for View-Dependent Referring in 3D Gaussians
summary: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting have enabled open-vocabulary and referring segmentation by distilling semantic knowledge from 2D foundation models into 3D representations. However, existing referring fields embed language features in a globally view-invariant space, making them fundamentally unable to resolve observer-centric spatial relations (e.g., "to the left of") that depend on camera pose. We propose DSSR-3D, an inference-time framework for view-dependent referring segmentation on continuous 3D Gaussian fields, formalized as two interfaces - pose-invariant semantic localization and pose-conditioned spatial reasoning - such that any pair of functions satisfying these constraints yields a valid instantiation, requiring no retraining of the underlying semantic field and no reliance on discrete geometric proxies such as bounding boxes. We instantiate the two interfaces with a temperature-sharpened softmax localization mechanism and a projection-based directional scoring function, fused via a lightweight, training-free step, and show they transfer zero-shot to structurally distinct semantic fields without adaptation. We further propose ViewRef-GS, a benchmark isolating view-dependent segmentation on 3D Gaussian fields, evaluated jointly with an augmented Ref-LERF to provide a comprehensive testbed for viewpoint-dependent spatial grounding. Experiments show consistent gains over existing 3DGS-based referring methods, with no additional training beyond the base semantic field
full_text: DSSR-3D: Decoupled Reasoning for View-Dependent Referring in 3D Gaussians Anonymous Author(s) Thanh-Khoi Nguyen Thien-Phuc Tran Minh-Triet Tran University of Science, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam Viet Nam National University, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam\\ Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting have enabled open- vocabulary and referring segmentation by distilling semantic knowledge from 2D foundation models into 3D representations. However, existing referring fields embed language features in a globally view-invariant space, making them fundamentally unable to resolve observer-centric spatial relations (e.g., "to the left of") that depend on camera pose. We propose DSSR-3D, an inference-time framework for view-dependent referring segmentation on continuous 3D Gaussian fields, formalized as two interfaces - pose-invariant semantic localization and pose-conditioned spatial reasoning - such that any pair of functions satisfying these constraints yields a valid instantiation, requiring no retraining of the underlying semantic field and no reliance on discrete geometric proxies such as bounding boxes. We instantiate the two interfaces with a temperature-sharpened softmax localization mechanism and a projection-based directional scoring function, fused via a lightweight, training-free step, and show they transfer zero-shot to structurally distinct semantic fields without adaptation. We further propose ViewRef-GS, a benchmark isolating view-dependent segmentation on 3D Gaussian fields, evaluated jointly with an augmented Ref-LERF to provide a comprehensive testbed for viewpoint-dependent spatial grounding. Experiments show consistent gains over existing 3DGS-based referring methods, with no additional training beyond the base semantic field. Introduction sec:intro Beyond novel view synthesis~ kerbl20233dgs,mildenhall2020nerf , 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has enabled 3D segmentation by distilling 2D foundation models (CLIP~ radford2021clip , SAM~ kirillov2023sam ) into queryable semantic fields~ qin2024langsplat,zhou2024feature3dgs,ye2024gaussiangrouping , recently extended to natural-language referring segmentation by ReferSplat~ he2025refersplat . Yet these methods~ qin2024langsplat,he2025refersplat,zhou2024feature3dgs,zhao2024fmgs,shi2024language,ji2025fastlgs encode semantics in globally view-invariant spaces without camera-pose conditioning, making observer-centric spatial relations difficult to resolve, leading to severe spatial hallucinations and physical inconsistencies in dynamic interactive scenarios. The problem is compounded on the 2D side: foundation models such as GroundingSAM~ ren2024grounded operate directly on isolated image frames without any notion of depth or 3D structure, so their spatial reasoning breaks down under occlusion and view inconsistency (Fig.~ fig:motivation ). Recent 3D Scene Graph methods~ tao2026geocga,xie2026relags model spatial relations (e.g., ``above'') explicitly, but as static, view-invariant edges, remaining ill-suited to relations whose meaning shifts with viewpoint. To address perspective-dependent queries, pioneering works explicitly incorporate observer viewpoints, either by conditioning 3D multimodal models on camera poses~ nanri2026viewpoint3dseg or training dedicated viewpoint prediction networks for scene alignment~ shi2024viewpointaware . However, these approaches face three critical bottlenecks. First, they operate on traditional point clouds, omitting the real-time rendering advantages of 3DGS. Second, they incur substantial training overhead, as camera dependence is implicitly learned through additional viewpoint supervision and pretraining, rather than being directly available for inference-time evaluation. Finally, they rely heavily on discrete 3D bounding boxes. Gathering dense box annotations is prohibitively expensive, and forcing spatial reasoning through such rigid proxies introduces quantization errors that affect fine-grained geometric fidelity. This leaves a critical gap: how can we achieve true viewpoint-aware spatial reasoning natively on 3D Gaussian fields without relying on point clouds, discrete bounding boxes, or heavy training overhead? To address these limitations, we propose a verifiable, training-free reasoning layer that decouples spatial reasoning to achieve interpretable, evidence-grounded spatial grounding natively on continuous 3DGS. Rather than costly bounding-box annotations or scale-sensitive, noise-prone fixed top- selection, we propose a Temperature-Sharpened Softmax mechanism for scale-adaptive, bounding-box-free localization, paired with a Direction-Aware Scoring mechanism that projects Gaussians onto the observer's local horizontal -plane with a soft spatial decay to inject directional bias, without task-specific retraining. Both instantiate a single principle: we formalize view-dependent spatial grounding as two independent, interface-constrained sub-problems (Sec.~ sec:problem-formulation ), decoupling spatial reasoning from the underlying semantic field and enabling zero-shot composition with structurally distinct frozen fields (Table~ tab:cross-backbone ). Finally, we propose ViewRef-GS, to our knowledge the first benchmark isolating view-dependent, observer-centric spatial relations for 3DGS referring segmentation, combined with a directional-query augmentation of Ref-LERF into a six-scene evaluation suite. Our main contributions are as follows: We formalize view-dependent 3D spatial grounding as two independent sub-problems: pose-invariant localization and pose-conditioned relational scoring. This training-free decomposition acts as a plug-and-play reasoning layer, achieving consistent gains across structurally distinct, frozen 3DGS backbones without per-backbone tuning. We instantiate this via two inference-time mechanisms: a Temperature-Sharpened Softmax for scale-adaptive, bounding-box-free reference localization, and a Direction-Aware Scoring function that resolves pose-conditioned relations through projection and spatial decay. We propose ViewRef-GS, a synthetic benchmark that, together with an augmented Ref-LERF, provides a comprehensive testbed for evaluating viewpoint-dependent spatial grounding under diverse observer-centric configurations. Related Work sec:related-work 3D Semantic and Referring Segmentation sec:related-semantic-segmentation 3DGS~ kerbl20233dgs has become a dominant explicit representation for real-time novel-view synthesis, extending earlier neural radiance fields (NeRF)~ mildenhall2020nerf . A large body of work embeds semantic or language features into Gaussians: LERF~ kerr2023lerf first volume-rendered CLIP embeddings inside NeRF, and subsequent 3DGS methods-Feature3DGS~ zhou2024feature3dgs , LangSplat~ qin2024langsplat , LEGaussian~ shi2024language , FMGS~ zhao2024fmgs , FastLGS~ ji2025fastlgs -distill CLIP/SAM features per-Gaussian for open-vocabulary querying, while GaussianGrouping~ ye2024gaussiangrouping combines SAM masks with contrastive grouping for instance-level segments. ReferSplat~ he2025refersplat formalized referring segmentation on 3DGS via spatially-aware referring fields and the Ref-LERF benchmark. Successors enrich relational modeling through cross-modal graph alignment or explicit relational embeddings (GeoCGA~ tao2026geocga , ReLaGS~ xie2026relags ), or inject camera geometry with cross-view logit alignment (CaRF~ tao2025carf ). Yet all encode semantics in a globally view-invariant space, limiting their ability to resolve observer-centric spatial relations whose meaning depends on camera pose. Viewpoint-Aware Spatial Reasoning sec:related-viewpoint-reasoning Spatial language in 3D is inherently viewpoint-dependent, with relations such as "left/right" or "front/behind" shifting with the observer's pose. Early work conditions grounding on the predicted speaker viewpoint~ shi2024viewpointaware , and Nanri et al.~ nanri2026viewpoint3dseg introduce a large-scale benchmark that isolates observer-centric relations under camera-pose conditioning. Subsequent methods target multi-view consistency and relational reasoning-ViewSRD~ huang2025viewsrd decomposes multi-anchor queries across viewpoints, Position3D~ wang2026position3d injects spatial relations into point-cloud queries, and others explore relationship graphs, zero-shot view retrieval, or VLM-guided novel-view selection on 3DGS~ shi2025semanticsprogramming,liao2025gvr,mvggt2026,kim2026gaussexplorer -but all either operate on point clouds/ meshes, rely on discrete bounding boxes, require viewpoint-specific training, or treat relations as view-invariant. DSSR-3D instead natively targets continuous 3D Gaussian fields with two training-free interfaces-pose-invariant localization and pose-conditioned directional scoring-requiring neither boxes nor per-backbone retraining, accompanied by ViewRef-GS, the first benchmark isolating view-dependent referring segmentation on 3DGS. Rendering projects Gaussians onto the image plane via depth-sorted alpha compositing (Eq.~ eq:color-rendering ). For referring segmentation, we associate each Gaussian with a semantic feature and replace with a scalar alignment score , yielding the query-conditioned response map (Eq.~ eq:score-rendering ), where measures 's relevance to the text query. 0.49 0.49 Problem Formulation sec:problem-formulation Let be a 3D Gaussian scene. Given a camera viewpoint and a query , we aim to localize the target object. We focus on observer-centric, view-dependent relations (e.g., "left", "front") and isolate viewpoint ambiguity by projecting geometry onto the camera's local horizontal plane. Motivated by ground-based robotics, we constrain to near-planar cameras (excluding aerial views where lateral constraints become ill-defined) and focus on single-anchor queries. Prior work conflates semantic identification and spatial reasoning into a single scoring function, forcing retraining per semantic field. We decompose the problem into two independent sub-problems, applied atop the frozen field's native scoring of the anchor or target span: Problem I (View-Invariant Localization): Given , estimate a pose-invariant reference that is scale-adaptive and bounded within the anchor's semantic support. Problem II (View-Conditioned Relational Scoring): Given , pose , and directional constraint , estimate a spatial score that is pose-conditioned, sign-consistent, and locality-aware (decaying with distance from ). Pipeline Overview sec:pipeline-overview Our training-free pipeline maps a query to a 2D mask over a frozen semantic field (Figure~ fig:pipeline ). Query Rewriting extracts ; Pose-Invariant Semantic Localization (Sec.~ sec:anchor-localization ) estimates the reference ; Pose-Conditioned Directional Scoring (Sec.~ sec:direction-scoring ) evaluates the relation under camera pose ; and Semantic-Spatial Fusion (Sec.~ sec:semantic-spatial-fusion ) renders the final mask. title: Towards a General Humanoid Loco-Manipulation Model via Egocentric Whole-Body Human Data Pretraining
summary: Humanoid whole-body manipulation has advanced rapidly, enabling policies to coordinate locomotion, posture, bimanual interaction, and dexterous hand movements. Meanwhile, egocentric human videos provide diverse examples of everyday interactions across objects and scenes, offering scalable supervision without robot operation. However, existing supervision from these videos provides limited coverage of whole-body movement and coordination with hand-object interaction, while obtaining such supervision through humanoid teleoperation is also costly and difficult to scale. We therefore explore how human experience can support scalable learning of humanoid loco-manipulation. To support this study, we introduce HumanVerse-500, a 500-hour dataset of diverse human loco-manipulation behaviors in open-world environments, collected with a lightweight wearable system that synchronizes egocentric video with body and hand motion. Building on this dataset, we develop $λ_0$, a whole-body humanoid vision-language-action policy, through three-stage training that first learns interaction from diverse egocentric datasets, then coordinates body and hand motion using HumanVerse-500, and finally adapts the policy to downstream tasks and robot embodiments. Across these stages, $λ_0$ learns a shared representation space for human experience transfer, while domain-specific interfaces handle differences between human and robot states and actions. We evaluate $λ_0$ on SIMPLE and 4 real-world loco-manipulation tasks, achieving state-of-the-art performance, and further analyze its scaling behavior, generalization, and training-stage contributions to understand how human data support downstream whole-body humanoid control. We will release our code, models, and data to support further research.

Introduction Humanoid whole-body manipulation has advanced rapidly, enabling robots to coordinate locomotion, posture, and dexterous manipulation within a unified policy~ jiang2026wholebodyvla,shi2026egohumanoid,wei2026psi0,hu2026openhlm,figure2026helix02,figure2026helix25 . Learning these coordinated behaviors requires demonstrations that capture both whole-body movement and interaction with objects. Such demonstrations can be collected through whole-body teleoperation, where human operators guide humanoids through coordinated movements and object interactions~ fu2025humanplus,he2025omnih2o,luo2025sonic,gear2025grootn16,li2026omega0 . Collecting diverse demonstrations this way requires substantial robot time and human effort, making it difficult to scale across tasks and environments~ shi2026egohumanoid,punamiya2026egoverse . Egocentric human videos offer a scalable alternative, capturing diverse everyday interactions without requiring robot operation~ grauman2022ego4d,kareer2024egomimic,hoque2025egodex,punamiya2026egoverse,figure2026index . Recent methods recover wrist and hand trajectories from these videos, turning observed interactions into action supervision for robot learning~ li2025vitra,yang2025egovla,wang2026ego2robot . Pretraining on these action-labeled videos can improve downstream manipulation, supporting the use of human experience for scalable robot learning~ zheng2026egoscale,punamiya2026egoverse . However, wrist and hand trajectories alone do not fully capture the whole-body coordination required for humanoid loco-manipulation. A humanoid must approach an object, adjust its posture to reach it, and maintain its grasp while carrying it elsewhere~ shi2026egohumanoid,zhao2026halomi . Learning these behaviors requires supervision that preserves the temporal coordination between body movement and hand--object interaction. We therefore ask how diverse human experience can provide scalable whole-body supervision for humanoid loco-manipulation. To address this question, we introduce , a 500-hour dataset of human loco-manipulation collected across diverse activities in open-world environments. We use a lightweight wearable system to capture egocentric video and body motion, then reconstruct hand motion from video to provide synchronized whole-body supervision. Building on , we develop , a whole-body humanoid vision--language--action policy that transfers human experience to robot control (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). We train the policy in three stages to learn interaction from diverse egocentric datasets, coordinate body and hand motion using , and adapt to downstream tasks and robot embodiments. A shared representation space enables transfer across stages, while domain-specific interfaces handle differences between human and robot states and actions. We evaluate on SIMPLE and four real-world loco-manipulation tasks, improving success rates over the strongest evaluated baselines by 3.9 and 22.5 percentage points, respectively. Across the evaluated data scales, more whole-body human data reduces validation loss and improves real-world task progress. Ablations further identify whole-body mid-training as the larger contributor to real-world success among the two human-data stages, while human demonstrations improve progress on robot-unseen objects. These results support scalable whole-body human data as a source of supervision for humanoid loco-manipulation. Our contributions are summarised as follows: We introduce , a 500-hour dataset of open-world human loco-manipulation with synchronized egocentric video, body motion, and hand motion. We develop , a whole-body humanoid vision--language--action policy that transfers human experience through three-stage training in a shared human--robot representation space. We reveal a consistent scaling trend in whole-body human pretraining and demonstrate its benefits for downstream performance and generalization in humanoid loco-manipulation. Related Work Generalist Robot Policies Large-scale robot datasets bring together demonstrations across tasks and embodiments, supporting the development of generalist policies~ dasari2020robonet,jang2022bcz,walke2023bridgedata,openx2024,brohan2023rt1,zitkovich2023rt2,khazatsky2024droid,bu2025agibot,zhao2025humanoideveryday . These policies learn from diverse demonstrations within a shared model~ ghosh2024octo,kim2025openvla,chi2025diffusion , motivating more scalable ways to collect training data. Advances in teleoperation and portable demonstration interfaces reduce collection effort~ dass2023pato,qin2023anyteleop,zhao2023aloha,fu2025mobilealoha,chi2024umi . However, robot-based collection remains tied to hardware availability and repeated environment resets, while portable interfaces capture motion within their supported action spaces. Learning from Human Videos Human video datasets capture diverse activities, objects, and environments, providing rich experience for robot learning~ grauman2022ego4d,damen2022epic,goyal2017something,grauman2024egoexo4d,wang2023holoassist,detone2026nymeriaplus,lightwheel2026egosuite . Learning from it requires connecting observations to actions. Temporal and geometric annotations describe when interactions occur and how hands and objects move~ liu2022hoi4d,wang2025hocap,sener2022assembly101,ragusa2021meccano,huang2024egoexolearn,banerjee2025hot3d , while motion tracking and reconstruction provide human trajectories for action learning~ hoque2025egodex,punamiya2026egoverse,li2025vitra,zheng2026egoscale,wang2026ego2robot . Complementary approaches learn visual representations from human videos~ nair2023r3m,sontakke2023roboclip,kumar2020subroutines or connect human demonstrations to robot control through imitation and alignment~ mandlekar2022offline,shao2020concept2robot,bahl2022whirl,wang2023mimicplay,bharadhwaj2023zeroshot,kareer2024egomimic,lepert2025phantom,yang2025egovla . Human videos offer scalable supervision for manipulation, but capturing whole-body coordination remains challenging for humanoid learning. Humanoid Whole-Body Control Humanoid whole-body control coordinates locomotion, posture, and manipulation to support complex physical interactions~ fu2025humanplus,he2025omnih2o,luo2025sonic . Building on this control foundation, humanoid policies learn task-level behaviors from human experience through latent video actions, geometric pretraining, or joint training on human and robot demonstrations~ jiang2026wholebodyvla,wei2026psi0,shi2026egohumanoid,hu2026openhlm,bjorck2025groot,beingbeyond2026beingh . Predictive models and integrated whole-body systems offer complementary ways to connect perception, motion, and control~ li2026omega0,symbiosis2026dpc,figure2026helix02,parada2026geminirobotics2,zheng2026motionwam,ye2026dreamzero,nvidia2026dreamdojo . A remaining challenge is to turn diverse human experience into scalable supervision for humanoid whole-body control. title: Evaluating the Robustness of Anti-UAV Detection under Controlled Fog Degradation: Fog-Aware Training and Clear-Sky Tradeoff
summary: Vision-based anti-UAV systems must function in poor visibility, yet most benchmarks use only clear-sky footage, and previous robustness studies treat adverse weather as a simple present/absent condition. As a result, the impact of fog severity on ground-to-air UAV detection remains poorly understood. This work presents the first severity-controlled fog benchmark for this task: synthetic fog at ten severity levels is applied to the RGB modality of the Anti-UAV300 dataset, comparing a clear-trained YOLOv5m baseline to a fog-aware model trained on both clear and foggy images. Detection performance drops sharply and non-linearly: degradation is front-loaded across light-to-moderate fog (beta approximately 0.05-0.10), with a 96% reduction in mAP@0.5:0.95 from clear to thickest fog, mainly due to lost recall and confidence. On the comparable metric (mAP@0.5), this collapse exceeds the most extreme rain degradation reported in the closest prior benchmark. Fog-aware training boosts detection across all severities (up to +0.320 mAP@0.5:0.95) with only a 9.1% drop in clear-sky accuracy, raising the threshold for reliable detection while not preventing collapse under extreme fog. Since reliability is lost within a narrow visibility range, simple clear vs adverse tests underestimate operational risk.

Introduction sec:introduction Object tracking is one of the most important and innovative tasks in computer vision, aiming to detect and track objects across image sequences soleimanitaleb_object_2019, smeulders_visual_2014 . This task has many applications including video surveillance zhao_fine-grained_2020, jha_real_2021 , traffic monitoring ghahremannezhad_object_2023, el-alami_review_2024 , and even medical diagnosis systems albuquerque_deep_2025,ragab_comprehensive_2024 . The growing importance of object tracking is particularly evident in the context of Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) wang_progress_2025, jiang_anti-uav_2023, huang_anti-uav410_2024, ding_vision-based_2025 . UAV accessibility and popularity have transformed them from recreational novelties into significant instruments for surveillance and monitoring; however, their misuse now poses escalating risks to public safety and personal privacy aldosari_drone-type-set_2024,coluccia_drone-vs-bird_2024,cubber_standardized_2025,ding_vision-based_2025 . In safety-critical surveillance contexts, unauthorized UAV incursions present severe threats: sightings at airports have repeatedly halted air traffic, leading to massive economic losses and significant operational disruptions ding_vision-based_2025,jiang_anti-uav_2023,aldosari_drone-type-set_2024,cubber_standardized_2025 . A prominent illustration of this vulnerability occurred during the 36-hour closure of London Gatwick Airport, where over 1000 flights were canceled following multiple drone sightings. Reports from this incident indicated that dense fog and light precipitation significantly reduced the effectiveness of visual and thermal cameras hudson_gatwick_nodate . Because poor visibility prevented consistent tracking, law enforcement was unable to identify the culprit or confirm whether the threat was still present. This incident highlights a reliability gap in existing vision-based detection algorithms when deployed in high-stakes environments munir_impact_2024, mudavath_object_2025, tahir_object_2024, appiah_object_2024 . Most existing benchmarks are constructed under clear atmospheric conditions, failing to account for the uncontrollable weather artifacts that safety-critical systems must endure to provide 24/7 protection ding_vision-based_2025,feng_hazydet_2025,munir_impact_2024,xie_cst_2025 . For instance, existing large-scale anti-UAV benchmarks, despite comprising hundreds of thousands of manually annotated bounding boxes across hundreds of video sequences, contain only clear-sky conditions jiang_anti-uav_2023, huang_anti-uav410_2024, xie_cst_2025 . Recent studies confirm that even top-tier detectors suffer performance degradation, when confronted with rain streaks, fog, or motion blur munir_impact_2024, agarwal_warlearn_2024,feng_hazydet_2025 . However, while the sensitivity of detectors to adverse weather has been acknowledged, no existing benchmark provides a parametric, severity controlled fog evaluation framework specifically targeting ground-to-air anti-UAV detection, where fog intensity is varied continuously as a function of a single scattering coefficient. This research addresses this gap by applying a physically inspired atmospheric scattering model to generate controlled fog severity levels agarwal_warlearn_2024 , enabling systematic robustness evaluation of anti-UAV detectors under adverse visibility conditions. Finally, YOLOv5m is selected as the detection architecture, following Munir et al. (2024) munir_impact_2024 who demonstrate it outperforms later YOLO generations under adverse weather conditions. Using the same architecture and variant ensures that degradation results reported here are directly comparable to the closest related benchmark. A more in-depth research design can be found in the methodology section. The study further dedicates a focused sub-analysis to UAV targets across size categories, with particular attention to small targets (those below 50 pixels, including the rare tiny instances below 10 pixels jiang_anti-uav_2023, huang_anti-uav410_2024 ), which are especially vulnerable to visibility degradation due to their minimal pixel footprint and heightened sensitivity to resolution downscaling song_review_2025, hu_improved_2024, sdraka_deep_2022, wang_research_2026 . This study examines whether fog affects UAVs differently depending on their apparent image size, since distant or visually small UAVs may provide fewer visual cues for detection. This study investigates the robustness of YOLOv5m-based UAV detection under controlled fog degradation and evaluates whether synthetic fog augmentation can improve performance under adverse visibility conditions without imposing a substantial cost under clear-sky conditions. The analysis characterises detector performance across ten progressively increasing fog severity levels, with particular attention to changes in mean Average Precision ( ), precision, recall, and F1 score. To examine whether visibility degradation affects targets differently according to their apparent size, detection performance is further analysed across small, medium, and large UAV categories. The clear-trained baseline is then compared with a fog-aware model trained on a mixture of clear and synthetically degraded images, allowing the robustness gains under fog to be assessed alongside any corresponding reduction in clear-sky performance. Through this controlled evaluation, the study establishes a severity-dependent benchmark for ground-to-air anti-UAV detection under synthetic fog. Rather than treating adverse visibility as a binary clear-versus-fog condition, the proposed framework quantifies how detector reliability changes across a continuous range of fog intensities and identifies the visibility regimes in which performance degradation becomes most pronounced. Related Work sec:related_work Vision-based UAV detection has seen substantial progress, yet a persistent reliability gap remains: most systems are developed and evaluated under clear atmospheric conditions, while real-world deployments must operate under uncontrolled environmental degradation, particularly fog munir_impact_2024, ding_vision-based_2025 . Anti-UAV Tracking Benchmarks Large-scale benchmarks for vision-based object detection of UAVs have been designed and researched substantially. Jiang et al. jiang_anti-uav_2023 introduce Anti-UAV300, the first large-scale benchmark specifically designed for ground-to-air UAV tracking. Comprising of 318 RGB-T video pairs and 558k manually annotated bounding boxes, across diverse scenes and lighting condition, the benchmarks addresses challenges such as scale variation, occlusion, fast motion, and thermal crossover, and proposes a dual-flow semantic consistency (DFSC) training strategy that improves tracker robustness by leveraging cross-sequence semantic information. However, all sequences are recorded under clear atmospheric conditions, even on night time videos, leaving the benchmark's utility for evaluating detector robustness under adverse weather unaddressed. Huang et al. huang_anti-uav410_2024 expanded this research by incorporating more realistic wild scenes with diverse backgrounds such as forests, mountains, and urban areas. Anti-UAV410 is a large-scale thermal infrared benchmark comprised of 410 sequences with over 438k manually annotated bounding boxes. Unlike Anti-UAV300 which features predominantly large-sized targets against simple sky or building backgrounds, Anti-UAV410 emphasizes tiny and small UAV targets, defining tiny targets as bounding boxes with a diagonal length below 10 pixels, along with challenging attributes such as dynamic background clutter and thermal crossover. However, like its predecessor, all sequences are captured under clear atmospheric conditions, providing no evaluation coverage for weather-induced visibility degradation. Xie et al. xie_cst_2025 introduced CST Anti-UAV, another example of a thermal infrared benchmark of 220 sequences with over 240k annotated bounding boxes, incorporating a substantially larger proportion of tiny UAV targets, 4.5 times more than existing datasets, alongside genuinely complex urban scenes with dynamic distractors such as pedestrians and vehicles. The benchmark is also the first to provide complete manual frame-level attribute annotations across all sequences, enabling more precise evaluation of tracker performance under specific challenges. Evaluation results reveal that even the state-of-the-art tracker achieves only state accuracy on CST Anti-UAV, compared to on Anti-UAV410, quantifying the performance gap that complex scenes and tiny targets introduce. However, CST Anti-UAV contains no sequences captured under adverse atmospheric conditions, leaving adverse weather unaddressed. Finally, Feng et al. feng_hazydet_2025 introduced HazyDet, the first large-scale benchmark specifically designed for drone-view object detection in hazy conditions, comprising 383k annotated instances drawn from both real-world foggy captures and physics-based synthetic scenes generated using the Atmospheric Scattering Model. To address haze-induced feature degradation, they propose DeCoDet, a depth-conditioned detector that dynamically modulates feature representations using estimated depth cues and a Progressive Domain Fine-Tuning strategy to bridge the synthetic-to-real domain gap, achieving mAP over the closest competitor on real-world hazy data. While HazyDet represents an important step toward adverse-weather drone detection, it focuses on object detection from a UAV-to-ground perspective and does not address the ground-to-air anti-UAV tracking problem under fog, leaving the specific impact of fog severity on UAV target detection uncharacterised. Recent multimodal anti-UAV studies have also examined reliability from the perspective of sensor uncertainty and fusion rather than atmospheric visibility. Suttorp et al.~ suttorp_uncertainty_2026 evaluate evidential RGB--thermal fusion with conflict-aware belief aggregation, while Golovchits et al.~ golovchits_evidential_2026 study evidential learning, Dempster--Shafer fusion, and uncertainty-driven sensor gating across thermal, RGB, audio, and RF anti-UAV settings. These studies broaden the analysis of anti-UAV reliability under modality disagreement and sensor-specific failure, but they do not provide a severity-controlled evaluation of fog-induced visibility degradation. title: Same Scene, Different Task: Skill Alignment for Compositional Generalization in VLAs
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models often struggle to generalize to skill combinations absent from their fine-tuning demonstrations, even when every constituent skill has been demonstrated. We focus on a vision shortcut as one failure mode: during fine-tuning, visual observations can serve as a proxy for the instruction, so a policy may execute a demonstrated combination associated with similar observations rather than the instructed combination. This motivates training with counterfactual pairs formed by holding a demonstration observation fixed while changing the instruction to specify an undemonstrated combination. These pairs, however, lack corresponding demonstrated action targets. Crucially, the currently required skill has already been demonstrated, but actions from those executions cannot serve as direct targets because the same skill can require different actions across observations. We propose CRAFT, which transfers supervision from demonstrated executions of the required skill to counterfactual pairs using skill representations that can be reused across executions of the same skill. Across three VLA models and two simulation benchmarks, CRAFT improves success on undemonstrated combinations while maintaining high success on demonstrated ones; it also improves compositional generalization on a real robot. Project website: https://taegeunyang.github.io/craft/

Introduction sec:intro Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and natural-language instructions to robot actions~ brohan2023rt2, kim2024openvla, black2024pi0, black2025pi05, bjorck2025gr00t . Adapting these models to a target robot embodiment, sensor configuration, or environment often involves fine-tuning on robot demonstrations collected in that setting~ kim2025oft . Because collecting demonstrations that cover every task of interest is costly, scalable adaptation requires generalization beyond the demonstrated tasks. Prior work has studied how adapted VLAs retain capabilities from pretraining~ yadav2026robust, guo2026priorvla , generalize across objects and visual conditions~ dey2025revla , and remain robust to language variation~ grover2025enhancing . In this work, we study a complementary form of generalization: whether a VLA can recombine skills demonstrated during adaptation into combinations absent from those demonstrations. Many robotic tasks can be viewed as compositions of skills, such as picking an object and then placing it at a target location~ ahn2022can, shi2025hi . We define a skill as an operation paired with the entity specified for that operation, such as picking a red cube or placing an object on a blue plate. For example, demonstrations of ``pick the yellow cube and place it on the yellow plate'' and ``pick the green cube and place it on the green plate'' contain all the constituent skills needed for ``pick the yellow cube and place it on the green plate,'' even though that combination is absent from the demonstrations (Figure~ fig:teaser ). As the number of possible entities grows, collecting demonstrations for every skill combination becomes increasingly costly. This motivates a compositional generalization setting in which all required skills appear in the fine-tuning demonstrations, but their combination does not. Yet even when every constituent skill is demonstrated, we observe that fine-tuned VLAs often perform well on demonstrated combinations but struggle with new combinations (Appendix~ app:compositional-failure ). =-1 To address this gap, we focus on one failure mode: a vision shortcut, in which fine-tuned VLAs use visual observations as a proxy for the instruction~ xu2025bayesvla, lian2026langforce . Under such a shortcut, a policy may execute a demonstrated combination associated with similar observations even when instructed to perform a new one (Figure~ fig:teaser ). To mitigate this shortcut, we form counterfactual pairs during fine-tuning by keeping a demonstration observation fixed while changing the instruction to specify a combination absent from the demonstrations. The resulting pair, however, has no corresponding demonstrated action target. Crucially, the skill currently required under the changed instruction has already been demonstrated. Nonetheless, actions from those demonstrations cannot generally serve as direct targets for the counterfactual pair, because the same skill can require different actions across observations. Thus, the key challenge is to transfer supervision from demonstrated executions of the required skill to the counterfactual pair while accounting for how the required action varies across observations. We propose CRAFT (Counterfactual Skill-Representation Alignment for Fine-Tuning), which addresses this challenge by learning skill representations that can be reused across executions of the same skill while allowing action prediction to vary with the observation. CRAFT introduces a skill representation that reflects the currently required skill and a state representation derived from the visual observation; together, they condition action prediction. For each counterfactual pair, CRAFT selects a demonstrated execution of the required skill. It combines the pair's skill representation with that execution's state representation and supervises the prediction with that execution's action target. This supervision trains the counterfactual pair's skill representation to reflect the required skill in action prediction. Thus, CRAFT transfers supervision from demonstrated executions of the required skill to the counterfactual pair without requiring a demonstrated action target for that pair. We evaluate CRAFT across -family~ black2024pi0, black2025pi05 and GR00T~ bjorck2025gr00t VLA models on two compositional benchmarks in simulation, with additional evaluation of on a real robot. CRAFT substantially improves success on undemonstrated skill combinations while maintaining high performance on demonstrated combinations. Our contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=1.2em, topsep=0pt, itemsep=2pt, parsep=0.5pt] We propose CRAFT, a counterfactual supervision approach that uses existing demonstrations of constituent skills to train VLAs to execute skill combinations absent from the original demonstrations, without collecting demonstrations for those combinations. We introduce two compositional benchmarks for two- and three-skill tasks, with demonstration datasets that cover every constituent skill but only a subset of skill combinations; we will release the datasets and simulation environments. Across -family and GR00T VLA models, CRAFT improves success on skill combinations absent from the original demonstrations while maintaining high success on demonstrated combinations; we additionally validate CRAFT with on a real robot. Related Work sec:related Compositional Generalization in VLAs sec:related-vla Compositional generalization concerns generalizing to new combinations of components encountered during training~ lake2018generalization and has been studied in computer vision~ uselis2025does and large language models~ sakai2025revisiting . In robot learning, prior work has studied generalization to new combinations of environmental factors, such as object type and table height~ gao2024efficient , as well as recombining demonstrated behaviors to execute new tasks~ mandlekar2020learning . More closely related to our setting, recent work has shown that VLAs can struggle to generalize to new combinations of previously learned skills~ xieskillnet . One line of work composes learned behaviors at deployment, either by interpolating task-specific text representations from different tasks~ li2025vlas or by learning reusable skills that can be recombined for new task combinations~ zhai2026skillvla . Another approach expands the training data by generating execution trajectories for new skill combinations and retaining successful ones as synthetic demonstrations~ peng2026unleashing . We instead exploit constituent-skill coverage in existing demonstrations to provide supervision during fine-tuning, without generating execution trajectories for new combinations. Shortcut Learning and Counterfactual Supervision sec:shortcut-counterfactual =-1 Shortcut learning occurs when models exploit predictive correlations in the training data that allow accurate predictions with limited reliance on task-relevant information~ geirhos2020shortcut, si2022language, elisha2026concept . In robot demonstrations, the task being executed can often be inferred from the visual observation, allowing a fine-tuned policy to fit demonstrated actions with limited reliance on the instruction~ fang2026vision, xu2025bayesvla, lian2026langforce . This can produce a vision shortcut, in which the policy uses the visual observation as a proxy for the instruction when predicting actions~ xing2025shortcut . In our compositional setting, such a shortcut can cause the policy to execute a demonstrated combination associated with similar observations rather than the new combination specified by the instruction. =-1 Counterfactual training has been used to reduce shortcut reliance by varying a task-relevant factor while holding other inputs fixed and supervising models on the resulting examples~ kaushik2020learning, wan2025eliminating . The vision shortcut therefore motivates counterfactual pairs that keep the observation fixed while changing the instruction. Such a pair, however, may lack a corresponding demonstrated action target. Prior work provides action supervision for such changed instructions by synthesizing counterfactual actions using policies trained on simpler instructions~ glossop2025cast or by constructing action sequences that connect trajectories for the original and changed instructions~ chen2026resteer . In our compositional setting, the changed instruction specifies an undemonstrated combination of demonstrated skills, so the skill currently required under that instruction has already been demonstrated. Rather than constructing an action target for the counterfactual pair, we use demonstrated executions of the required skill to train the policy so that its action prediction under the changed instruction reflects that skill. title: Token-World: World Modeling in Vision-Language Model Token Space for Robot Manipulation
comment: Submitted to IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA) 2027
summary: A common approach to world-model simulation for vision-language-action (VLA) systems is to predict future RGB observations and then re-encode them into policy inputs, introducing an indirect interface between simulation and downstream policy execution. We instead investigate whether world dynamics can be modeled in a compact, policy-oriented state derived from VLM visual tokens. A key challenge is that raw VLM visual tokens are high-dimensional, making efficient and accurate autoregressive dynamics modeling challenging. To address this, we introduce Token-World, an action-conditioned world model that compresses VLM features into a compact token state, learns future dynamics in this reduced space, and maps predicted states back to the original policy-facing representation for downstream use. Across manipulation benchmarks, Token-World improves open-loop feature fidelity and policy-action consistency over recent world-model simulators, with slower degradation over long rollout horizons. In closed-loop evaluation, its simulated policy performance correlates more strongly with reference policy performance than Ctrl-World ($r=0.794$ vs.\ $0.583$), while requiring lower simulation latency. Ablations further show that compact-representation design and dimensionality substantially affect future-state prediction. Code will be available at https://chuyaofu.github.io/Token-World/.
full_text: Token-World simulates directly in compact VLM visual-token space. Unlike RGB-based world models that generate future images and re-encode them into policy inputs, Token-World models action-conditioned dynamics directly in compact VLM tokens. This design avoids intermediate RGB generation, reduces simulator step time to \,s, and yields more reliable closed-loop policy evaluation ( vs.\ for Ctrl-World). fig:teaser A common approach to world-model simulation for vision-language-action (VLA) systems is to predict future RGB observations and then re-encode them into policy inputs, introducing an indirect interface between simulation and downstream policy execution. INTRODUCTION World models ha2018world offer a promising route toward scalable embodied learning by serving as learned simulators of action-conditioned environment dynamics finn2017deep,hafner2019dream,hafner2019learning,wu2023daydreamer . Instead of executing every behavior in the physical world, an agent can roll out future observations inside the model, which is especially valuable in robotics where real-world interaction is costly and slow wu2023daydreamer . Recent work has therefore explored world models as simulators from several perspectives: using predicted futures to evaluate policies quevedo2025worldgym, wang2026echoarena , synthesizing additional interaction data for policy learning guo2025ctrl,chi2025wow , and performing reinforcement learning through imagined rollouts zhu2025wmpo,jiang2025world4rl,jiang2026wovr . As world models are increasingly used as learned simulators, they are often paired with VLA policies that map visual observations and language instructions to actions team2024octo,kim2024openvla,pi0,pi05 . However, existing pipelines often use an indirect simulation interface, where future RGB observations are first predicted by the world model, then re-encoded into VLA visual tokens before being consumed by the VLA policy quevedo2025worldgym,guo2025ctrl,zhu2025wmpo,jiang2025world4rl,jiang2026wovr . As world models move toward scalable simulators for VLA agents, this indirect interface becomes a critical bottleneck: the simulator predicts human-viewable pixels, whereas the downstream policy ultimately consumes policy-facing visual tokens.This mismatch is not merely computational: RGB reconstruction encourages the simulator to allocate capacity to visual details that may be irrelevant to the policy, while token-space rollout directly targets the representation used for downstream action generation. A representation-aligned alternative is to simulate the future directly in the VLM visual-token space consumed by the policy. Such an interface avoids repeatedly reconstructing RGB observations and re-encoding them into policy inputs during imagined rollouts. However, policy-facing VLM tokens are high-dimensional representations optimized primarily for perception and action rather than generative dynamics modeling~ kim2024openvla,pi0,pi05 . Directly predicting their temporal evolution therefore imposes both a substantial modeling burden and considerable computational cost. In this work, we introduce Token-World, an autoregressive action-conditioned world-model simulator that rolls out in compact policy-aligned VLM token space. Its dynamics model is a flow-matching DiT, without relying on pretrained video-generation models. To make high-dimensional policy-facing VLM features tractable for dynamics learning, Token-World compresses the feature dimension into a compact semantic token state. Future states are predicted in this compact space and mapped back to the original VLM visual-token space only when consumed by the downstream policy, avoiding intermediate RGB generation throughout the rollout. Across manipulation benchmarks, Token-World improves open-loop feature fidelity and policy-action consistency over recent world-model simulators, while degrading more slowly over long rollout horizons. In closed-loop evaluation, its simulated success rates track reference policy performance more closely than Ctrl-World ( vs.\ ), while providing higher simulation efficiency. Controlled ablations further show that both the design and dimensionality of the compact VLM representation substantially affect future-state prediction. In summary, our contributions are threefold: We study direct VLM visual-token simulation as an alternative to RGB-based world-model pipelines, enabling the simulator to operate on the representation interface consumed by downstream VLA policies. We present Token-World, an autoregressive action-conditioned world-model simulator that uses a flow-matching DiT to model dynamics in a compact VLM visual-token space, without relying on pretrained video-generation models. We validate Token-World through open-loop prediction, closed-loop policy evaluation, and representation ablations, showing improved long-horizon feature and policy-action fidelity, more reliable policy success estimation, lower simulation cost, and the importance of compact-representation design for dynamics prediction. Related Work World Models as Learned Simulators World models learn action-conditioned dynamics to support planning and policy learning through imagined rollouts ha2018world,hafner2019dream,hafner2019learning,wu2023daydreamer . Recent robotic world models have been used for policy evaluation li2025worldeval,quevedo2025worldgym , synthetic interaction generation guo2025ctrl,jang2025dreamgen , and policy optimization zhu2025wmpo . Recent VLA-oriented methods move prediction closer to policy representations: DIAL predicts futures in VLM feature space chen2026dial , LaWAM uses latent visual subgoals chen2026lawam , and LaST reasons through token-efficient latent spatio-temporal states liu2026last . Related generative models have also studied representation design for diffusion. Representation Autoencoders use pretrained semantic features as diffusion latents zheng2026diffusion , while PS-VAE maps high-dimensional representation features into a compact, KL-regularized latent space for image generation and editing zhang2025both . title: When Reasoning Helps Action: Monitoring and Steering Chain-of-Thought in Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Reasoning-enabled VLA policies expose chain-of-thought (CoT) traces that appear to explain and guide their actions, creating a potential interface for runtime safety through reasoning monitoring and correction. In this work, we define and operationalize two evaluation axes for assessing when this interface can improve embodied behavior: correctability, which measures whether unreliable reasoning can be detected and improved during generation, and actionability, which measures whether reasoning corrections produce behaviorally meaningful changes in the intended direction. To enable correctability, we introduce Token-level Reward for Utility-Steered Chain-of-Thought (TRUST), an offline-trained value model that predicts eventual reasoning correctness from partial prefixes and uses these estimates to monitor and selectively steer reasoning generation in frozen VLA policies. On the Alpamayo 1.5 driving VLA, TRUST monitors correctness with 88.9% accuracy and improves reasoning correctness from 75.9% to 90.0%. On a baseline-defined challenging subset in AlpaSim, TRUST reduces collision rate by 30.4% and maximum trajectory error by 11.5% relative to the unsteered policy, outperforming a compute-matched Best-of-4 baseline. On the DeepThinkVLA manipulation VLA, TRUST improves the correctness of grasp-state claims from 69.3% to 90.2% and action-choice claims from 68.8% to 85.9%, yet closed-loop task performance on LIBERO-Plus remains largely unchanged. Empirical analysis reveals intent-consistent behavioral effects in Alpamayo 1.5 but limited effects in DeepThinkVLA, helping interpret these different task-level outcomes. Together, our results show that gains in reasoning correctness do not automatically imply gains in embodied performance, motivating evaluation of correctability and actionability when using CoT as a runtime safety interface.

Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models~ brohan2023rt have become a dominant paradigm for robot policies, mapping visual observations and natural-language instructions directly to action sequences. Recent reasoning-enabled VLA models further incorporate the chain-of-thought (CoT) capabilities of multimodal large language models (LLMs)~ yin2024survey , generating textual scene interpretations, intentions, and high-level plans before predicting actions. Such explicit reasoning has been shown to improve long-horizon manipulation~ zhao2025cot and robustness in driving~ wang2025alpamayo . It also offers an appealing interface for runtime safety: if the model's reasoning becomes inconsistent with the observation or task, we may be able to detect and correct that reasoning before unsafe actions are executed. In this work, we define and operationalize two evaluation axes for assessing when CoT can serve as a runtime safety interface for embodied policies. Correctability assesses whether unreliable reasoning can be detected and steered during generation. Actionability assesses whether corrections to action-relevant reasoning produce meaningful behavioral changes in the intended direction. These axes distinguish the ability to improve reasoning from the policy's ability to act on those improvements. This distinction is critical because a policy's reasoning may become accurate while its actions remain insensitive to the corrected trace. Fig.~ fig:faithfulness illustrates the actionability of correcting the reasoning. In the Alpamayo~1.5 wang2025alpamayo driving example, the policy focuses on a green straight-through signal while approaching a yellow left-turn arrow. Substituting reasoning that identifies the arrow and calls for stopping changes the predicted trajectory, causing the vehicle to decelerate toward a stop and reducing the minimum average displacement error (ADE) from 8.83~m to 2.02~m over six samples. Here, the reasoning correction is actionable: it produces the intended behavioral effect. In the DeepThinkVLA yin2025deepthinkvla manipulation example, the policy incorrectly claims that an object has been grasped. Correcting this claim, however, produces little change in the generated action chunk. Here, the reasoning can be corrected, but the correction is not actionable in the tested setting. These examples suggest that reasoning corrections may not always translate into corresponding changes in action, motivating a systematic investigation of their behavioral consequences in VLA policies. To enable correctability during generation, we introduce Token-level Reward for Utility-Steered Chain-of-Thought ( ), an offline-trained value model that predicts, from the visual observation and a partial reasoning prefix, whether the completed reasoning trace will be correct. As a runtime monitor, flags prefixes predicted to lead to incorrect reasoning. As an inference-time steering mechanism, applies gated value-augmented sampling (VAS)~ han2024value to flagged prefixes, reweighting the policy’s next-token distribution toward higher-valued continuations. The value model uses only observations and reasoning tokens, requires no access to the VLA policy's weights or hidden states, and leaves the policy frozen during monitoring and steering. We evaluate on Alpamayo~1.5 for driving and DeepThinkVLA for manipulation. In both domains, improves reasoning correctness, demonstrating correctability. In AlpaSim~ alpasim_2025 , this reasoning improvement translates into better trajectory and safety metrics on a baseline-defined challenging subset, outperforming a compute-matched Best-of-4 baseline. On LIBERO-Plus~ fei2025libero , however, DeepThinkVLA’s reasoning improves while task performance remains largely unchanged. Through reasoning-substitution and intent-level analyses, we show that these analyses help interpret the contrasting task-level outcomes: Alpamayo~1.5 exhibits intent-consistent behavioral changes under corrected reasoning, whereas DeepThinkVLA is less responsive to the tested reasoning corrections. To summarize, our main contributions are: (1) we define and operationalize two evaluation axes for using CoT as a runtime safety interface in embodied policies; (2) we introduce , an offline-trained value model that predicts eventual reasoning correctness from partial prefixes and enables token-level monitoring and selective inference-time steering in frozen VLA policies; and (3) we provide closed-loop evaluations and reasoning-substitution analyses showing that improved reasoning correctness can improve behavior when corrections are actionable, but may leave task performance unchanged when the policy is weakly responsive to corrected reasoning. Related Work CoT Reasoning in VLA Models. CoT reasoning has been extended from LLMs to VLA models in both manipulation~ zhao2025cot and autonomous driving~ wang2025alpamayo . Prior work develops these reasoning capabilities through supervised fine-tuning and RL post-training. complements this with runtime monitoring and selective steering in frozen VLA policies. Reasoning-Action Faithfulness. Recent work examines whether VLA reasoning causally influences actions~ mayumu2026vla,nguyen2026vladrivebench . VLADriveBench~ nguyen2026vladrivebench uses controlled CoT interventions to measure this influence in autonomous driving. ``Do What You Say''~ wu2025you selects candidate actions that follow a fixed textual plan. ``Altered Thoughts, Altered Actions'' trinh2026altered corrupts the reasoning trace of DeepThinkVLA adversarially, evaluated on LIBERO liu2023libero and measures the effect on task success, finding that the action decoder is sensitive to object references but insensitive to sequential structure, spatial terms, and token-level coherence. We connect faithfulness to runtime reasoning correction: steers the VLA reasoning generation, and our analyses evaluate whether these corrections lead to behavioral effects in actions. Runtime Failure Monitoring in Embodied Systems. Runtime monitors often detect failures from perception inputs or from the executed actions, using learned risk models~ chakraborty2025system , latent-space failure prediction~ cheng2025lsre , anomaly detection~ balakrishnan2021percemon , LLM-based monitoring~ semanticanomaly , embedding-based detection with VLM reasoning~ sinha2024real , and context-aware VLM safety assessment~ gupta2025perception . monitors the reasoning stage, using a scalar value head to predict eventual reasoning correctness from observations and partial prefixes before actions are generated. LLM Alignment. Preference-based alignment modifies model weights through RL~ ouyang2022training or direct optimization~ rafailov2023direct . Decoding-time methods use learned discriminators or value functions to predict sequence-level outcomes and guide token generation~ mudgal2023controlled, han2024value , including preemptive LLM safety monitoring and steering~ karnik2025preemptive . extends this inference-time paradigm to the visually grounded VLA reasoning. title: TacDyn-WAM: Learning Implicit Tactile Dynamics in a Heterogeneous Visuo-Tactile World Action Model
summary: World action models improve robotic manipulation by conditioning actions on predicted futures, yet existing tactile variants largely inherit video-generation pipelines that reconstruct future tactile observations through iterative denoising. Such prediction can become unreliable under deployment drift: small changes in contact position or force may substantially alter tactile pixels even when the underlying contact evolution remains predictable. We introduce TacDyn-WAM, a heterogeneous visuo-tactile world action model that predicts implicit tactile dynamics rather than reconstructing future tactile observations. It learns TacRep, a dynamics-aware tactile target space trained through masked spatio-temporal prediction on tactile clips and regularized by relational structure distillation. A visual expert and an Implicit Tactile Dynamics Expert predict future visual and tactile representations in separate target spaces while interacting through joint attention; the tactile expert predicts future representations and their changes at multiple horizons in a single forward pass, and a read-only tactile memory supplies the current tactile state. On UniVTAC, TacDyn-WAM achieves an average success rate of 81.5% using only the provided demonstrations, reaching state-of-the-art-level performance and remaining competitive with models pretrained on large-scale visuo-tactile trajectories. Ablations confirm the benefits of both tactile pathways and TacRep over pixel-reconstruction and static alternatives. On five real-robot tasks, TacDyn-WAM reaches 71.0% average success, and modest-scale pretraining raises it to 85.0%, further validating our method.
