Introduction sec:intro World models forecast how observations evolve, while world action models use this foresight for policy learning, allowing actions to depend on predicted futures rather than current observations alone~ cai2026internvla,li2026causal,yuan2026fast,ye2026gigaworld . Yet in existing world action models, this foresight comes primarily from vision. In contact-rich or precision manipulation tasks, such as insertion and alignment under occlusion, cameras cannot fully resolve contact states, local geometry, or interaction forces. Early efforts incorporated tactile sensing into VLA models, giving rise to vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) models that encode tactile observations alongside vision and language~ huang2025tactilevla,zhang2025vtla,bi2025vlatouch,cheng2025omnivtla . By understanding the current tactile state, they improve contact-rich manipulation over vision-only policies. However, they do not predict how this state will evolve, leaving policies reactive to tactile feedback. Recent tactile world action models close this gap by predicting future tactile observations as part of the world model~ neoteai2026n0twam,lou2026dreamtac,yuan2026vtam,wu2026tactilewam . These models have achieved promising results, with some further benefiting from large-scale visuo-tactile pretraining. Despite this progress, a core design question remains: what should tactile world models predict? Most existing methods simply reuse video-generation pipelines: the same VAE encodes camera and tactile frames, while video backbones iteratively denoise future tactile latents. This slows inference and ties prediction to pixel reconstruction, which is poorly suited to tactile observations. Expert demonstrations cover only tactile images near correct contacts, whereas closed-loop errors may cause policies to drift from them. This drift may leave camera views nearly unchanged, yet even slight changes in contact position or force can substantially alter tactile images, pushing them farther from the demonstration distribution. Despite these pixel-level changes, contact evolution---whether an imprint deepens, slides, or rotates---often remains predictable. We therefore argue for implicit tactile dynamics modeling: predicting contact evolution in a dynamics-aware representation space rather than reconstructing future tactile observations. Latent prediction is a step toward this goal, but not every latent space is equally suited to forecasting tactile evolution. -VTLA~ neoteai2026n0vtla predicts the net tactile change at a single horizon in the feature space of a frozen DINOv2~ oquab2023dinov2 . However, DINOv2 is trained on static natural images and is not explicitly optimized to capture frame-to-frame tactile evolution; recent tactile representation learning also shows the limitations of single-frame encoders in modeling such dynamics~ feng2026anytouch . In contrast, V-JEPA~2.1~ mur2026v learns representations by predicting masked spatio-temporal features in videos, encouraging its encoder to capture predictable motion rather than exact pixel details. Building on this objective, we learn a target space from tactile video clips that captures temporal change, while preserving spatial structure to support robust prediction under tactile distribution shifts. Moreover, because a single net change can hide intermediate contact events when a squeeze or slip returns to a similar final state, we predict both future representations and their changes from the present at multiple horizons. This captures contact evolution rather than only its endpoint. In this paper, we present TacDyn-WAM, a heterogeneous visuo-tactile world action model whose two world-model experts use separate parameters and target spaces. The visual expert predicts future visual latents, while the Implicit Tactile Dynamics Expert (ITDE) predicts tactile evolution in the TacRep space. Joint attention couples their predictions at every layer and allows the Action Expert to use both. The ITDE requires only a single forward pass without iterative denoising. A separate Tactile Understanding Memory provides direct access to the current tactile state, while staged training progressively integrates the tactile modules with the pretrained experts. On UniVTAC~ chen2026univtac , TacDyn-WAM achieves state-of-the-art-level performance using only the provided demonstrations. It is competitive with the two strongest models on this benchmark, -VTLA and -TWAM, both of which rely on large-scale visuo-tactile pretraining. Notably, -TWAM follows the video-generation recipe and has roughly twice the parameters of TacDyn-WAM. Ablations show the benefits of both tactile pathways and TacRep's advantage over pixel-reconstruction and static alternatives. On five real-robot tasks, TacDyn-WAM trained on per-task demonstrations alone reaches 71.0 average success, 16 points above the tactile policy FTP-1, and modest-scale pretraining on about 6,000 real visuo-tactile trajectories raises it to 85.0 . In summary, this work makes the following contributions: We propose TacDyn-WAM, a heterogeneous visuo-tactile world action model that jointly predicts future visual latents and tactile evolution in distinct target spaces, while a read-only Tactile Understanding Memory provides the current tactile state. We introduce TacRep, a dynamics-aware representation space for implicit tactile dynamics prediction, enabling one-pass multi-horizon prediction without pixel reconstruction or iterative denoising. TacDyn-WAM achieves state-of-the-art-level performance on UniVTAC using only the provided demonstrations, and ablations validate the design. On a real robot, it outperforms vision-only and tactile baselines and benefits further from modest-scale tactile pretraining. Method sec:method Problem Setup and Overview sec:overview Base Model. We build on the 3B checkpoint of InternVLA-A1~ cai2026internvla , a mixture-of-transformers world action model with three experts coupled through block-wise causal joint attention. The Understanding Expert, a Qwen3-VL-2B vision-language model~ bai2025qwen3 , encodes the current RGB observations and language instruction into a prefix block . The Visual Generation Expert receives a visual history block , encoded by a frozen Cosmos tokenizer~ agarwal2025cosmos , and predicts the future visual latent . The Action Expert receives the robot state and a noisy action block , then denoises an action chunk of length through flow matching~ lipman2022flow . The ITDE operates on a tactile block encoded by the frozen TacRep Encoder and predicts future tactile representations and their changes at multiple horizons. The Action Expert can therefore combine predicted visual and tactile futures with the current tactile state. TacRep: A Dynamics-Aware Tactile Representation Space sec:tacrep Why the Target Space Matters. As argued in Section~ sec:intro , deployment drift can expose a policy to tactile images outside the demonstration distribution. Their pixels may change substantially even when the underlying physical trend remains broadly consistent. Reconstructing future pixels or VAE latents ties predictions to these unstable pixel patterns and may therefore produce unreliable forecasts under such shifts. We instead let the ITDE predict tactile dynamics in a representation space designed to capture contact evolution while tolerating pixel-level deviations. title: DITTO-X: Forward and Reverse Teleoperation for Dexterous Manipulation and Human Intervention
summary: Teleoperated demonstrations are a primary source of data for robot manipulation, and teleoperated interventions are a primary mechanism for correcting policies at deployment. Yet most teleoperation systems close the loop through vision alone and are built around parallel-jaw grippers, limiting both what the robot can execute and what the operator can express through it. This is most damaging in shared autonomy, where the operator sees the scene only through occluded cameras and must take over a dexterous hand mid-task, often with an object already grasped. We present DITTO-X, a hand-agnostic dexterous teleoperation interface that renders joint-level force and fingertip contact events from sensing already on the robot hand, and drives three commercial dexterous hands (Sharpa, Wuji, and Inspire) without per-hand redesign. Because the exoskeleton is actuated, DITTO-X also supports reverse teleoperation, in which the robot back-drives the operator's fingers into its own configuration before control is transferred, so the human enters the loop already matched to the state they inherit. Our results show that DITTO-X improves demonstration quality and throughput over a commercial hand-tracking glove, both in regular data collection and in human intervention during policy deployment for contact-rich manipulation tasks. More information can be found from our website: https://tml.stanford.edu/ditto-x/.

Introduction sec:intro Teleoperation plays a fundamental role in modern robotics, letting humans directly supervise, guide, and demonstrate complex manipulation tasks~ intelligence2025pi, bjorck2025gr00t . In robot learning, teleoperated demonstrations remain a critical complement to scripted motion, human video, and handheld collection devices~ chi2024universal, fang2025dexop , capturing the precise, contact-rich interactions that passive or ungrounded approaches struggle to reproduce. At deployment time, shared autonomy and human-in-the-loop frameworks rely on teleoperation to let operators intervene at uncertain or safety-critical moments~ he2025uncertainty, hoque2021thriftydagger, agia2024unpacking , and the interventions they produce can be used to improve the policy. Despite their widespread use, most teleoperation systems are poorly matched to dexterous manipulation. They are built around parallel-jaw grippers, which bound the natural movement an operator can demonstrate in the first place, and they close the loop through vision alone. Humans do not manipulate this way; we regulate contact forces, detect incipient slip, and reshape a grasp from cues we feel rather than see. Without those cues, the operator is blind to contact, and demonstrations are rendered slow and conservative. The limitation is therefore not only what the robot can execute, but also what the human can express through it. This limitation becomes a failure mode in shared autonomy. When collecting demonstrations from scratch, the operator can both position themselves to see the scene and restart a failed attempt at little cost. Intervening on a running policy affords neither. Perception is restricted to onboard cameras, under which self-occlusion by the arm and hand is often unavoidable, especially at critical contact moments. The operator also inherits the robot's state mid-task, so the kinematic mismatch between the human hand and the robot hand must be resolved at that exact moment. During tool use or in-hand manipulation, a non-smooth transition at takeover is enough to drop or break the object, resulting in unrecoverable failures. We present , a dexterous interface for transparent teleoperation that works across different robotic hands for both regular data collection and human intervention. Improving the design of DITTO~ ditto , which requires strict 1-to-1 kinematics between leader and follower and instruments only two fingers, is a hand-agnostic framework and currently drives three commercial, five-finger dexterous hands (Sharpa Wave, Wuji 2, and Inspire RH56DFX) without per-hand redesign. It closes the feedback loop at two levels: sustained joint-level force via motors on the exoskeleton and discrete fingertip contact events via haptics from sensing already available on the robot hand. This allows the operator to feel both when contact is made and how hard the robotic hand is squeezing, restoring cues that vision-only interfaces lack. Our actuated exoskeleton can also be used to improve human intervention through a novel operating mode we call ``reverse teleoperation'': while an operator is supervising an autonomous policy deployment, the exoskeleton can actively drive the operator's fingers to match the robot's current configuration. This allows for a seamless transition of control once the operator takes over and gives them a kinesthetic sense of the policy actions. Our user study and policy learning results show that improves both the throughput and the quality of data collected for contact-rich policy training. With reverse teleoperation, operators intervene on a running policy fluently, without dropping objects already in hand, yielding better data for subsequent policy improvement. We summarize our contributions as follows: We present a dexterous teleoperation framework, equipped with force and haptic feedback, with support for three commercial robotic hands, spanning 6 to 22 actuated DoF, without hand-specific redesign. We introduce reverse teleoperation, in which the actuated exoskeleton back-drives the operator's hand to match the robot's configuration, so that intervention on a running policy begins from a matched state rather than a discontinuous handoff. We open-source the full system, including hardware design, forward and reverse teleoperation, and policy training and fine-tuning details. We also release all 1.8k episodes of contact-rich manipulation data from three embodiments, spanning teleoperated demonstrations, human interventions, and autonomous policy rollouts. Related Work sec:related Teleoperation for dexterous hands. Dexterous teleoperation has largely been studied as a problem of closing the kinematic gap between the operator's hand and the robot's: vision-based hand tracking~ qin2023anyteleop , non-wearable leader-follower designs~ tilde , and learned retargeting priors~ dexterity_gen each attack it differently, but none renders contact back to the operator, who is left to infer it from vision alone. Motorized exoskeletons do render force, yet packaging actuators alongside the fingers forces a choice about what to render. DOGlove~ doglove reduces feedback to a single axis per finger, while GEX~ gex and N2D~ huang2026n2d map forces in task space; neither tells the operator which joint is loaded. DITTO~ ditto recovers joint-level feedback by enforcing a one-to-one correspondence between leader and follower joints, at the price of being tied to a single two-fingered manipulator. In this work, we remove that restriction and extend the design to five-fingered hands. Shared autonomy, human intervention and DAgger. A large body of work improves manipulation policies with human feedback, including interventions~ mandlekar2020human, spencer2020learning , preferences~ lee2021pebble , rankings~ pmlr-v97-brown19a , and scalar rewards~ macglashan2017interactive . Interactive imitation learning, in which the agent queries an expert during execution and aggregates the resulting corrections~ ross2011reduction, kelly2019hg , underpins systems that collect data where the policy actually fails~ liu2022robot, luo2024hilserl . Because continuous supervision is costly, much of this literature concerns when to request help~ hoque2023fleet, hoque2021thriftydagger, agia2024unpacking, lee2024diff, zhao2025conformalized , and a parallel line supplies it through language rather than teleoperation~ cui2023lilac, shi2024yay . Most of these works study when a human should intervene. In this work, we look into the problem of how to intervene on a policy. How authority passes between an autonomous controller and a human has also been studied. Blended and traded control arbitrate continuously, predicting the operator's goal and blending toward it~ dragan2013policy, javdani2015shared or applying guidance forces that shift authority without a discrete switch~ abbink2012haptic ; when a switch is unavoidable, the resulting transient is well documented in automated driving~ eriksson2017takeover . Our setting differs in what must be made continuous. A dexterous hand transferred mid-task is usually already holding an object, so a pose mismatch at the instant of transfer releases or displaces it rather than merely perturbing a trajectory. Reverse teleoperation removes this discontinuity in the operator's state rather than the controller's, conforming the human to the robot before authority passes. Method sec:method supports two modes of operation: forward teleoperation (human-to-robot) and a novel reverse teleoperation (robot-to-human). In the forward direction, used for data collection, it transmits the operator's hand motion to a dexterous robot hand while rendering the contact the robot experiences back to the operator via force and haptic feedback. In the reverse direction, which is intended for intervention during policy deployment, it drives the operator's fingers to match the robot's configuration, which enables a fluent transition when the operator takes over. We first describe how supports high-quality forward teleoperation across different robot hands, augmented by force and haptic feedback (Sections~ sec:forward and~ sec:feedback ). We then describe how we leverage the same actuation to support fluent takeover via reverse teleoperation (Section~ sec:reverse ). Forward Teleoperation Across Dexterous Hands sec:forward is designed to support bilateral teleoperation for a diverse set of robotic hands, with vastly different kinematic designs and sensing capabilities. We select DITTO as a starting point due to its kinematic design of thumb and index fingers, which aligns with the user's anatomical joint axes, allowing for joint-level position control and force feedback. However, DITTO relies on a kinematically equivalent leader-follower pair, which limits its applications to other manipulators and five-finger hands. To address these problems, we extend its design by adding a third motorized finger module interfacing with the user's middle finger, which mirrors the index design to the ulnar side of the hand, aligning actuators with the middle finger's joint axes (Fig. fig:ditto_hardware_updates .A Left). To support five-finger hand control, we couple the motion of the ring and pinky fingers on the target hand with the middle finger, positing that three independent fingers suffice for a variety of dexterous primitives, while the coupled ring and pinky fingers allow for power grasps (Fig.~ fig:ditto_hardware_updates ). We also remove one joint from the original thumb design (3rd joint from the base, i.e. proximal flexion joint) to reduce weight (Fig. fig:ditto_hardware_updates .A right); we find this removal does not degrade our ability to capture thumb motion. Additionally, we expand the modalities of contact feedback by embedding Linear Resonant Actuators (LRAs) (Fig.~ fig:ditto_hardware_updates B) underneath the operator's fingertips for vibro-tactile feedback. We use on three different robotic hands: Sharpa, Wuji2, and Inspire with vastly different kinematic designs and sensing capabilities (Table tab:hand_comparison_expanded ). To support this heterogeneity, we select both the position mapping and the force and haptic feedback for each hand according to its kinematics and available sensing. title: ECoMEM: Explicit Concept Memory for Memory-Dependent Robot Control
summary: A robot may lose sight of an object it must later retrieve, need to recall what a person demonstrated earlier, or track which steps of a task it has already completed. Current vision-language-action (VLA) policies often fail once the information needed for action disappears from the current observation, making memory critical for long-horizon robot behavior. Existing approaches typically provide longer histories or learn implicit memory from observation-action trajectories. But action supervision tells a policy how to act, not what to remember: it does not specify which past facts should persist or how they should change as new evidence arrives. We therefore separate maintaining an evidence-grounded account of the past from learning how to act on it. This insight motivates Explicit Concept Memory (ECoMEM), which represents task-relevant history with a reusable library of grounded concepts. An evidence-based Writer selects and updates these records, while a learned Reader turns them into memory tokens that directly condition the VLA. Across 16 RoboMME tasks, ECoMEM leads the evaluated robot policies on 15 tasks. On two new real-robot tasks, the same memory library either transfers directly or requires only one new concept, achieving 86.1% success versus 8.6% for a no-memory VLA. These results show that explicit concepts provide a reusable and extensible memory interface for robot control. Project website: https://ecomem.github.io/

Introduction sec:intro A robot that acts over extended periods cannot treat every observation as a fresh start. It may need to remember where an object was last seen after it becomes occluded, which object a person interacted with earlier, what parts of a task have already been completed, or the order in which previous events occurred. In each case, the information needed for the next action is no longer available in the current observation. Yet the relevant past is often much smaller than the full interaction history: what matters is a compact set of task-relevant facts about entities, states, events, and progress. Vision--language--action (VLA) policies increasingly incorporate history through extended context, recurrent representations, learned memory banks, and test-time adaptation~ ptp,hamlet,memoryvla,ttt . These mechanisms can preserve rich perceptual history, but they leave an important question implicit: what from that history should become memory? Action supervision specifies what the robot should do, but not which past facts should be retained, when a belief should be revised, or when two observations correspond to the same event. When memory is learned only through the control objective, the policy may instead rely on shortcuts in current observations, previous actions, or trajectory-specific correlations~ causalconfusion,copycat, proprioshortcut . Successful action prediction therefore does not by itself establish that the task-relevant history has been represented reliably. Making memory explicit helps, but does not remove the problem of memory construction. Keyframe memories preserve visual evidence ~ eventvla,fang2025sam2act , leaving the policy to recover the relevant facts from stored images. VLM-based approaches summarize histories~ sridhar2026memer,remembr , but place entity tracking, state estimation, and temporal interpretation inside long-video reasoning, where spatial and temporal errors remain challenging ~ beyondsemantics,egoillusion . Textual world states ~ statler,liu2023reflect and scene graphs ~ gu2024conceptgraphs,sayplan,dynamem provide more structured representations, but a robotic memory must additionally decide how observations become persistent facts: what should survive occlusion, what should be revised, what constitutes a completed event, and how repeated evidence should be reconciled. Our key idea is to separate maintaining an evidence-grounded account of the past from learning how to act on it. Rather than asking the policy to infer memory implicitly from history, we represent task-relevant history as explicit facts about entities, states, completed events, progress, and temporal order. These facts are updated only when supported by visual and robot-state evidence, while the policy learns how they should influence action. This separation also keeps task requirements distinct from observations: the instruction specifies what should be achieved, while memory records what has actually happened. We instantiate this principle in Explicit Concept Memory ( ), an explicit memory channel for VLA policies (Figure~ fig:org ). First, a shared concept library provides reusable memory primitives spanning entity and spatial grounding, state and relations, events and progress, and temporal and procedural structure. Second, an evidence-based Writer selects the concepts required by the instruction, grounds them to task entities, and maintains their records over time, while a learned Reader maps the resulting structured memory into latent tokens. Third, these memory tokens directly condition the VLA alongside visual and language inputs. Recognition and memory writing remain fixed during policy training, so evidence determines what is remembered, while action supervision learns how that memory should be used. Across the 16 memory-dependent tasks of RoboMME~ dai2026robomme , achieves the highest average success among the evaluated robot policies and leads on 15 of 16 tasks. Controlled experiments show that spatial grounding, event and progress information, temporal structure, task-conditioned selection, and language grounding each contribute to effective memory construction. More importantly, the same abstraction transfers to new physical-robot tasks: reuses the existing library without adding a new recognizer, while requires only one new event concept composed with the existing memory machinery. Across shared real-robot conditions, succeeds in trials ( ), compared with ( ) for the no-memory baseline. These results suggest that explicit, compositional concepts can serve not merely as task-specific memory annotations, but as a reusable and extensible interface between a robot's accumulated experience and learned control. Related Work sec:related Implicit memory in robot policies History-aware robot policies typically learn a latent representation of past observations and actions. Long-context policies directly attend to extended trajectories~ ptp,hamlet ; recurrent architectures propagate learned state across time~ rememvla ; memory-bank methods compress and retrieve past perceptual features~ memoryvla ; and test-time adaptation stores history in model weights~ ttt . Predictive world models similarly maintain latent state for control~ daydreamer,r2i . These approaches can capture rich temporal dependencies without prescribing what the representation must contain. However, what is retained, forgotten, or updated is learned largely through downstream objectives and remains difficult to inspect independently of the policy. ECoMEM instead externalizes a sparse set of task-relevant facts and fixes their evidence-based updates, while learning only how the policy should use them. Explicit and latent memory are therefore complementary rather than mutually exclusive. Explicit memory in robot policies A second line of work stores selected parts of experience explicitly. Keyframe and retrieval methods retain event-triggered images or trajectory segments~ eventvla,fang2025sam2act,strap,vid2robot ; MemER retrieves task-relevant visual experiences and uses a high-level VLM to condition a low-level policy~ sridhar2026memer . Other approaches summarize experience into language ~ remembr,liu2023reflect , maintain textual world states ~ statler , or organize persistent information in scene graphs ~ gu2024conceptgraphs,sayplan,dynamem . These representations improve access to past information, but visual memories still require the controller to recover facts from stored observations, while language and graph memories are commonly consumed by high-level reasoning or planning modules. ECoMEM instead maintains typed, evidence-linked records of states, events, progress, and temporal structure, and feeds them directly to a low-level VLA through a learned Reader. Neuro-symbolic methods in robotics Neuro-symbolic robotics combines learned perception and control with explicit, compositional abstractions. Knowledge representations such as KnowRob organize persistent robot knowledge~ tenorth2009knowrob ; neuro-symbolic concept learning and structured world models ground symbolic concepts in perception and compose them for reasoning ~ mao2019nscl,pdsketch ; and learned or invented predicates provide compact abstractions for task planning ~ visualpredicator,pix2pred,predicateinvention . Related work also uses symbolic concepts to structure learned generative models for manipulation and geometric reasoning~ setitup,stackitup . Recent systems further use vision--language models to construct symbolic planning abstractions from demonstrations~ buildonpriors , while knowledge graphs provide structured memory for language-model agents ~ arigraph . ECoMEM follows the same principle of grounding reusable symbolic concepts in learned representations, but uses them for a different role: as the interface between perceptual history and a learned control policy. Preliminaries sec:prelim Memory-dependent tasks. Given an instruction , a VLA policy observes (camera images and robot state) at decision and predicts an action chunk . The history contains all observations and executed actions up to , plus any demonstration given with the task. A task is memory-dependent if two histories with the same instruction and current observation require different expert actions: Pressing a button three times illustrates this: the scene may look identical after the first and third press, yet the correct action differs. A policy conditioned only on cannot distinguish them. Memory-conditioned policy. The history is long, but what separates from is usually a few facts. We therefore compress the history into a memory : a set of concept records, each stating one fact about the task entities (Figure~ fig:concept-library ). We separate what to remember from how to use it: We construct a Writer that selects concepts, harnesses pretrained perception models to recognize them, and updates records using only the history available at (Section~ sec:constructing-memory ). We keep fixed, because action supervision alone does not specify which facts to keep; a learned memory can instead exploit shortcuts~ causalconfusion,copycat . We then train a Reader jointly with the VLA on expert action chunks . The Reader encodes the records into memory tokens that condition the policy (Section~ sec:memory-vla , Appendix~ app:training ). sec:method adds an explicit memory channel to a VLA (Figure~ fig:org ), following the factorization in . The Writer determines what to remember: it draws from a shared concept library (Section~ sec:concept-library ), selects the concepts required by the task, recognizes them from visual and robot-state evidence, and updates the memory records (Section~ sec:constructing-memory ). The Reader learns how to use this memory by encoding the records into tokens that condition the VLA (Section~ sec:memory-vla ). Concept Library sec:concept-library A shared concept library. Memory-dependent tasks differ, but the facts they need recur. Counting button presses and counting placements both need the number of completed events. Finding a hidden cube and re-picking a demonstrated object both need a remembered location. We therefore define each type of fact once, as a concept in a shared library. A new task reuses these concepts instead of building from scratch, and a single Reader serves all tasks. Robot knowledge bases and neuro-symbolic concept learners follow the same principle~ tenorth2009knowrob,mao2019nscl . Four concept families. title: TRACE: Privacy-Preserving Next-Best-View Selection over Distributed 3D Gaussian-Splat Maps
summary: Share the light, not the map. We study next-best-view selection for a team of robots, each of which builds its own 3D Gaussian Splatting map and keeps it private. A robot picks the view with the largest expected information gain (EIG) about the splats along its own path. This gain depends on the other maps. Their splats occlude its own and shine behind them, so the gain has to be evaluated against the pooled map. No robot has this map. We show that the coupling passes through only two ray quantities, the transmittance in front of a splat and the radiance behind it, and that both are sums over the hits of the ray. Hence, they decompose across the robots, and each robot sums them over depth bins in its own map, along the rays of a candidate view, and sends the sums with their pose derivatives. The robot planning the view turns them into its EIG and gradient on SO(3). Transmittance and Radiance Aggregates, communicated for the EIG, give the protocol its name: TRACE. No robot shares its splats, and the message size does not grow with a map. We prove that the reconstruction is exact unless a depth bin behind a splat mixes hits of two robots, and we bound the error otherwise. Over 100 next-best-view decisions in Habitat-Sim, TRACE picks a heading within 15 degrees of the centralized one in 83.3% of the cases, and its views reach 97.9% of the centralized EIG.

Introduction sec:introduction A team of robots enters a building after an earthquake. Each robot maps what it sees and plans where to look next, in order to reconstruct the part of the scene it must traverse well enough to move through safely. The difficulty is that no robot sees everything it needs from where it stands. The far side of a corner ahead of it is already behind a second robot, and the top of a shelf it passes under was seen by a third that flew over it. Such viewpoints are out of reach, yet they hold the geometry that keeps the first robot safe. The value of a view is therefore a team quantity~ Di_NeRF,MAC_Ego3D,khass2026multi . A robot that scores its views on its own map alone looks where the team has already looked, and still misses what it cannot see. Coordinating these views is hard under limited bandwidth, energy and computation~ HAMMER,MAGiC_SLAM,Zhao2025RSS . We build these maps with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d . A 3DGS map is a set of anisotropic Gaussian primitives, and a view is rendered by projecting them onto the image plane and compositing them front to back along each ray~ ye2025gsplat,Matsuki . The render is differentiable in the parameters of the map and in the pose of the camera. Next-best-view (NBV) methods exploit this property to pick poses that reduce the uncertainty of the map~ Fisherrf,xue2026gavis,khass2025active,chen2026cover . The rendering Jacobian gives the sensitivities that build a Fisher information objective, which is then optimized over the pose. In a team of robots, this objective couples the maps at the level of the render. A centralized method sends the observations or the local maps to a server, which builds one 3DGS map and evaluates the team objective on it~ Chen_Su_Wang_Han_Xia_Bu_Li_Hu_Meng_Wang_2026,li2026compact . A distributed method keeps them on board, and then no robot holds the whole scene. Along a shared ray, the contribution of a primitive depends on the light that reaches it through the hits in front of it, and on the radiance behind it. Both are set by the joint depth order of all primitives on the ray, which no robot knows from its own map. A robot that renders only its own map therefore biases the objective and its gradient. We propose TRACE, a distributed NBV method that rebuilds these two quantities without sharing observations or Gaussian parameters. Along the rays of a candidate view, each robot reports the transmittance and radiance aggregates communicated for the EIG, which is where the name comes from. These aggregates are sums over depth bins. Hence, they carry what the other maps place along a ray without revealing which splats placed it. Each robot then evaluates the pooled-map gradient on its own and turns its camera, with no consensus over viewpoints. (i) We show that the EIG of a view, and its pose-gradient, depend on the maps of the other robots only through two quantities on each ray, the transmittance in front of a splat and the radiance behind it. (ii) We derive the pose-gradient of the masked EIG on in closed form from the outputs of a standard rasterizer. (iii) We propose TRACE, a protocol in which the robots exchange these two quantities in depth bins, with their pose derivatives, and never their splats; the message size does not depend on the number of splats. (iv) We prove that the EIG and its gradient are exact when no depth bin behind a splat mixes hits of two robots, and we bound the error otherwise. (v) We test TRACE in simulation against the centralized computation. NBV methods select camera poses that maximize information gain or improve coverage. FisherRF~ Fisherrf scores a view by the trace of a diagonal Fisher information matrix, and COVER~ chen2026cover builds an efficient coverage surrogate from an approximation of it. GAVIS~ xue2026gavis models view-dependent uncertainty with an anisotropic visibility field, and RT-GuIDE~ RT_guide uses the updates of the Gaussian parameters as a cheap information proxy. Others add risk-aware masks~ liu2024beyond or couple information gathering with safety-critical control~ khass2026conflict,khass2026splat . Across a team, views are classically picked from finite candidate sets by greedy submodular maximization on one shared map~ lauri2020multi . All of these score a view on a map the planner can access. Multi-agent neural mapping solves the other half of the problem, which is to build one consistent model from distributed observations. Di-NeRF~ Di_NeRF trains a NeRF by consensus and RAMEN~ Zhao2025RSS maps asynchronously. For 3DGS, MAGiC-SLAM~ MAGiC_SLAM merges local submaps by loop closures, MAC-Ego3D~ MAC_Ego3D enforces geometric consistency by Gaussian consensus, and CoMA-SLAM~ Chen_Su_Wang_Han_Xia_Bu_Li_Hu_Meng_Wang_2026 works on Gaussian surfels, while others cut communication with compact submaps~ HAMMER,li2026compact . All of these build one map of the whole scene. Closest to our goal is distributed risk-averse NBV over 3DGS maps~ khass2026multi , where each robot scores its views on its own map and consensus reconciles the team. That work distributes the optimization, and the splats of the other robots never enter a local render. TRACE distributes the render instead. No global map is formed, and each robot evaluates the gain of the pooled map from what it receives along the rays of its own view. title: UniTrackPLA: Unified Panorama-Language-Action Model for Instruction-Guided Navigation and Dynamic Person Tracking
comment: The project page is at https://tw5775.github.io/UniTrackPLA
summary: General-purpose embodied robots should support both navigation toward language-specified destinations and dynamic person tracking under arbitrary initial target azimuths. However, existing methods typically rely on forward-facing observations and address these tasks with separate policies, limiting omnidirectional perception and unified closed-loop control. We present UniTrackPLA, a unified panorama-language-action model for instruction-guided navigation and dynamic person tracking. Its Panoramic-Aware Encoding (PAE) preserves the temporal and azimuthal structure of perspective views projected from each panorama, enabling perspective-pretrained visual encoders to process omnidirectional observations. A shared vision-language backbone grounds instructions in the panoramic context and predicts continuous robot-centric waypoint chunks for both tasks. World-Action Consistency (WAC) further predicts action-conditioned future visual states and verifies waypoint prefixes online, allowing reliable actions to be reused while triggering replanning upon inconsistency. We also introduce OmniTrackNav-Bench, comprising 5,000 simulated tracking trajectories, 10,000 simulated VLN routes, and 96 verified real-world routes, providing 919,978 waypoint-supervision instances. UniTrackPLA improves overall tracking SR from 23.50% to 35.00% and Omni-VLN SR/SPL from 13.00%/12.77% to 19.75%/19.29%. Incorporating 76 real-world routes further improves held-out EP@0.2m from 42.92% to 92.08%. Closed-loop experiments on a Go2-W robot demonstrate unified panoramic tracking and navigation across indoor and outdoor environments. The project page is at https://tw5775.github.io/UniTrackPLA.

Introduction Embodied navigation enables robots to move through an environment according to visual observations and task instructions, constituting a fundamental capability for household assistance, human accompaniment, inspection, and mobile manipulation~ wang2022towards,zhang2026embodied_foundation,cai2026navigation_wayfinding,yang2026learning_panorama . Existing studies, however, have largely evolved along two separate paradigms. Vision-language navigation mainly focuses on reaching static semantic goals specified by language instructions~ zhang2024uni_navid,qiao2025navbench,lu2025monovln,dai2026thinkmatter , whereas embodied visual tracking emphasizes continuously following dynamic targets whose positions evolve over time~ wang2025trackvla,wu2025vlm,sun2026instance,liu2026trackvla++,ye2026refertrack . Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate visual perception, language understanding, and action prediction, improving instruction following and generalization in unseen environments~ zhang2026embodied_foundation,zhang2024uni_navid,wang2025trackvla,li2026urbanvla . Nevertheless, static-goal navigation and dynamic person tracking are still commonly treated separately, with task-specific observations, action spaces, and policies. We argue that these two tasks should instead be viewed as complementary instances of a broader embodied navigation problem. Instruction-guided navigation is primarily driven by relatively static semantic goals, while person tracking requires continuous adaptation to dynamically evolving physical targets. Despite this difference, both require the robot to ground task-relevant entities, reason about their spatial relationships, and continuously translate visual-language observations into motion decisions. A more general embodied navigation system should therefore be able to bridge these two regimes within a shared perception-language-action paradigm. This raises a fundamental question: can a single policy support both instruction-guided navigation toward static goals and continuous tracking of dynamic persons under a unified observation and action interface? Bridging static navigation and dynamic tracking requires a shared omnidirectional perceptual representation. Panoramic perception provides a natural means of removing this heading dependence by exposing the surrounding scene within a single omnidirectional observation space~ zhang2026embodied_foundation,zhang2024uni_navid,luo2025omnitrack . Prior studies have explored panoramic RGB-D observations~ watkins2020learning,kawaharazuka2024reflex , omnidirectional images~ wang2024enhanced , multiple perspective views~ lu2025monovln , panoramic environment generation~ li2023panogen,wang2025panogen++ , and latent panorama prediction~ dai2026thinkmatter for static-goal search and vision-language navigation. Recent approaches further incorporate panoramic scene parsing~ jin2026panonav , dynamic memory~ sheng2026p2dnav , and global-to-local reasoning~ liu2026omnivln,damodaran2026eagor . Nevertheless, existing panoramic systems mainly focus on static object search, route following, and scene reasoning, while dynamic target localization across arbitrary orientations and panorama boundaries remains insufficiently explored. More importantly, panoramic observations introduce a representation gap: most pretrained visual encoders are optimized for perspective images, whereas panoramic perception requires explicit reasoning over circular spatial structure and temporal evolution. Therefore, the key challenge is not merely to enlarge the field of view, but to retain the transferable representations of pretrained perspective-image encoders while recovering the spatial and temporal structure required for unified panoramic embodied navigation. A unified policy must also handle the different temporal dynamics of static navigation and dynamic tracking. Continuous waypoint heads improve efficiency by predicting short-horizon action chunks~ zhang2024uni_navid,wang2025trackvla , but fixed-horizon execution may become unreliable as the visual world evolves: trajectories that remain valid in relatively stable navigation can quickly become stale when a tracked person changes direction, local traversability changes, or execution errors accumulate. Executing the full chunk risks propagating invalid actions, while using only the first waypoint sacrifices most of the predicted trajectory. The key challenge is therefore how long a predicted trajectory should remain trusted. Since pixel-level world models are costly for real-time control~ nie2025wmnav,yao2026sc2wm , we instead employ lightweight action-conditioned latent future prediction to adaptively regulate the execution horizon. To bridge static instruction-guided navigation and dynamic person tracking across both perception and execution, we propose UniTrackPLA, a unified Panorama-Language-Action framework. UniTrackPLA formulates both tasks under shared panoramic observations and a continuous waypoint action space. Panoramic-Aware Encoding (PAE) captures visual content, view azimuth, and temporal position while preserving compatibility with pretrained perspective-image encoders, and a shared multimodal policy predicts waypoint chunks for both navigation and tracking. We introduce World-Action Consistency (WAC), which predicts action-conditioned future states in latent space and adaptively determines whether to continue the current chunk or replan, enabling efficient yet responsive closed-loop control. To support unified training and evaluation, we construct OmniTrackNav-Bench, comprising Omni-Tracking with dynamic-following trajectories and Omni-VLN with language-annotated panoramic navigation routes. Both tasks share the same panoramic observation and continuous waypoint representation, enabling unified multi-task learning within a single policy. We introduce a real-world panoramic navigation dataset comprising routes. Closed-loop experiments show that UniTrackPLA achieves a success rate on Omni-Tracking, compared with for our reproduced TrackVLA baseline, and reaches SR and SPL on Omni-VLN, outperforming the baseline results of and . Ablation studies verify the effectiveness of PAE and WAC. With this dataset, EP@0.2m on held-out real-world routes improves from to . Real-world deployment on a Go2-W robot with an Insta360 X4 further demonstrates both dynamic person tracking and instruction-guided navigation using the same policy. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: We propose UniTrackPLA, a panoramic VLA framework that bridges dynamic person following and vision-language navigation through shared panoramic perception, visual-language representations, and a continuous waypoint action space. Its PAE module jointly models panoramic azimuth and temporal context while reusing pretrained perspective-image encoders. We introduce a lightweight World-Action Consistency module that unifies temporal action execution across static navigation and dynamic tracking. By predicting the latent future consequences of waypoint prefixes, WAC adaptively regulates the effective action horizon and dynamically determines whether to continue the current chunk or trigger replanning. We construct the OmniTrackNav-Bench to support joint training and consistent evaluation across static navigation and dynamic tracking, comprising Omni-Tracking for arbitrary-orientation human following and Omni-VLN for dense panoramic language navigation. Extensive simulation experiments and real-robot deployments validate the effectiveness and generality of the overall framework. Related Work Embodied Navigation Existing embodied navigation methods can be broadly divided into static-goal navigation and dynamic-person following. Static-goal navigation guides a robot toward a specified location according to language instructions, target categories, or reference routes. Recent methods unify multiple navigation tasks and improve generalization across environments, embodiments, and long-horizon routes~ zhang2026embodied_foundation,zhang2024uni_navid,li2026urbanvla , while observation-instruction augmentation further facilitates transfer to unseen environments~ wei2026unseen_seen . Dynamic person following instead requires continuous target identification and motion adaptation. Hierarchical approaches bridge high-level user instructions and low-level tracking actions through intermediate spatial goals~ wu2025hierarchical . Other modular approaches employ visual foundation models, offline reinforcement learning, and vision-language models to improve target representation, failure recovery, occlusion handling, and cross-embodiment adaptation~ wu2025vlm,sun2026instance,zhong2024empowering,wu2026adatracker . End-to-end methods further incorporate referring comprehension, target memory, competitive interaction, and trajectory planning into vision-language-action policies~ wang2025trackvla,liu2026trackvla++,ye2026refertrack,liu2026comatrack , while recent benchmarks evaluate long-term tracking, socially aware following, and unified target seeking and following~ ye2025tpt_bench,ye2025follow_bench,yu2026uesf . However, most existing tracking methods rely on limited-FoV forward-facing cameras and assume that the target is initially visible in front of the robot, leaving side, rear, and panorama-boundary initialization underexplored. Panoramic-Aware Embodied Navigation Panoramic-aware navigation methods can be broadly divided into panoramic-perception-based navigation and panorama-assisted navigation. The former directly uses panoramic RGB-D observations, omnidirectional images, or multiple perspective views for target-driven, open-vocabulary, and language-guided navigation~ watkins2020learning,kawaharazuka2024reflex,wang2024enhanced . In particular, view-decomposed panoramic representations preserve local visual details while retaining compatibility with visual encoders pretrained on perspective images. The latter leverages generated panoramic environments, complementary views, or predicted latent panoramic features to bridge the observation gap between monocular and panoramic navigation~ lu2025monovln,dai2026thinkmatter,li2023panogen,wang2025panogen++ . title: TOAST: Stochastic Robot Action Tokenization for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action models often represent continuous robot actions as discrete token sequences, enabling action prediction with standard next-token objectives. FAST has substantially improved this representation by compactly encoding action containing diverse temporal frequencies into relatively few tokens. However, while such compression reduces the number of action tokens required for autoregressive prediction, it does not necessarily improve the efficiency of policy learning from limited demonstrations. In particular, FAST typically assigns a single deterministic tokenization to each quantized action sequence, although multiple token sequences can represent and decode to the same robot motion. We investigate whether exploiting this representational redundancy can improve policy learning. In this paper, we propose TOkenization of Action sequences with STochastic sampling (TOAST), a stochastic action tokenization method that samples alternative tokenizations of the same quantized action sequence during policy training. This diversifies the discrete supervision while preserving the underlying robot action and requires no additional demonstrations. Experiments on LIBERO show that TOAST consistently improves over its deterministic counterpart, with the improvement increasing as training data decreases, achieving a 6.8 point gain in success rate when only 1/16 of training data is available. Across four real-robot manipulation tasks, TOAST further improves mean success rate by 15.8 points over the deterministic counterpart. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of stochastic action tokenization for autoregressive robot policy learning, particularly when training data are limited.

Introduction sec:introduction Vision-language-action models (VLAs), backed by the success of imitation learning~ osa2018algorithmic , have been drawing attention as an approach for realizing general-purpose robot policies~ zitkovich2023rt2,reed2022gato,ghosh2024octo,kim2024openvla,black2025pi0,nvidia2025gr00tn1,liu2025rdt1b,lee2025molmoact . Autoregressive VLAs~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,pertsch2025fast,lee2025molmoact are policies that use a backbone multimodal large language model (MLLM) to predict action sequences as tokens via next-token prediction. Autoregressive VLAs offer advantages over flow matching-based ones~ black2025pi0,nvidia2025gr00tn1 of having a simpler architecture~ liang2025discrete , leveraging MLLM's pre-trained knowledge effectively~ liu2026hybridvla , and realizing faster convergence~ pertsch2025fast . In building autoregressive VLAs, the tokenizer determines what the policy has to predict, and recent work has explored efficient compression of action chunks in two ways: learned vector quantization, as in VQ-VLA~ wang2025vqvla , or training-free frequency-based compression, as in FAST~ pertsch2025fast , which applies byte pair encoding (BPE)~ sennrich2016neural to the quantized coefficients of a discrete cosine transform. Both make prediction easier by shortening the token sequence. However, the tokenization boundaries produced by frequency-based compression such as BPE are not necessarily physically meaningful for robot actions. Once the vocabulary contains tokens spanning multiple quantized action values, the same quantized action sequence can be represented by different token sequences, all of which decode to exactly the same motion. Deterministic tokenizers nevertheless select a single tokenization according to corpus-level frequency statistics, and the policy is trained under cross-entropy to reproduce only that sequence. A similar ambiguity has long been recognized in natural language processing, where stochastic tokenization~ kudo2018subword,provilko2020bpedropout,wang2021multiview mitigates over-reliance on a single segmentation and has shown particular benefits when training data are limited. This issue can be especially important in robot learning, where demonstrations are costly to collect. When only limited training data are available, repeatedly supervising each action sequence with the same deterministic tokenization may encourage the policy to overfit to specific token patterns or segmentation boundaries that are not uniquely tied to the underlying motion. To address this issue, we propose kenization of ction Sequences with ochastic Sampling ( ), the first stochastic action tokenization framework for autoregressive robot policy learning. As shown in , samples multiple tokenizations of the same action sequence during training, exposing the policy to different discrete representations while preserving the underlying motion. Moreover, because multiple valid token sequences can be obtained from each demonstration without collecting additional robot trajectories, increases the diversity of supervision available from limited data. We therefore hypothesize that stochastic action tokenization becomes increasingly beneficial when fewer demonstrations are available. We instantiate this framework with a unigram tokenizer that enables probabilistic segmentation, together with dimension-major flattening for frequency-based action sequence compression. We evaluate this hypothesis through both controlled simulation and real-world manipulation task experiments. The results show that stochastic tokenization consistently improves policy performance over its deterministic counterpart across training-set sizes, flattening orders, and vocabulary corpora. Notably, the relative benefit of stochastic tokenization is greater when fewer demonstrations are available, indicating improved data efficiency in policy learning. We further observe substantial gains on real-robot manipulation tasks, where collecting demonstrations is particularly expensive. These results show that stochastic action tokenization provides a simple and effective means of extracting more useful supervision from limited robot demonstrations. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We identify deterministic action tokenization as a source of over-reliance on a single discrete representation and formulate stochastic tokenization as a representation-level regularization effect for autoregressive VLAs. We introduce , which samples equivalent tokenizations of the same motion during training, yielding more diverse supervision from each demonstration without additional robot data. Related work sec:related_work Vision-language-action models and action tokenization. Inspired by advances in foundation models for natural language processing and computer vision~ hurst2024gpt,comanici2025gemini,beyer2024paligemma,bai2025qwen3,deitke2025molmo , Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising approach to generalist robot policy learning~ reed2022gato,brohan2023rt1,zitkovich2023rt2,ghosh2024octo, kim2024openvla,black2025pi05,nvidia2025gr00tn1,geminiroboticsteam2025geminiroboticsbringingai . Autoregressive VLAs formulate action prediction as next-token prediction~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla,pertsch2025fast,lee2025molmoact , making the representation of continuous robot actions as discrete tokens an important design choice. Early approaches use uniform binning to discretize each action dimension and timestep independently~ zitkovich2023rt2,kim2024openvla . More recent methods exploit temporal or cross-dimensional structure to obtain more compact action representations. BEAST~ zhou2025beast represents action sequences using B-spline control points, while vector-quantization-based methods~ lee2024behavior,liu2026faster , such as VQ-VLA~ wang2025vqvla , learn discrete latent representations of continuous actions. FAST~ pertsch2025fast instead provides a training-free tokenizer by applying the discrete cosine transform (DCT) followed by byte pair encoding (BPE)~ sennrich2016neural . Our work builds on this frequency-based approach, but focuses on stochastic tokenization of action sequences rather than introducing another compression scheme. Stochastic tokenization with frequency-based tokenizers. In natural language processing, subword tokenizers such as BPE~ sennrich2016neural and unigram language model~ kudo2018subword tokenization construct vocabularies from corpus statistics. Given a fixed vocabulary, the same underlying sequence can generally admit multiple valid segmentations, although standard tokenization selects a single one deterministically. Subword regularization~ kudo2018subword instead samples alternative tokenizations during training, and subsequent work has explored related stochastic tokenization strategies~ provilko2020bpedropout, wang2021multiview,cognetta2024distributional,sims2026stochastok . These methods have been shown to enable efficient learning in low-resource settings. Frequency-based action tokenizers such as FAST~ pertsch2025fast admit the same segmentation ambiguity, but whether sampling equivalent tokenizations improves robot policy learning has remained unexplored. The action horizon is fixed by the policy configuration, whereas the number of tokens depends on the tokenizer and the action sequence. Action sequence tokenization and compression. The action chunk is first transformed and discretized into , for example by scalar binning or by applying DCT followed by discretization. title: eRLT: Efficient VLA Reinforcement Learning via Action-Relevant Token Routing
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models provide strong behavioral priors for robotic manipulation, yet efficiently adapting them to downstream tasks remains challenging. Recent work addresses this challenge by adapting frozen VLAs through online reinforcement learning (RL), whose sample efficiency depends on the quality of the state representation used by the actor and critic. Existing methods construct such representations either with VLA-independent visual encoders or through fixed compression of internal VLA representations. Neither design explicitly extracts the task-specific action-relevant VLA features most useful for downstream action refinement and action-value estimation, therefore limiting sample efficiency. To address this limitation, we introduce eRLT, which constructs an effective state representation by routing task-specific action-relevant information across both tokens and layers of the frozen VLA. Specifically, learned routing tokens dynamically aggregate visual-language features at multiple depths, while a lightweight layer router combines these summaries into a fixed-dimensional RL token. The routing module is initialized using expert demonstrations to capture features predictive of expert actions and then refined using critic feedback from online interactions for action-value estimation. Across seven LIBERO and RoboTwin tasks, eRLT improves mean normalized learning-curve AUC by up to 23.7% over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments on USB connector insertion and motherboard ribbon-cable insertion further show AUC improvements of 108.9% and 46.7%, respectively, over the strongest baseline.

Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models inherit broad visual and semantic knowledge from internet-scale pretraining and learn generalist control from diverse robot data, enabling generalization across tasks and environments kim2025openvla,black2026pi0 . However, achieving high reliability on a specific downstream task often requires further adaptation. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is effective, but heavily relies on collecting additional high-quality task-specific demonstrations, whose coverage of states encountered during deployment is inherently limited. Online reinforcement learning (RL) provides a complementary approach by collecting experience from the policy's own deployment distribution and learning from both successful and failed interactions physicalintelligence2025pi06,xu2026rltoken,wagenmaker2025dsrl,xiao2025pld, zhu2026learning, gao2026smoothrl . In this work, we focus on lightweight online RL methods that keep the pretrained VLA frozen and adapt its behavior through a small actor-critic. The success of lightweight online RL depends critically on the state representation supplied to the actor and critic. A VLA trained for generalist control encodes rich information about visual observations, language instructions, robot states, and actions. For task-specific adaptation, an effective state representation should retain the task-specific action-relevant information needed for action refinement and action-value estimation, including robot-object relations that determine appropriate corrections and task-progress cues that determine the expected return of those corrections. Such information is distributed across the VLA's tokens and layers, and the most useful features vary across tasks. Existing methods construct the state representation either with visual encoders independent of the VLA wagenmaker2025dsrl,xiao2025pld or by compressing representations from a predetermined layer and token set kowshik2026midas,xu2026rltoken . The former constructs the state representation outside the VLA and therefore cannot directly reuse its internal task-specific action-relevant features. The latter reuses VLA features, but restricts feature extraction to a predetermined layer and token set regardless of which features are most useful for the target task. Neither design explicitly extracts the task-specific action-relevant VLA features most useful for downstream action refinement and action-value estimation, limiting sample efficiency under constrained online interaction budgets. To address this limitation, we introduce eRLT, which constructs an effective state representation by routing task-specific action-relevant information across the tokens and layers of the frozen VLA. At each selected VLM layer, learned routing tokens dynamically aggregate visual-language features, while a lightweight layer router combines these layer-wise summaries into a fixed-dimensional RL token. The routing module is firstly initialized by predicting expert action chunks from existing VLA SFT demonstrations, encouraging the RL token to retain information useful for action refinement. Then, during online RL stage, the critic's Bellman objective further refines the routing module using online transitions, adapting the retained information for action-value estimation. The VLA remains frozen throughout both stages. By focusing the RL token on task-specific action-relevant VLA features, eRLT facilitates action refinement and action-value estimation, thereby supporting sample-efficient actor-critic learning from limited online interactions. We evaluate eRLT on manipulation tasks from LIBERO liu2023libero and RoboTwin chen2025robotwin , as well as two real-world high-precision manipulation tasks: USB connector insertion and motherboard ribbon-cable insertion. Across the seven simulation tasks, eRLT improves mean normalized learning-curve AUC by relative to baselines with fixed VLA feature compression and by relative to baselines with VLA-independent state encoders. On the two real-world tasks, eRLT improves learning-curve AUC by and , respectively, relative to the strongest baseline, and on USB connector insertion raises the final-window success rate from to under the same interaction budget. Ablations further validate the complementary roles of layer-wise routing, token-wise routing, task-specific action-relevant initialization, and online adaptation. In summary, our contributions are three-fold: 2pt 0pt 0pt 0pt 0pt We provide controlled evidence that the VLA layers and tokens most useful for online RL vary across downstream tasks. We propose eRLT, which constructs an effective RL token by routing task-specific action-relevant information across VLA tokens and layers. The routing mechanism is initialized via expert action prediction and subsequently refined online using critic feedback. We evaluate eRLT across LIBERO, RoboTwin, and two real-world precision high-precision manipulation tasks, demonstrating improved sample efficiency over existing state representations. Related Work Lightweight Online Reinforcement Learning for VLA Models Lightweight online RL adapts a pretrained policy through small trainable modules while preserving its behavioral prior. Early residual RL learns corrections for conventional controllers ; recent VLA methods instead keep the pretrained policy frozen and train a lightweight actor to correct its actions or steer its generative process xiao2025pld,wagenmaker2025dsrl,li2025grrl,xu2026rltoken,zhu2026learning,gao2026smoothrl,kowshik2026midas,zheng2026torlvla . Some further incorporate human guidance or improved initialization lu2026unisteerunifiednoisesteering,frs . eRLT adopts this frozen-VLA actor-critic framework and studies how to construct the state representation supplied to the actor and critic from the VLA's internal representations. Within this framework, the actor and critic must infer which decisions lead to higher returns from an effective state representation, making the task-specific action-relevant information retained in this representation central to sample-efficient learning. Existing methods construct the state representation either with VLA-independent visual encoders or by compressing a predetermined layer and token set. DSRL and PLD use the former design wagenmaker2025dsrl,xiao2025pld ; MiDAS mean-pools internal VLM tokens, while RLT compresses final-layer tokens using reconstruction kowshik2026midas,xu2026rltoken . The former constructs state representations separately from those already available in the VLA, while the latter uses only prescribed layers and tokens. Both designs therefore lack a mechanism for selecting the internal VLA information most relevant to task-specific action refinement and action-value estimation, limiting sample efficiency under constrained online interaction budgets. eRLT instead learns to aggregate task-specific action-relevant information across VLA tokens and layers into an effective RL token. Internal VLA Representations and Feature Aggregation Frozen VLA representations encode object relations, robot and action states, task progress, failures, transitions, and future success lu2025probing,gu2025safe,bhardwaj2026taskprogress,zhang2026frozenvlasuccess,molinari2025emergent . Intervention studies further show that motion- and action-related features can influence robot behavior haon2025mechanistic,buurmeijer2026observing,swann2026sparsevla,grant2026features . These signals are distributed: different layers provide complementary representations wang2026vlaadapter,yao2024denseconnector,cao2024mmfuser,lin2025multilayer,shi2026vlatrace , while selective token aggregation can improve action generation xiao2026avavla,ji2026actionqformer . These findings support eRLT's use of frozen internal VLA representations as the source of the RL token supplied to the actor and critic. Feature aggregation methods extract such distributed information either by compressing tokens within a layer or by combining representations across layers. Learned tokens and queries compress visual or multimodal features within a layer ryoo2021tokenlearner,li2023blip2,li2025tokenpacker , and recent VLA methods use related mechanisms for action generation xiao2026avavla,ji2026actionqformer,kim2026progvla . Other methods combine hidden representations across depths yao2024denseconnector,cao2024mmfuser,lin2025multilayer,wang2026vlaadapter . These representations target visual-language understanding or VLA action generation; eRLT adapts both forms of aggregation to construct a fixed-dimensional RL token that retains task-specific action-relevant information for the actor and critic. A pretrained VLA provides a strong behavioral prior for generating task-relevant robot actions. Lightweight online RL keeps the VLA frozen as the action prior and generator and improves its behavior by training only lightweight modules around it, such as an actor and critic. The frozen VLA and the trainable actor jointly produce an executable action chunk from the current observation and the actor's RL state. Different lightweight RL algorithms may combine the actor and VLA in different ways; their concrete implementations are specified in the experimental setup. Online training alternates between environment interaction and actor-critic updates. After executing an action chunk, the robot receives a reward , the next observation , and a termination indicator . The interaction is stored in a replay buffer and repeatedly reused for off-policy learning haarnoja2019sac . The critic learns which decisions of the lightweight actor lead to high long-term return, and the actor is updated to favor decisions assigned higher value by the critic. Thus, the lightweight modules improve from both successful and failed trials, while the pretrained VLA remains unchanged throughout online learning. title: NarrativeFlow: Flow-Based Vision-Language-Action Model Using Robot Velocity Fields
summary: We focus on language-conditioned flow-based manipulation, where robot flows (robot velocity fields) serve as embodiment-agnostic, motion-centric representations for leveraging data collected from multiple robot platforms. This task is crucial because language-conditioned manipulation is essential for practical robotic systems, yet scaling robot foundation models remains limited by the labor-intensive collection of embodiment-specific data. Existing methods either coarsely approximate robot flows with sparse keypoint displacements, or cannot handle language-conditioned manipulation. To address this limitation, we propose NarrativeFlow, which models robot flows as continuous velocity fields using a flow-matching formulation conditioned on language. Accordingly, NarrativeFlow generates robot flows that are physically consistent with real-world manipulation. To validate NarrativeFlow, we have conducted experiments on standard datasets for language-conditioned manipulation. The experimental results show that NarrativeFlow outperforms representative baseline methods on standard evaluation metrics. Furthermore, through real-world experiments, we show that NarrativeFlow achieves higher success rates than baseline methods across multiple manipulation tasks. The project page is available at https://shota0520.github.io/NarrativeFlow-project-page/
