The project page is available at Introduction sec:intro Labor shortages have increased demand for robotic systems that support workers and reduce physical burden in manufacturing, logistics, and healthcare. To meet this demand, such systems must perform diverse tasks across a wide range of real-world environments, while following natural language instructions. In this direction, recent work has explored robot foundation models, which are often pretrained on large-scale data collected from multiple robot platforms~ pi0-black25rss, pi05-black25corl, oxe-neill24icra, openvla-kim24corl . This line of work indicates that the scale and diversity of training data are critical to model performance, yet training these models still requires labor-intensive collection of embodiment-specific data~ pi0-black25rss, pi05-black25corl, oxe-neill24icra, openvla-kim24corl . In this study, we focus on language-conditioned flow-based manipulation. In this task, a model generates a robot flow (robot velocity field) conditioned on an instruction, and then a robot performs object manipulation based on the robot flow. Robot flows serve as embodiment-agnostic intermediate representations that bridge visual observations and robot actions. Because such flows can be extracted from arbitrary robot videos, flow-based approaches can leverage large-scale data collected from multiple robot platforms rather than relying on costly embodiment-specific data collection. However, this task remains challenging: indeed, a representative method, Im2Flow2Act~ im2flow2act-xu24corl , still underperforms a method using oracle robot flows by 21 percentage points in average success rate (see ). Many existing flow-based manipulation methods~ flip-gao25iclr, im2flow2act-xu24corl, track2act-bharadhwaj24eccv do not formulate robot flows as dense velocity fields, but as displacements of sparse keypoints, even though robot manipulation is inherently a time-evolving physical process. Specifically, these methods predict sparse keypoint coordinates and then derive robot flows from their displacements, yielding only a coarse approximation of continuous robot motion. These formulations can be problematic because they assume that the displacements are deterministic, although such an assumption is rarely satisfied in practice. By contrast, Flow as Flow~ faf-seno26 can model robot flows as dense velocity fields; however, it cannot handle language-conditioned settings. Moreover, existing methods~ flip-gao25iclr, im2flow2act-xu24corl, track2act-bharadhwaj24eccv, faf-seno26 typically rely only on primary flow-generation objectives during training, which provide no explicit supervision for capturing task-relevant semantics. As a result, such models can be misled by task-irrelevant visual details, such as background appearance and lighting. To address these limitations, we propose , a language-conditioned robot flow generation method that formulates robot flows as probability velocity fields within a flow-matching framework. By modeling velocity fields, generates robot flows that are more physically consistent with real-world manipulation. Moreover, we introduce an auxiliary loss that aligns the model’s intermediate representations with task-relevant scene changes, enabling the model to capture task-relevant semantics. shows an overview of our approach. We first train our model on cross-embodiment datasets. At deployment, given an instruction and an initial image, the model generates a robot flow that represents the robot motion required for the specified task (e.g., picking up the can and placing it on the table). Subsequently, the robot executes the manipulation based on the generated flow to complete the task. The contributions of this study are as follows: We propose , a language-conditioned robot flow generation method that formulates robot flows as probability velocity fields within a flow-matching framework, enabling high-quality robot flow generation. We introduce the loss as an auxiliary objective that aligns the model’s intermediate representations with task-relevant scene changes. We further introduce two tokens to mitigate interference between this auxiliary objective and the primary flow-generation objective. We show that outperforms baseline methods across standard datasets. Through real-world experiments, we show that achieves higher success rates than baseline methods across multiple manipulation tasks. Related Work Robotic foundation models aim to address diverse tasks across varied environments and have been actively investigated~ surveyA-kawaharazuka2025vla-survey, surveyB-zhong2025survey . Recent language-conditioned manipulation policies build on pretrained foundation models such as multimodal large language models (MLLMs), adopting them as semantic backbones coupled with action heads that map language and observations to control~ pi0-black25rss,pi05-black25corl,evo1-lin2026cvpr . This design inherits semantic and perceptual priors from large-scale pretraining, which transfer to unseen tasks and objects~ pi05-black25corl,instructvla-yang25iclr . A separate line of work introduces an explicit intermediate representation between language and action~ im2flow2act-xu24corl,vidbot-chen25cvpr,ghost-krishna26rss . Such methods predict task- or scene-level targets, including 3D affordance maps (e.g.,~ robobrain-ji25cvpr,ghost-krishna26rss ) and visual subgoals (e.g.,~ susie-black24iclr,cotvla-zhao25cvpr ), rather than conditioning the policies directly on latent features from the backbones. Among such targets, robot flows represent task progress as point or end-effector motion, bridging language specifications and the low-level trajectories that execute them~ tramoe-yang25cvpr,im2flow2act-xu24corl,flip-gao25iclr,lilac-kambara26ral . Flow-based manipulation methods use robot flows as embodiment-agnostic motion representations that bridge vision and action~ track2act-bharadhwaj24eccv,ec-flow-chen25iccv,g3flow-chen25cvpr,generalflow-yuan25corl,im2flow2act-xu24corl . These representations can be extracted from heterogeneous robot videos (e.g.,~ robotap-vecerik24icra,atm-wen23rss ) and from web-scale human videos (e.g.,~ track2act-bharadhwaj24eccv,faf-seno26,egoscaler-yoshida25cvpr ). Moreover, a large body of work has demonstrated the effectiveness of robot flows across diverse real-world tasks including rigid, articulated, and deformable object manipulation (e.g.,~ flow-bot-pp-zhang23corl,im2flow2act-xu24corl ). Although earlier methods generate robot flows over the entire frame (e.g.,~ track2act-bharadhwaj24eccv,atm-wen23rss ), some studies use object-centric or hand-centric flows to further reduce the influence of embodiment-specific factors (e.g.,~ im2flow2act-xu24corl,lilac-kambara26ral,ec-flow-chen25iccv,egoscaler-yoshida25cvpr ). Other approaches adopt flow-conditioned video generation to predict the future scene (e.g.,~ flip-gao25iclr ), or extend 2D flows into 3D using depth estimation (e.g.,~ g3flow-chen25cvpr,ppi-yang25rss ). These methods derive robot flows from the displacements of sparse keypoints. As an alternative, Flow as Flow~ faf-seno26 directly predicts robot velocity fields via flow matching, a framework that predicts probability velocity fields in a generation space. However, this method is limited to goal-conditioned manipulation and hence it is unable to address language-conditioned settings. In contrast, generates robot flows using the flow-matching formulation conditioned on language. To model temporal dynamics and task-relevant transformations, prior work has leveraged scene-change information in visual representation learning. For example, procedure-planning methods predict sequences of high-level action labels from a current visual observation toward a visual goal in instructional video understanding~ pdpp-wang23cvpr,skipplan-li23iccv,kepp-nagasinghe24cvpr . Other work has focused on scene changes for object-centric localization (e.g.,~ oscs-xue24cvpr ), procedural modeling (e.g.,~ niu2024schema ), and fine-grained temporal modeling (e.g.,~ hifvla-lin26cvpr,progress-xue25cvpr ). In parallel, recent work has explored efficient temporal representations using video codecs, further leveraging temporal and scene-change cues (e.g.,~ remora-yashima26cvpr ). In manipulation tasks, goal images are often used to specify desired final scene configurations~ rtsketch-sundaresan24corl, susie-black24iclr . These images provide fine-grained details of the scene change to be achieved, but are typically unavailable at inference time in language-conditioned settings. To leverage this information for language-conditioned manipulation, GRIF~ grif-myers23corl uses initial--goal image pairs during training to learn scene-change representations aligned with instructions. In addition, world models and dynamics models predict how objects and scenes change conditioned on actions. They model such changes through future observation prediction, learned physical dynamics, or dense geometric motion~ susie-black24iclr, graphdynamics-deng24icra, pointworld-huang26cvpr . Method Problem Statement In this study, we address language-conditioned flow-based manipulation. This task consists of two subtasks: robot flow generation and object manipulation conditioned on the generated robot flow. In the robot flow generation subtask, given an initial image and an instruction, the model generates a robot flow, which is expected to be aligned with the ground-truth robot motion. Subsequently, in the object manipulation subtask, at each timestep, given the current observation and the generated robot flow, the model outputs a robot end-effector pose. shows an example of this task. Given the initial image and the instruction “Pick up the gold can, and place it on the table,” the model is required to generate the corresponding robot flow. Based on the generated robot flow, the robot then moves the gold can onto the table. In this study, we assume that the end-effector is visible in an initial image under a fixed camera setup. We focus on the flow generation subtask. For the object manipulation subtask, we use a flow-conditioned manipulation policy, such as those adopted in prior methods (e.g., faf-seno26,im2flow2act-xu24corl,track2act-bharadhwaj24eccv ). title: Divide-and-Remember: Recursive Action-Relevant Memory for Long-Horizon VLA Policies
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models struggle on history-dependent manipulation tasks, where the current observation alone does not determine the action, and the policy needs a memory of the history. Existing memory methods decide what to remember by design, for example, keeping frames with large pixel changes, and show inconsistent gains across tasks. We view what to remember as an optimisation problem. From the POMDP formulation of imitation learning, we show that the optimal memory maximises the conditional mutual information $I(a_t; m_t \mid o_t)$ between the action and the memory given the current observation. Intuitively, this means preserving the action-relevant information in the history that is not already contained in the current observation. Based on our analysis, we propose Divide-and-Remember (D&R), a recursive memory method that learns a memory function $m_t = M(h_t)$ and scales to long contexts while staying compute-light. It involves two strategies: (1) the selection over the full history is divided recursively into subproblems of top-$K$ selection over $2K$ tokens, so that fixed-size, lightweight selectors learned end-to-end support an unbounded history; (2) all recursion blocks share one selector, which captures the selection rule common to every block and keeps the method efficient. On RoboMME, a benchmark of 16 long-horizon manipulation tasks that require remembering when, where, what, and how to act, D&R achieves a state-of-the-art average success rate with consistent gains across all four suites under a budget of only 64 tokens; real-robot experiments show the same gain. Code, checkpoints and more results are at https://dnr-memory.github.io/

Introduction Vision--language--action (VLA) policies are visuomotor policies trained by imitation learning, a.k.a.\ learning from demonstrations (LfD): a policy is learned from a dataset of demonstrations, each an observation--action sequence . Powered by large-scale robotic datasets and pretrained vision--language models, VLAs have achieved remarkable progress in robotic manipulation. However, many long-horizon tasks are partially observable, where the current observation alone cannot determine the correct action. In Figure~ fig:intro (a), the robot must move a cube ``in the same manner as before'', as shown in a video it has just watched; after either video it faces the same observation, and only the history tells it how to act. When the task's memory length, the shortest history the task requires, exceeds the policy's context length (Definition~ def:long-horizon ), such ambiguity can only be resolved by the history . In this case, the policy needs memory, the ability to retain and reuse relevant information across time; we refer to this as the memory problem. A growing body of research has integrated memory into VLAs, differing in what the memory encodes, from latent memory~ koo2026hamlet,memoryvla2025,cronusvla2025 to perceptual memory~ yang2026eventvla,dai2026robomme , and alleviates the memory problem to some extent. However, what information the memory should carry remains fragmented. Latent memory learns a dense compression of the history , which tracks temporal facts well (e.g., a count of events) but aligns poorly with the pretrained token space of the VLA and loses spatial detail. Perceptual memory keeps a subset of the history chosen by an inductive bias (e.g., the frames with the largest pixel change, or those picked by a VLM verifier); its verbatim snapshots preserve spatial facts (object locations and spatial relations) and object identity, but often miss some key robot behaviour, and the selection is not optimised for control. This diversity reflects that existing work designs memory from task-specific~ yang2026eventvla,kemo2026 perspectives, yielding inconsistent gains and a limited understanding of what the optimal formulation of memory is. Starting from information theory and POMDPs, we cast the memory problem of a visuomotor policy as an optimisation problem: the optimal memory maximises the conditional mutual information between the action and the memory given the current observation (formal definition in Section~ sec:analysis ); intuitively, it keeps the key facts that lacks but depends on, such as the grasp pose in Figure~ fig:intro (b). This objective gives a unified view of existing memories. Perceptual heuristics keep the frames that differ most in pixels. This is a proxy for the conditional entropy , i.e., how much a candidate frame differs from the current observation . It is only a loose upper bound on what the frame adds, , and spends the memory budget on information that does not help control, such as when the observation changes for reasons unrelated to the action (e.g., a lighting change). Latent memory does optimise through its variational lower bound; the action log-likelihood is maximised jointly over the policy weights and the memory , but it learns in a new latent space and loses the spatial detail that the pretrained tokens of the VLA carry. Thus, we ask: Can a memory be trained to maximise directly, without heuristics, while staying in the pretrained token space of the VLA, so that it is optimised for control and still keeps the spatial details? We answer this question with Divide-and-Remember ( ), which optimises the memory against in the pretrained token space of the VLA, so that choosing becomes a discrete optimisation over the history tokens . is a recursive memory method, in which the full history is divided recursively into slices of tokens and a fixed-size, lightweight selector keeps tokens of each slice. The tokens kept from two neighbouring slices are merged into a new -token slice and selected again (see Figure~ fig:tree ), and the composition of these selections solves the memory selection over the full history. This design lets the history scale up while the learnable parameters stay light. The selector is trained end-to-end by the policy's action loss, the variational lower bound of . We evaluate on RoboMME~ dai2026robomme , a benchmark of long-horizon manipulation tasks that each require a different fact from the past. Under a memory budget of only tokens, reaches a state-of-the-art average success rate of , against for the best latent memory and for the memoryless policy. leads on every memory demand of the benchmark, whether the policy has to accumulate a count over repeated events, track an object after it is hidden, refer back to an earlier moment of the episode, or reproduce a demonstrated sequence. We also evaluate on a real robot over several long-run tasks, with a person intervening mid-task and under perception noise, where achieved the highest success rate. Related work Memory-augmented VLAs. Existing memory methods for VLAs differ in what the memory encodes, and each fixes what to remember by design. (1) Latent memory compresses the history into a compact representation, by merging each step into learnable moment tokens (HAMLET~ koo2026hamlet ) or by a recurrent belief state trained with world-model objectives (RB-VLA~ bagaria2026rbvla ); it tracks temporal facts well but loses spatial detail. (2) Perceptual memory keeps a subset of the raw history chosen by a fixed selection rule: frames a VLM labels as events (EventVLA~ yang2026eventvla ), the patches with the largest pixel change (TokenDrop~ dai2026robomme ), or uniformly sampled frames (FrameSamp~ dai2026robomme ); the snapshots preserve spatial and object detail, but the rule is hand-designed and not optimised for control. (3) Parametric memory folds the history into fast weights by test-time training (TTT)~ sun2024ttt,dai2026robomme ; a fact stored in weights is written by gradient descent, which is slow, and is hard to read back exactly. Routes to the optimal POMDP policy. Classical solutions differ in which statistic of the history the policy conditions on. (1) The full history, , by solving the associated dynamic decision network (Figure~ fig:gm (a)); the policy grows exponentially with the history's length, so this works only for short histories~ poole2023artificial . (2) The belief state, the posterior over the current state and a sufficient statistic for prediction, as in RB-VLA~ bagaria2026rbvla ; its recurrent update makes compute and activation memory grow linearly with the episode length and cannot be parallelised over time, which is costly when every step runs a full forward pass of the VLA. Our analysis gives all of these designs a common objective, ; is an approximation that optimises it in the pretrained token space, conditioning the policy on a bounded statistic, so that the memory stays small and the facts it keeps can be read back exactly. Such a dynamic system is defined by a POMDP with states , actions , and observations , as depicted by the decision diagram in Figure~ fig:gm (a). title: Online Planning for Sparse Ground Target Search from a High-Altitude UAV under Partial Observability
summary:
Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) searching for ground targets from a high altitude face a unique challenge, particularly when the target is already within the field of view but effectively unobservable because of its small apparent scale. Standard object detectors often underperform in such scenarios because of resolution downscaling and limited context. In contrast, active object search frameworks address this challenge by directing the agent to a suitable pose to gather richer visual information. However, flight regulations in urban airspace often restrict such physical movements for UAVs. As an alternative active sensing approach, the UAV can leverage the pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) mechanism of the onboard camera to dynamically adjust its field of view and sequentially gather enhanced visual information from specific regions of interest. Once the candidate locations of the target are identified, it can deploy more expensive object detection schemes, such as an ensemble of multiple models, to get better reasoning at a fixed scale. In this work, we formulate the sequential exploration with PTZ operation as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), in which the agent maintains a belief state over the target's true location. To solve the POMDP, we deploy partially observable Monte Carlo planning (POMCP), where we condition the sensing reliability on target object scale and deploy selective ensemble detection as an additional reasoning step.
  We validate our methodology with experiments in a photorealistic simulator under different environmental conditions and vehicle states, showing detection of ground targets at variable scales with significantly fewer steps and minimal dependence on sensor resolution compared to baseline methods.

This capability allows us to detect small objects at a distance, even if they occupy a tiny area within our field of view (FOV). Emulating such adaptive perception capability is crucial for efficient object search and has been extensively studied in the computer vision community as human eye movement models~ butkoIPOMDPInfomaxModel2008,butko2009optimal . However, these models assume that the object of interest is always present in the input image, that the image already contains sufficient features of the target object, and that the sensor has a high detection probability with negligible noise in the operating range. In a real-world object search scenario, most images collected by a mobile robot may not contain the target object, the target object may be occluded or may not reveal sufficient features, and the detector itself may be noisy. There has been significant advancement in object search in indoor environments by the robotics community, where these challenges are handled by physically moving the agent to a suitable pose to gather enhanced visual information~ xiao2019online, zheng2021multi . These works assume the observation uncertainty mostly arises from object occlusion or hidden features for the object's relative pose, as the target object scale variation within the FOV is often negligible in indoor settings. For unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), searching for a sparse ground target from high altitude, such physical movement is not feasible due to flight regulations in urban airspace. Moreover, even if the target is visible within the FOV, it may be tiny, and the input image resolution may not be enough to reveal sufficient features. In this scenario, standard object detectors often struggle to produce reliable detections. Computer vision methods for tiny object detection also suffer in this case, as a higher-resolution version of the input image may not be available, and approaches such as slicing~ akyon2022slicing , that attempts to enhance the size of the target by exhaustive slicing of the whole image with overlaps, or coarse-to-fine~ huang2022ufpmp detection, that runs a coarse detector to find the candidate regions and runs a fine detector on the candidate regions for finding the target, leads to significant resolution downscaling that produces uncalibrated confidence scores and a number of false positive detections. Though the detection accuracy can be further enhanced with more expensive ensemble methods~ solovyev2019weighted , which run inference with multiple models trained on a subset of data (bagging~ breiman1996bagging ) or with random initialization~ lakshminarayanan2017simple , they can still struggle under scale and resolution variation of the target image. The UAV can leverage the pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) mechanism before capturing the images to selectively enhance the size, clarity, and position of the object of interest, while maintaining a fixed input resolution, as illustrated in Figure~ fig:UAV_carla . However, such selective enhancement can be expensive, and any exhaustive exploration may be limited by on-board computational resources and time-sensitive mission objectives. Conventional autonomous PTZ camera control follows a preloaded policy, often learned offline, that assumes complete environmental observability and focuses primarily on target tracking rather than ensuring detection reliability~ sandha2023eagle, fang2025automatic . For the sparse target search scenario, these assumptions do not hold, as the UAV cannot access the full information about the environment simultaneously and can only receive noisy observations with variable uncertainty conditioned on the PTZ settings, environmental conditions, and the target's relative pose. In other words, the environment is partially observable, and the UAV must maintain a belief state, which is an internal estimate of its surroundings, to effectively choose the next sequence of actions. At every time step, the UAV has to trade off between wide-scan exploration for quick area coverage to receive noisy observations and precise-scan exploration for slower area coverage to receive more reliable observations. In this work, we formulate the sparse target search problem from a high altitude using camera PTZ functionality as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP)~ kaelblingPlanningActingPartially1998 . In this setting, the control policy operates directly on the belief space to sequentially actuate the PTZ operation of the camera to optimize the long-term objective of finding the target with minimum steps. The belief gets updated as the UAV receives new observations. Unlike conventional approaches that assume complete knowledge of the environment (i.e., complete observability of the environment), assuming near-perfect sensors or fixed uncertainty across actions, we explicitly model the observation uncertainty conditioned on different object appearances within the FOV. To solve the POMDP, we deploy Partially Observable Monte Carlo Planning (POMCP)~ silver2010monte . To address the variation of the observation model in different deployment environments and UAV states, we formulate the detection reliability with a Beta-Bernoulli conjugate model that allows us to incorporate prior knowledge about the observation uncertainty as well as update the model iteratively as we gather more experiences from the deployment scenarios. Additionally, we selectively deploy an ensemble of DNNs at a fixed scale, conditioned on belief concentration, to improve prediction and enable successful target search. Our proposed methodology is illustrated in Figure~ fig:ptz_framework . To evaluate our approach, we use a simulation environment~ bansal2025airtaxisim built in Unreal Engine that models realistic aerial scenarios, including cluttered urban landscapes, varying altitudes, camera attributes (Field of view, focal length, and aperture control), and dynamic lighting. This environment enables thorough testing of the proposed framework, allowing us to study the effect of uncertainty, limited observability, and PTZ camera control against the baselines. Our key contributions are: We formulate the PTZ camera operation, by a high-altitude UAV searching for a sparse ground target, as a POMDP. We formulate the observation model uncertainty as a Beta-Bernoulli conjugate model, conditioned on the object appearance, with a prior assignment. We deploy POMCP to solve the POMDP that sequentially selects the informative actions for environmental exploration. Within the POMCP implementation, we integrate our defined observation model and selectively deploy ensemble detection to enhance reasoning when belief concentration is already high. Finally, we validate our method in a photo-realistic simulation environment to show the confident discovery of the targets with significantly fewer steps, with minimal dependency on camera resolution, compared to traditional tiny-object detection methods. title: What Builds the Scene? Luminance Dominates Geometry Formation in 3D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Standard 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) learns geometry and appearance jointly from RGB supervision, making it difficult to isolate how luminance and chroma contribute to the learned representation. We study this by training models under different channel supervision, freezing their non-appearance parameters (position, scale, rotation, and opacity), and re-estimating appearance with the same solver before comparing held-out reconstruction. Across eleven benchmark scenes with four independent runs each, geometry learned from luminance alone supports held-out reconstruction 0.085 dB below RGB-trained geometry on average. If chroma is deleted from a trained model, a sufficiently expressive solver can re-fit it on the frozen geometry to the original quality or slightly better. Higher-order spherical harmonics contribute much more reconstruction quality to luminance than to chroma, improving PSNR by 1.44 dB versus 0.19 dB on average, although on mirror-like surfaces hue does still change with viewpoint. The luminance advantage is even larger when geometry is being formed. Chroma-only supervision produces geometry 3.9-5.5 dB worse than luminance-only supervision after the same appearance solve; densification explains part of this gap. Overall, geometry formation in standard 3DGS is strongly luminance-dominated but not luminance-exclusive, and much of the chromatic appearance can be recovered after spatial support has formed.

Introduction sec:intro Standard RGB optimization in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233d combines two roles of the image signal: building the scene and coloring the scene. A standard degree-3 model represents appearance with 16 spherical-harmonic (SH) coefficients per color channel, or 48 appearance coefficients per Gaussian. Because SH evaluation is linear in its coefficients, these appearance parameters can be re-expressed under a linear change of color basis. For example, YCbCr separates the image signal into one luminance-like channel, \(Y\), and two chromatic channels, \(Cb\) and \(Cr\). Yet these appearance parameters are not learned independently of scene structure. Standard 3DGS jointly optimizes Gaussian positions, scales, rotations, opacities, and SH coefficients against the same image-space reconstruction loss, while densification and pruning are driven by statistics of that optimization. An RGB residual therefore does not reveal which part of the color signal caused the representation to form. A simple training intervention exposes this ambiguity. We withhold chromatic supervision during the first half of training and optimize using only \(Y\); \(Cb\) and \(Cr\) supervision are introduced later (Fig.~ fig:experimental_overview b). When chroma is released, held-out reconstruction quality rises sharply, yet the delayed schedules often converge near ordinary RGB training. This does not tell us why. Luminance may already have built the geometry, with chroma filling in appearance; alternatively, the later full-color phase may repair geometry left incomplete by luminance. A successful final reconstruction after delayed chroma therefore does not tell us which signal actually built the representation. Several results already point to a separation of these roles along the luminance--chroma axis. Monochromatic reconstruction followed by colorization shows that a useful spatial representation can be learned without observed chroma and colored afterward cheng2024colorizing,dhiman2025chromadistill,color3d2026 . Instant Colorization shows that appearance can be re-estimated on a fixed Gaussian representation without further geometric optimization lieber2026instant . LCD-GS and palette-based editing separate luminance-like and chromatic components explicitly, for HDR reconstruction and for appearance manipulation lcdgs2026,chao2026palette . GSICO, HiGS, and YUV-domain channel decorrelation show that higher-order chromatic SH can be pruned or coarsely quantized at little cost gsico2026,higs2026,sony2026decorrelation . Outside neural rendering, image coding has long subsampled chroma and geometric vision runs on intensity alone jpeg_chroma_subsampling,sift,colmap . Together these results establish feasibility: structure can exist without observed chroma, color can be fitted after geometry exists, and chromatic appearance can be stored compactly. Natural-image statistics supply a prior for what to expect. In natural images, luminance carries most of the spatial detail and contrast, while the chromatic channels are smoother and lower in amplitude ruderman1998statistics,mullen1985contrast . That prior predicts that luminance should matter more for geometry. It does not tell us how much worse chroma-only training will perform, or how much of that gap comes from densification, the process that adds Gaussians during training. We test whether the gap persists when both conditions keep the same set of Gaussians. We also measure how much chroma can be fitted on fixed geometry and how much each channel group benefits from view-dependent SH terms. These prior methods do not establish what chromatic supervision contributes to geometry learned during RGB training. Nor do they measure how changing when observed chroma enters the loss affects the learned geometry. The Delayed-Chroma result shows that final reconstruction quality alone cannot distinguish the possible explanations. To separate them, we freeze Gaussian position, scale, rotation, and opacity after training and apply the same full degree-3 appearance solve \(A^*\) to each geometry (Fig.~ fig:two_arm_setup ; Sec.~ sec:luminance-geometry ). This measures the reconstruction each geometry can support after appearance is re-estimated under the same conditions. Throughout, geometry means the non-appearance parameters of the model, including opacity, and every model starts from the SfM initialization provided with its dataset. Our claims therefore concern reconstruction of the captured benchmark images after standard 3DGS optimization and densification from that initialization; they do not concern the physical accuracy of its surfaces, and they do not concern geometry formed without a spatial prior. We combine this comparison with fixed-geometry chroma recovery and the SH-capacity sweep (Sec.~ sec:appearance-capacity ), and with direct changes to channel supervision (Sec.~ sec:channel-geometry ). All experiments use BT.601 YCbCr and the eleven-scene 3DGS benchmark unless stated otherwise. 1.~Geometry trained on luminance alone supports nearly the same reconstruction as RGB-trained geometry. After the same appearance solve, validated in contribution 4, with four independent runs per condition on every scene, the average difference in held-out PSNR is dB, a small advantage for RGB (95 CI ). Eight of eleven scenes fall inside the dB band we set before the comparison. The three outliers are , , and , where RGB-trained geometry keeps an average advantage of -- dB over four independent runs. At seed 0, SSIM moves in the same direction by , and LPIPS slightly favors luminance-trained geometry on average while favoring RGB-trained geometry on two of the three departure scenes. Controls for Gaussian count, appearance basis, and solver iteration budget support this interpretation in the tested settings. 2.~Luminance provides most of the signal for learning geometry. On three scenes, geometry trained on chroma alone supports -- dB less reconstruction than geometry trained on luminance alone. Part of this gap comes from densification, because chroma produces smaller positional gradients and therefore fewer new Gaussians. However, when both conditions start from the same Gaussians with densification turned off, chroma-only geometry is still -- dB worse. Chroma does still affect geometry. Giving each training view the chroma of another view, while leaving luminance unchanged, lowers reconstruction by -- dB, and the drop appears in all four adversarial seeds. This effect is consistent but much smaller than the effect of removing luminance. 3.~Higher-order SH matters far more for luminance than for chroma. Removing SH degrees 1--3 lowers held-out PSNR by dB for luminance but only dB for chroma on average, and luminance loses more on every benchmark scene. In linear terms, held-out MSE rises by for luminance and for chroma. The same ordering holds on specular scenes. This does not mean that chroma is view independent. On the chrome ball, measured directly from the ground-truth views, chromaticity changes substantially with viewpoint. 4.~Chroma can be fully re-estimated on fixed geometry. We remove the chroma from trained RGB models and re-estimate it from the training images with the geometry frozen. Recovery rises from with a single scene-wide tint to with coupled degree-3 fitting, where matches the trained model. Most of the chroma loss seen with simpler solves therefore comes from the solver, not from the geometry. Because this solve recovers appearance fully, we use it to compare geometries trained under different supervision without carrying over the appearance each model learned. 5.~Delayed chroma follows the same asymmetry. Withholding chroma for the first half of training preserves final quality on two of three replicated scenes and costs dB on . When chroma is introduced, quality rises sharply, and the rise moves with the release time rather than with other training events such as the end of densification. When training continues from the same luminance-only checkpoint, adding chroma improves the reconstruction the final geometry supports by about dB, which matches the RGB advantage measured in the main comparison. The pattern largely holds in an independent 3DGS implementation and in BT.709, YCoCg, and YIQ. Together, these results show that luminance provides most of the signal for learning geometry that supports reconstruction, and most of the benefit of view-dependent appearance. Chroma plays a smaller role in forming geometry, and most of its appearance can be fitted afterward with little higher-order SH. However, the asymmetry is not absolute. Chroma can still change the learned geometry, RGB-trained geometry keeps an advantage on three scenes, and view-dependent chromatic reflections can require higher-order chromatic SH. Related Work sec:related The distinction between luminance and chroma has appeared in several areas of 3D reconstruction and Gaussian Splatting. It has been used for monochromatic reconstruction and colorization, appearance editing, progressive training, and compression. These works provide useful evidence about what can be learned from luminance alone and how chromatic appearance can be represented after training. They do not directly measure what chroma contributes while standard RGB-supervised 3DGS learns its geometry. ChromaDistill dhiman2025chromadistill studies a similar problem primarily with Plenoxels and also reports a 3DGS variant in its supplementary material. In that variant, the model is trained with luminance alone, and chroma is introduced through knowledge distillation from an image colorization model. title: WBAG: A Whole-Body and Attached-Geometry Safety Framework for Vision-Language-Action Manipulation
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have demonstrated impressive capabilities in generalizable robotic manipulation, but their deployment in the real world remains challenging due to potential collisions involving different parts of the robot, manipulated objects, and the surrounding environment. Existing inference-time VLA safety frameworks typically rely on simplified end-effector-centered representations that do not explicitly model the full articulated robot and attached-object geometry. In this paper, we present WBAG, a safety framework that models the robot's whole-body and grasp-dependent attached geometry. WBAG constructs a grasp-conditioned safe set that adapts the protected geometry as objects are grasped, then converts this evolving geometry into differentiable CBF constraints that minimally modify the VLA's native six-dimensional operational-space action for collision avoidance across robot, scene, and attached geometry. On the SafeLIBERO benchmark, a variant of LIBERO augmented with obstacles for safety evaluation, WBAG achieves the best overall safety and safe task success among the evaluated methods under a scene-level safety evaluator that monitors all eligible non-task objects, reaching 97.38\% aggregate Scene Safety and 59.38\% Safe Success.

Existing inference-time VLA safety frameworks typically rely on simplified end-effector-centered representations that do not explicitly model the full articulated robot and attached-object geometry. In this paper, we present WBAG, a safety framework that models the robot's whole-body and grasp-dependent attached geometry. WBAG constructs a grasp-conditioned safe set that adapts the protected geometry as objects are grasped, then converts this evolving geometry into differentiable CBF constraints that minimally modify the VLA's native six-dimensional operational-space action for collision avoidance across robot, scene, and attached geometry. On the SafeLIBERO benchmark, a variant of LIBERO augmented with obstacles for safety evaluation, WBAG achieves the best overall safety and safe task success among the evaluated methods under a scene-level safety evaluator that monitors all eligible non-task objects, reaching 97.38 aggregate Scene Safety and 59.38 Safe Success. Introduction Vision-language-action (VLA) models map visual observations and language instructions directly to robot actions across diverse manipulation tasks pi05 , but their task-level generalization does not provide an explicit geometric safety model to consistently safeguard robot motions. In cluttered environments, a VLA action may move the end effector toward the target while causing an upstream link, wrist, gripper, or manipulated object to collide. The relevant collision geometry spans the articulated robot and changes when the robot grasps an object. Recent benchmark evaluations further show that task completion alone can obscure physical safety violations during manipulation~ fan2026safevlabench,cui2026liberosafety . Control-theoretic safety methods, particularly control barrier functions (CBFs), provide a principled mechanism for enforcing collision avoidance during robotic control ames_cbf_qp . CBFs constrain control inputs to maintain forward invariance of a prescribed safe set, but their effectiveness depends on how that set is represented. For geometric collision avoidance, the safety function must capture separation between the protected robot geometry and surrounding obstacles. The geometric representation therefore determines which collision modes can be enforced. Recent work on safety-critical control with VLA-based policies safevla,vlsa_aegis,knows,english2026neurosymbolic,sinaei2026barrier spans both training-time and inference-time interventions. SafeVLA safevla incorporates safety constraints during policy optimization through constrained reinforcement learning. At inference time, AEGIS vlsa_aegis combines perception-derived geometric information with CBF constraints to filter a pretrained VLA, while KNOWS knows combines VLA-based target identification with online obstacle tracking. Other methods enforce safety directly within flow-matching action generation. Recent work in~ english2026neurosymbolic apply predictive trajectory-level barrier constraints through minimum-norm corrections during iterative denoising, while~ sinaei2026barrier modify the flow-matching dynamics using an aggregate CBF over the generated action chunk. However, existing inference-time safety frameworks typically enforce collision avoidance using simplified end-effector-centered geometry vlsa_aegis,knows, english2026neurosymbolic . Such end-effector-centered representations do not explicitly model the full articulated robot or the rigid geometry of an attached object: the end effector may remain separated while an upstream link, wrist, or attached geometry collides with an obstacle. Geometric methods such as Bernstein-polynomial signed distance fields (BP-SDFs) bpsdf provide smooth, differentiable representations of object geometry, enabling efficient distance queries and gradients that are well suited for optimization-based control. For articulated robots, BP-SDFs can represent individual links, whose poses are determined by forward kinematics as a function of robot configuration. Recent work geometry_cbf employs BP-SDFs to construct geometry-aware CBFs from the minimum distance between robot and obstacle geometries and derive corresponding safety constraints on the robot control input. Applying such geometric safety constraints to VLA manipulation requires connecting perception, manipulation state, and the policy's native action interface. In our setting, scene and target geometry are reconstructed from RGB-D observations rather than assumed known, while the protected geometry changes when the target becomes rigidly attached after grasping. At the same time, the resulting link- and object-level clearances are functions of robot configuration, whereas the frozen VLA produces six-dimensional operational-space actions. These factors must therefore be coupled so that perception-derived, grasp-conditioned geometric constraints can be enforced directly on the VLA action without retraining the VLA or modifying the operational-space controller. In this paper, we introduce WBAG, a whole-body and attached-geometry safety framework for pretrained VLA policies. WBAG reconstructs scene and target geometry from RGB-D observations and constructs a grasp-conditioned safe set: before grasping, it protects the articulated robot; after grasping, the protected set expands to include the rigidly attached object. We represent robot, scene, and attached geometry with differentiable BP-SDFs and enforce the resulting CBF constraints directly on the VLA's native six-dimensional operational-space action. WBAG minimally modifies the policy output while accounting for collisions involving the whole robot and attached geometry, without retraining the underlying VLA or modifying the operational-space controller. We evaluate WBAG on SafeLIBERO using a scene-level safety evaluator that monitors all eligible non-task scene objects. WBAG achieves the highest aggregate Scene Safety and Safe Success among the evaluated configurations, reaching \(97.38 \) and \(59.38 \), respectively. Our main contributions are summarized as the following: We formulate a grasp-conditioned geometric CBF over articulated robot links and dynamically attached geometry, with the protected set adapting across pre- and post-grasp manipulation. We develop WBAG, a novel perception-to-control safety framework that reconstructs scene and target geometry from visual observations, maintains grasp-conditioned protected geometry, and enforces the resulting constraints directly on the VLA’s native operational-space action without retraining the VLA or modifying the operational-space controller used to execute its actions. We conduct a controlled SafeLIBERO evaluation with scene-level safety measurement that isolates the effects of scene coverage, whole-body protection, and attached-geometry modeling on safe VLA manipulation. title: Experience-Based Feasibility-Aware Generative Adversarial Imitation from Observation under Embodiment Mismatch
summary: With the increasing use of robot-free demonstration interfaces that provide state trajectories without action labels, imitation from observation has become a promising approach for learning robot behaviors from human demonstrations. However, due to differences in embodiment and dynamics between humans and robots, demonstrated human motions may not be feasible for the robot, potentially degrading policy performance. In this study, we propose Experience-Based Feasibility-Aware Generative Adversarial Imitation from Observation (EF-GAIfO), which estimates the feasibility of state-only demonstrations from the robot's own experience rather than relying on explicit dynamics models or large prior exploration datasets. A key feature of EF-GAIfO is that the notion of feasibility evolves with policy learning: as the policy improves and the robot experiences a broader range of state transitions, the feasible region is progressively expanded, allowing additional demonstrations to be incorporated into learning. This enables feasibility-aware imitation that adapts to the current stage of policy learning, rather than relying on a pre-designed feasibility criterion. We validate the effectiveness of EF-GAIfO on a locomotion task in simulation and on a real quadruped robot performing a object-reaching-and-grasping task.

Introduction In recent years, imitation learning approaches using human demonstrations collected through robot-free demonstration interfaces have attracted increasing attention. Several approaches have been proposed, ranging from purely video-based ones young2021visual to those based on external infrastructures ohkawa2026yubi, sasaki2026robotic , and those based on self-contained onboard tracking ha2025UMI, shafiullah2023bringing . Such interfaces allow users to provide demonstrations through their own hand movements without directly teleoperating a robot. However, demonstrations collected through such interfaces typically consist of state trajectories without corresponding robot action labels. Imitation from Observation (IfO) torabi2018bco, torabi2019 , which learns policies from state-only demonstrations, is therefore a suitable framework for utilizing such data. However, due to an embodiment mismatch between humans and robots, demonstrated state transitions collected via robot-free demonstration interfaces are not necessarily feasible for the robot. Such demonstrations may contain state transitions that cannot be reproduced under the robot's embodiment. If these demonstrations are directly used for IfO, the learned policy may be influenced by robot-infeasible motions. Consequently, the learned policy may be encouraged to reproduce robot-infeasible motions, potentially resulting in falls or degraded task performance. To reduce the influence of infeasible demonstrations, model-based approaches evaluate whether demonstrated motions are feasible for the robot using a robot dynamics model takahashiICRA2025, chen2025 . These methods predict the feasibility of demonstrated motions using known or learned robot dynamics models. However, whole-body dynamics are strongly coupled, and contact interactions and balance constraints must also be considered. Therefore, constructing an accurate dynamics model is not straightforward. These limitations motivate a different approach to feasibility estimation: rather than explicitly modeling, what the robot can do, we infer feasibility from what it has actually experienced (Fig. fig:motivation ). During policy learning, the robot continuously generates state transitions that are physically realizable under its embodiment, providing direct evidence of feasible motion. We therefore use this experience distribution as an embodiment-specific reference: demonstration transitions well supported by the robot's experience are likely to be feasible, without requiring an explicit dynamics model. In this study, we propose Experience-based Feasibility-aware Generative Adversarial Imitation from Observation (EF-GAIfO). EF-GAIfO estimates the feasibility of state-only demonstration transitions using experience data collected during GAIfO-based policy learning and reduces the influence of demonstrations with low estimated feasibility. For feasibility estimation, we train a state-transition reconstruction model using the robot's experience data and evaluate demonstration transitions based on their reconstruction error. The estimated feasibility is incorporated into the discriminator objective as a weight, allowing the policy to preferentially imitate demonstration transitions that are supported by the robot's experience. We evaluate the proposed method through experiments in a point-mass environment and a quadruped robot environment. Related Work Imitation Learning from Observation Unlike behavior cloning, which uses state-action pairs, imitation from observation aims to learn from demonstrations consisting only of state sequences or visual observations. A possible approach to learn, despite the absence of expert actions, consists of inferring the missing actions through a learned inverse dynamics model that maps state transitions to actions torabi2018bco . Another approach to infer the missing action involves learning a latent action space directly from state observations that will be later aligned to the true action space using a small number of environment interactions edwards2019imitating . Liu et al. liu2018imitation , instead, translate a demonstrator's raw video observations into the imitator's own context, enabling imitation in scenarios where the demonstrator's viewpoint or environment configuration is not the same as that of the imitator. A separate line of work extends adversarial imitation learning to observation-only settings by matching distributions over state transitions instead of state-action pairs torabi2018gaifo , using a Wasserstein formulation to handle rough or partial demonstrations li2023agile , an inverse dynamics disagreement objective yang2019imitation , or off-policy reuse of past interactions to improve sample efficiency zhu2020off . Previous methods for learning from observation mainly focus on observation-only or partial demonstrations, but they do not fully address the feasibility problem caused by differences between the demonstrator and the robot. When the demonstrator and the robot have different physical capabilities, some observed transitions may be difficult or impossible for the robot to reproduce. In contrast, this work introduces an experience-based feasibility estimation mechanism to reduce the influence of robot-infeasible transitions during imitation learning. Imitation Learning from Imperfect and Infeasible Demonstrations In practical imitation learning, demonstration data are not always optimal, clean, or suitable for the robot. Demonstrations may contain suboptimal actions, mistakes, noisy trajectories, or motions that cannot be executed by the robot. To address imperfect demonstrations, several studies have investigated methods for estimating the quality or confidence of demonstration data. A common approach is to downweight low-quality demonstrations by estimating a per-sample confidence or quality score, either by using a subset of explicit confidence labels wu2019imitation , or by adding a negative-risk term to counteract bias toward frequently occurring state-action pairs liu2025pn . In offline settings, one can distinguish expert from non-expert data without environment interaction, using cooperative discriminator training xu2022discriminator or importance-sampling-weighted behavior cloning li2023imitation . Another popular approach consists of ranking the demonstrations by quality to extrapolate reward functions that can surpass the best available demonstration brown2019extrapolating , an idea later extended to incorporate the generator's own experience into the ranking process shi2024ranking . Wang et al. wang2021learning , instead, learn per-demonstration weights directly within the adversarial imitation learning framework. A paradigm more related to the proposed method, even though less explored, is feasibility-aware imitation learning, which considers whether demonstrated motions are executable by the imitator. Existing work addresses mismatched dynamics between demonstrator and learner cao2022learning , the question of whether to follow potentially non-reproducible behavior lee2020selective , and the estimation of feasibility for demonstrations collected via hand-mounted interfaces, using either a robot dynamics model takahashiICRA2025 or multimodal visual and haptic feedback takahashi2026multimodal . These methods focus on demonstration quality, require confidence labels, rely on explicit or learned robot dynamics models, or use prior robot execution data. In contrast, the proposed method estimates demonstration feasibility from state transitions collected online during policy learning. This enables the policy to reduce the influence of robot-infeasible demonstrations without requiring confidence labels, an explicit dynamics model, or a separate prior exploration dataset. Therefore, this work focuses on experience-based feasibility estimation for IfO with demonstrations that may contain robot-infeasible motions. Generative Adversarial Imitation Learning from Observation (GAIfO) The objective of GAIfO torabi2018gaifo, torabi2019 is to learn a policy that can reproduce the state-only demonstrations using reinforcement learning. In GAIfO, the policy is trained using a discriminator to estimate similarity between its behavior and the demonstration data. title: CtrlWAM: Controllable World Action Models with Aligned Intent and Foresight
summary: World action models (WAMs) jointly predict actions (intent) and visual future (foresight). Standard training adds noise to recorded actions and video simultaneously, but such training paradigms introduce a mismatch: perturbed actions imply counterfactual future visual, while the noised video remains tied to the GT recording. In low-noise regime, the scene geometry and even the dynamic behavior remain clearly visible from the noisy future frames despite the added noise. We present CtrlWAM, which executes perturbed actions in a simulator and pairs them with their noised visual consequences for joint WAM learning. To accommodate the different denoising requirements of video and actions, we introduce warped video--action noise schedules that aim to keep visual layout responsive as action predictions evolve. We further extend the action interface from ego-only control to a variable number of agent streams, allowing a unified model to represent predicted or commanded futures for multiple agents. Driving experiments show more accurate action forecasts, closer agreement between generated video and actions, and better following of supplied commands; robotics experiments show stronger motion fidelity and controllability. Matched controls support the benefit of off-path renders for command following and manipulation fidelity. Together, these findings contribute to a more controllable world action model. Project page: https://ctrl-wam.github.io/

Project page: Introduction sec:introduction World action models (WAMs) jointly predict an embodied agent's future actions (intent) and their visual consequences (foresight)~ zhu2025uwm,ye2026world . The imagined video should therefore remain consistent with the consequences of predicted actions. In unified models such as Cosmos~3~ agarwal2026cosmos3 , which perform both joint prediction and forward dynamics (action-conditioned video generation), this intent--foresight alignment is essential in both modes. r 0.42 fig:moti However, current training procedures do not explicitly preserve this alignment during denoising. Methods such as DreamZero~ ye2026world independently corrupt the recorded actions and video with Gaussian noise~ ho2020denoising . Perturbing the actions in this way does not change the motion depicted in the video: the corrupted video remains tied to the recorded future, even when the perturbed actions would produce a different trajectory. The model is thus trained to recover the paired clean targets, but it receives no explicit supervision on the physical correspondence between its intermediate action and video states. This gap matters because useful visual structure can emerge early in denoising. DIDO~ lyu2026dido observes that static scene structure forms before gripper--object dynamics are fully resolved. In its four-step video-model ablation, conditioning the action expert on first-step representations already achieves 97.7 success on LIBERO, compared with 98.4 after all four steps. These findings suggest that intermediate visual predictions already provide substantial information for action generation, which motivates closer attention to their physical consistency with the evolving action estimates. Without explicit alignment, an intermediate action estimate could veer toward an obstacle while the imagined video still depicts a safe pass (Figure~ fig:moti ). We introduce for physically aligned denoising in world action models. Its central idea, aligned noising, pairs each action perturbation with its visual consequence to construct physically corresponding training inputs (Figure~ fig:teaser ). Specifically, a simulator executes the perturbed actions and renders the resulting observations, and we use RoboTwin~ chen2025robotwin for manipulation and AlpaSim~ alpasim_2025 for driving. We then add noise to the rendered video and train the model to recover the recorded actions and video at the corresponding timestamps. These paired inputs provide a physically grounded training signal for flow matching~ lipman2023flow . Learning from these pairs also requires choosing how much visual evidence to expose at each stage of denoising. Video and actions can be assigned separate noise levels~ chen2024diffusionforcing and can therefore follow different noise schedules~ guo2026unified . Our preliminary inspection suggests that the video layout can stabilize and enter detail refinement while the action estimates are still changing (Figure~ fig:denoising_misalignment ). This observation motivates warped video--action noise schedules. By assigning video a higher noise level than actions, we aim to keep the video layout responsive to evolving action predictions, and then let it settle into detail refinement as the actions approach convergence. In interactive scenes, the future also depends on the behavior of other agents. A driving scenario, for example, may leverage a neighboring vehicle's maneuver in addition to the history ego trajectory for the action prediction. We therefore introduce structured multi-agent conditioning, which extends the ego action stream to a variable number of additional agents. Conditioning masks specify which futures are predicted and which are supplied as commands. This interface supports both joint multi-agent prediction and action-conditioned generation, and it reduces exactly to the ego-only model when no other agents are present. We evaluate on autonomous driving~ alpasim_2025 and bimanual manipulation~ chen2025robotwin . In driving, we assess action forecasting, video--action consistency, and adherence to supplied commands. In manipulation, we assess motion fidelity and video quality. In summary, our main contributions are as follows: [leftmargin=1.5em,itemsep=2pt] Physically aligned noising, which pairs perturbed actions with their simulator-rendered visual consequences and trains the model to recover the recorded actions and video, providing physically corresponding inputs for video--action denoising. Warped video--action noise schedules, which assign video a higher noise level than actions, aiming to keep the video layout adaptable while actions evolve and to shift toward detail refinement as they stabilize. Structured multi-agent conditioning, which extends the ego action stream with streams for additional agents, so that each agent's future can be either predicted to improve the ego-prediction or supplied as a command to enhance the controllability. Related Work sec:related Unified World Action Models Joint video--action models learn action prediction and visual dynamics within a shared generative model. The Unified World Models (UWM) framework couples video and action diffusion within one transformer zhu2025uwm . The Unified Video Action (UVA) model learns a joint latent representation with separate video and action decoders li2025uva . Both support policy learning and forward or inverse dynamics through flexible conditioning. VideoVLA and DreamZero adapt pretrained video generators for joint prediction of actions and visual futures in robotic control shen2025videovla,ye2026world,yuan2026fast . Controllable World Models Controllable world models condition visual futures on commands, actions, or scene structure. In robotics, action-conditioned video prediction supports model-predictive planning finn2017foresight , while Genie learns latent actions for interactive generation from unlabeled videos bruce2024genie . GAIA-1 uses video, text, and action inputs to steer driving scenarios hu2023gaia , while DriveDreamer learns structured traffic constraints for controllable generation wang2023drivedreamer . Vista supports controls ranging from high-level commands and goal points to trajectories, steering angles, and speeds gao2024vista . sec:method Physically Aligned noising sec:aligned-training A recorded action--video pair specifies how the two modalities agree at the clean endpoint. It does not specify how they should deviate together from that endpoint as noise is added. For example, noising an action trajectory produces a different ego camera path, implying a different visual future, yet adding Gaussian noise to the recorded video does not reflect this change (Figure~ fig:moti ). Aligned noising instead constructs an action perturbation and its visual outcome as a paired training input (Figure~ fig:teaser ). This gives the model physically related evidence in both modalities as it learns to recover their shared recorded future.
