Discussion and limitations app:discussion The experiments assess generated futures and offline open-loop metrics. Self ADE measures video--action consistency, Rollout ADE measures direct forecasting accuracy, and Cmd ADE/FDE measure agreement with supplied commands through an IDM. Most robotics metrics also rely on external models. Both the evaluation is heavily dependent on the used models, leading to a risk of the model bias. Limitations. The aligned noising pipeline requires a simulator to execute perturbed actions and render their consequences. The multi-agent extension is limited to driving because we lack suitable dynamic robotics datasets with actor-level action--observation pairs. We expect future real--sim--real workflows to enable reconstruction of multi-agent interactions, generation of controlled variations, and transfer of learned behavior back to real environments, making multi-agent prediction and control in robotics feasible.

title: Is Success All You Need? Investigating the Impact of Input Perturbations on VLA Behaviour in Tabletop Manipulation Tasks
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved high task success rates on robot manipulation task benchmarks. More recently, there has been an emphasis on evaluating the robustness of VLA models to perturbations. However, this robustness is still predominantly measured through Task Success Rate (TSR). In this work, we propose a benchmark-agnostic evaluation framework to measure the behavioural robustness of models by characterising how successful trajectories are executed under perturbation. We implement this methodology by extending the widely-used LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. Across three state-of-the-art VLA models, four LIBERO task suites and seven perturbation conditions, we evaluate changes in both typical successful behaviour and its variability, including metrics of motion smoothness, efficiency and gripper behaviour. We find that perturbations can alter the behaviour of successful trajectories, a phenomenon which cannot necessarily be inferred from TSR alone. Across LIBERO suites, we identify cases where state-of-the-art VLA models achieve comparable TSR under the same perturbation condition, yet behaviour on successful trajectories diverges substantially. Therefore, to have a more robust assessment of task performance, we argue that suitable measures of robustness should capture not only whether a task is completed, but also how the robot behaves while completing it. When evaluating the robustness of VLA models, TSR may be complemented by behavioural evaluation metrics that characterise the nature and variability of successful task execution by robots.
full_text: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved high task success rates on robot manipulation task benchmarks. More recently, there has been an emphasis on evaluating the robustness of VLA models to perturbations. However, this robustness is still predominantly measured through Task Success Rate (TSR). In this work, we propose a benchmark-agnostic evaluation framework to measure the behavioural robustness of models by characterising how successful trajectories are executed under perturbation. We implement this methodology by extending the widely-used LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. Across three state-of-the-art VLA models, four LIBERO task suites and seven perturbation conditions, we evaluate changes in both typical successful behaviour and its variability, including metrics of motion smoothness, efficiency and gripper behaviour. We find that perturbations can alter the behaviour of successful trajectories, a phenomenon which cannot necessarily be inferred from TSR alone. Across LIBERO suites, we identify cases where state-of-the-art VLA models achieve comparable TSR under the same perturbation condition, yet behaviour on successful trajectories diverges substantially. Therefore, to have a more robust assessment of task performance, we argue that suitable measures of robustness should capture not only whether a task is completed, but also how the robot behaves while completing it. When evaluating the robustness of VLA models, TSR may be complemented by behavioural evaluation metrics that characterise the nature and variability of successful task execution by robots. INTRODUCTION Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models brohan2023rt1roboticstransformerrealworld have emerged as a prominent paradigm in robotics, with the ability to map visual observations, natural language instructions and proprioceptive states directly to motor commands. Building upon large-scale pre-trained Vision-Language Models (VLMs), VLAs have progressed rapidly in recent years, demonstrating generalisation to unseen objects and language instructions brohan2023rt2visionlanguageactionmodelstransfer, black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel . Such models have shown strong performance across robotic tasks, including tabletop manipulation intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld, wu2026vlanextrecipesbuildingstrong, kim2025finetuningvisionlanguageactionmodelsoptimizing . More recently, increasing attention has been given to the robustness of VLA models, which have shown brittleness to environmental variations such as altered scene lighting and visual distractors liberoplus, liberopro . A number of works investigate this by introducing perturbations to the evaluation data, along dimensions including scene lighting and language instruction liberoplus, liberopro, morgan2026colosseumv2benchmarkinggeneralization, guo2026robustvlarobustnessvisionlanguageactionmodel . However, this robustness is typically measured by binary task success rate (TSR). Focussing primarily on TSR enables straightforward comparison; however, it may obscure other critical failures which aren't captured by this binary outcome alone rabanser2026scienceaiagentreliability, wang2026roboevalroboticmanipulationmeets . In their work on AI agent reliability, Rabanser et al. argue that once agents are deployed in the real world, they will inevitably face environmental perturbations, but that "robust agents should maintain comparable performance despite such perturbations" rabanser2026scienceaiagentreliability . We argue that, for embodied AI systems, the notion of comparable performance should account for the fundamentally embodied nature of the application. The decisions and control outputs of embodied AI agents translate into physical actions, which can have significant real-world consequences Roy2021FromML . Beyond binary TSR alone, behavioural metrics may more suitably reflect the deployability of VLA models. We consider a number of such metrics. The jerkiness of the trajectory may be important, as large acceleration changes can lead to higher mechanical stress and manipulator wear 10610437, 7069580 . Behavioural metrics also matter from a human acceptability perspective. Sheidlower et al. 10.1145/3776734.3794505 found that task completion speed data, a marker of efficiency, was requested by users. Additionally, perceived reliability and predictability are central factors affecting trust alhaji2021trust , and unexpected behaviour from robots can degrade the trust that users may have in the technology lyons2023explanationsTrust . In addition to TSR, we argue for the inclusion of behavioural metrics, which we find can offer greater insight into the comparative robustness of VLA models. We identify a gap in the evaluation of VLA and embodied AI models. Work exists which either (i) evaluates the trajectory behaviour beyond binary task success, or (ii) measures robustness to perturbations using task success as the primary metric. To our knowledge, these two practices have not yet been combined. As a result, current robustness evaluation cannot determine whether a policy's behaviour has meaningfully degraded when it continues to complete a task successfully. Two policies may achieve identical success rates under perturbation, while exhibiting substantially different trajectory quality. A demonstrative example is given in Figure originalvsperturb . Motivated by this gap, we propose a framework for evaluating the behavioural robustness of VLA models under perturbation by calculating metrics of motion smoothness, efficiency and gripper behaviour, to complement TSR. With this evaluation framework, we aim to answer the following research questions: RQ1: How does the typical behaviour of successful trajectories change under input perturbation? RQ2: Are perturbation-induced behavioural changes reflected by changes in the TSR? RQ3: Do perturbations alter the behavioural consistency of successful trajectories? We implement this framework by extending the LIBERO libero and LIBERO-Plus liberoplus benchmarks. While we use these benchmarks as an experimental testbed given their wide adoption kim2025finetuningvisionlanguageactionmodelsoptimizing, liberoplus , the proposed behavioural evaluation is benchmark-agnostic and could be applied to other benchmarks, as long as trajectory-level state and action information can be retrieved (e.g. MetaWorld) yu2021metaworldbenchmarkevaluationmultitask . Thus, through this work, we: Propose a benchmark-agnostic behavioural evaluation methodology that complements task success rate with trajectory-level behaviour metrics, enabling practitioners to derive a more complete performance assessment of the robustness of VLA models, and implement it on the popular LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus benchmarks. The metrics comprise the duration, total gripper movement, Cartesian jerk, joint jerk, Cartesian path length, and joint path length observed for the trajectories. Characterise perturbation effects in terms of the change in typical behaviour and consistency of behaviour. Demonstrate that for state-of-the-art VLA models, robustness of task success does not necessarily equate to robustness of successful execution behaviour. Under perturbations, successful trajectories can change substantially even when task success is preserved. RELATED WORK Vision-Language-Action models Building on advances in large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (VLMs), Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models extend multimodal language modelling by predicting robot control actions from visual observations and language instructions brohan2023rt2visionlanguageactionmodelstransfer, driess2023palm . Early VLA approaches represented robot control actions as discrete tokens alongside natural language tokens brohan2023rt2visionlanguageactionmodelstransfer . OpenVLA is an open-source model which adopted token-based action representation, and used large-scale robot demonstration data for pre-training kim2024openvlaopensourcevisionlanguageactionmodel . More recent approaches have used continuous action representation and action chunking. OpenVLA-OFT kim2025finetuningvisionlanguageactionmodelsoptimizing replaces OpenVLA's discrete action representation with continuous action prediction, training using an L1 regression objective. Models in the family use flow matching for continuous action generation black2026pi0visionlanguageactionflowmodel, intelligence2025pi05visionlanguageactionmodelopenworld . The VLANeXt open-source model similarly uses a dedicated policy module with action chunking and flow matching, conditioned on learned representations from a VLM backbone wu2026vlanextrecipesbuildingstrong . These developments have enabled increasingly capable models, which has motivated efforts to more rigorously evaluate their behaviour and robustness. Evaluation of VLA models The focus on TSR We observe that the majority of widely used benchmarks for evaluating the performance of embodied AI models emphasise the overall task success rate (TSR). See Table tab:evalembodied for a breakdown of this. Benchmarks include those in the LIBERO family (including LIBERO-Plus liberoplus and LIBERO-PRO liberopro ). The primary reported metric is the percentage of successful episodes, measured using task-specific goal logic. Other relevant robotic manipulation benchmarks include RLBench james2019rlbenchrobotlearningbenchmark , CALVIN mees2022calvinbenchmarklanguageconditionedpolicy , RoboCasa nasiriany2024robocasalargescalesimulationeveryday , MetaWorld yu2021metaworldbenchmarkevaluationmultitask and MolmoSpaces-Bench kim2026molmospaces . These benchmarks vary in terms of which skills are being evaluated and task complexity, however a commonality is that binary task success rates are reported. A number of works propose behaviour quality metrics beyond TSR, which can largely be grouped into metrics focussing on safety and metrics focussing on efficiency. In their RoboEval work, Wang et al. wang2026roboevalroboticmanipulationmeets propose computing and reporting on joint jerk, Cartesian jerk, self-collisions, environment collisions and object slips, arguing that evaluating TSR alone may conceal critical failures. Wang et al. wang2026roboevalroboticmanipulationmeets also propose the metrics of trajectory length, completion time, joint path length and Cartesian path length. In their BEHAVIOR benchmark srivastava2022behavior , Srivastava et al. incorporate a number of efficiency metrics, citing deployment infeasibility of policies which are overly inefficient. Specifically, they report on time taken, kinematic displacement (i.e., the displacement caused by an agent in the environment), logical disarrangement (i.e., the number of changes caused by the agent to the logical state of the environment), distance navigated (i.e., the accumulated distance travelled by the agent) and the displacement of hands (i.e., the accumulated displacement of each hand while manipulating objects). Introducing perturbations to measure robustness A number of works introduce perturbations to modify the evaluation data, and evaluate model robustness to distribution shift. Rather than evaluating models on tasks which are nearly identical to the training tasks, the LIBERO-Plus liberoplus benchmark introduces controlled perturbations along seven dimensions. These are the object layout, camera viewpoints, robot initial state, language instruction, lighting conditions, background textures and sensor noise. The authors find that, while several SOTA VLA models perform very well on the original LIBERO benchmark, under perturbations the performance of the models dropped substantially. Similarly, the LIBERO-PRO benchmark from Zhou et al. liberopro introduces variations along four dimensions: object attributes (e.g. colour, textures), initial configuration, task instruction, and environment (e.g. background, lighting). title: Completion Aware Guidance for World Action Models
summary: World Action Models (WAMs) predict visual futures and robot actions, yet they remain susceptible to task-incomplete imagination, where plausible, action-consistent predictions omit the transition needed for task completion. In this paper, we show that this failure is not inherent to the world model backbone, but emerges when adapted for short-chunk control, which can repeatedly favor plausible local continuations over task-completing transitions. To address this, we introduce Completion Aware Guidance (CAG), a training-free sampling method that guides generation toward task completion. Across representative WAMs, CAG improves success from 64% to 70% on a RoboTwin 2.0 subset and from 69% to 75% in zero-shot simulation, while reducing task-incomplete imagination from 79% to 40%.
full_text: Method Task-Incomplete Imagination. As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:overview , WAMs can repeatedly produce locally reasonable video-action continuations while failing to progress to the transition required for the next task phase. We refer to this failure as task-incomplete imagination; for example, the model may reach the target region yet continue holding the object instead of releasing it. Does this failure simply reflect a limitation of the underlying video diffusion backbone? Using the same video diffusion backbone, we compare its native generation horizon with the short chunk horizon used by the WAM. As shown in Fig.~ fig:result_summary (a), the native horizon produces the required completion event, whereas short-chunk autoregressive generation remains visually coherent but repeatedly omits it. This suggests that task-incomplete imagination is not an intrinsic limitation of the backbone, but arises from its adaptation to short-horizon control generation as follows: 1.4 ! lcc Task & DreamZero~ ye2026world & CAG \\ Cube to Bowl & 90 & 92 \\ Can to Mug & 60 & 72 \\ Banana to Bin & 56 & 60 \\ 0.17 1.4 Here, denotes the observation at time , the robot action, the language instruction, the proprioceptive state , the native video-generation horizon, and the WAM chunk horizon. Once the task reaches a completion-relevant phase, the WAM must select the required transition within a short horizon . However, a holding or hovering continuation can remain locally plausible and compatible with the instruction, providing no explicit preference for realizing the completion in the current chunk. Repeated generation can therefore defer the required transition. This raises the central question: how can we guide short-horizon generation to include the completion required by the current task phase? Completion Aware Guidance. Our algorithm, Completion Aware Guidance (CAG), tackles task-incomplete imagination as an elicitation problem. The video diffusion backbone represents the task-completing transition specified by the instruction, but short-horizon control can favor a plausible continuation that preserves the pre-completion state. CAG biases this selection toward a continuation that completes the current manipulation phase while remaining close to the WAM prior . title: ActiveWAM: Evidence-Aware Active Vision for World-Action Models
summary: Active vision manipulation requires a policy to control both its camera and its end-effectors, yet camera motion determines which evidence remains visible within finite observation windows. Acquiring a new view can displace task-critical cues, while retaining a view forgoes potentially useful observations. We formulate this as an evidence-aware retain--acquire problem and present ActiveWAM, a unified world--action model that learns observation and manipulation jointly. To this end, we propose training-time inversion which constrains a frozen video prior by task-bearing source evidence and visible temporal changes, eliminating the need for test-time inversion or candidate ranking. At deployment, the policy generates bimanual and pan/tilt actions-including stay and reacquisition behaviors-from view-aware history, and updates context from newly measured RGB observations. Future-video prediction serves as a co-training signal, while action generation requires neither future-video decoding nor optimal viewpoint annotations. We introduce RoboTwin-AV, a 50-task benchmark with executable pan/tilt control and automatically generated demonstrations. ActiveWAM improves TAVIS out-of-distribution success by up to 17.0 percentage points over the strongest baselines, achieves 20.0 additional points over Fast-WAM on RoboTwin-AV, and outperforms it by 26.7 points on real-world physical kitchen tasks.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiment Experimental questions Our experimental evaluation is organized around four central questions. (Q1) Does task-guided inversion preserve task-relevant evidence across view changes? (Q2) Do learned observation actions improve over fixed or rule-based control? (Q3) What roles do video co-training and paired learning play? (Q4) Can the system compose multi-stage physical tasks with acceptable efficiency? Benchmarks and Experimental Setup sec:data TAVIS~ tavis2026 provides native Head/Hands trajectories with 96 test episodes per task, seed, and split. Its pose-OOD condition perturbs end-effector positions ( \,cm) and neck yaw/pitch ( ) to test spatial robustness. We extend RoboTwin~2.0~ robotwin22025 with synchronized RGB observations and executable pan/tilt control across all 50 tasks, creating RoboTwin-AV. To generate active-vision demonstrations, we implement a gaze collector that uses instance masks and rendered depth to compute waypoints, with a 0.06-rad stay deadband to avoid unnecessary head motion. Collector-privileged inputs (masks, depth) are withheld at test time; success evaluation follows native task predicates. We train on 100 successful trajectories per task and evaluate on 100 test episodes per task, seed, and condition (clean, appearance, initial-head-pose, compound). Train/test splits are created before temporal windowing, and failures or timeouts are retained in the test set. Figure~ fig:tasks illustrates representative simulated and physical task sequences. For simulation results, each configuration is tested under three different seeds. Baselines and additional benchmarks We compare against per-task baselines (ACT~ act2023 , Diffusion Policy~ dp2023 ) and per-suite methods ( ~ pi02024 , Fast-WAM, EasyWAM-Unified). For fair comparison, all re-implemented baselines use identical RGB inputs, head--arm action interfaces, and native success predicates. Published benchmark scores (LIBERO~ libero2023 , LIBERO-Plus~ liberoplus2025 ) are reported separately with their native interfaces. Training and metrics We fine-tune DiT modules and the 16-token adapter where VAE, text encoder, and video prior are frozen. The policy receives nine RGB frames at resolution. For ablation studies, control experiments match the full training recipe except the ablated component, with head trajectories held consistent across matched conditions. Main Benchmark Comparisons sec:standard_results sec:active_results Results on TAVIS On TAVIS, ActiveWAM improves over the strongest listed baseline by up to 17.0 percentage points (Table~ tab:main_benchmarks ). The gains are pronounced under pose-OOD conditions: +13.0/+10.6\,pp on Head tasks and +12.0/+11.0\,pp on Hands tasks for GR1T2/Reachy2, respectively. These results show higher task success under end-effector and camera pose perturbations. We examine the contributions of history inversion and observation control through the controlled comparisons below. To characterize gaze timing, we measure gaze--action lead time on Head ID tasks. Mean lead times are 0.75\,s (GR1T2) and 0.78\,s (Reachy2), with 97 of gaze actions classified as valid (878 and 763 successful episodes, respectively). Results on RoboTwin-AV On RoboTwin-AV (Table~ tab:main_robotwin_av ), ActiveWAM achieves gains of +4.0, +14.4, +9.0, and +19.3 percentage points over the strongest listed baseline under clean, appearance, pose, and compound shifts, respectively. Under compound shifts, ActiveWAM exceeds Fast-WAM by 20.0 percentage points. It also achieves 53.3 1.5 success compared with 41.7 1.5 for the raw-history baseline. The matched ablations below examine which components contribute to this improvement. Fixed-camera generalization We also evaluate fixed-camera benchmarks to examine whether the training approach remains useful when the policy cannot move the camera. On LIBERO-Plus, ActiveWAM achieves 76.9 success compared with 68.2 for raw history, 72.5 for task-safe augmentation, and 71.9 for source-feature auxiliary supervision (Table~ tab:main_generalization ). On LIBERO, success is 98.7 compared with 98.4 for raw history. These results show an improvement on LIBERO-Plus while the reported LIBERO scores remain close. The interaction between inversion and head control is examined separately on RoboTwin-AV. Mechanism Validation and Control Experiments sec:history_results sec:interaction Retention--acquisition interaction We cross history inversion with active head control to examine whether their benefits depend on one another (Table~ tab:main_attribution ). Under compound shifts, success is 23.7 with neither component, 30.3 with inversion alone, 41.7 with head control alone, and 53.3 with both. The interaction estimate is approximately 5.0 percentage points, computed from the means displayed in the table. The corresponding estimates are approximately 1.6, , and 1.0 percentage points under clean, appearance, and pose conditions. This pattern suggests that inversion provides a greater benefit when head control is available under compound shifts. History inversion and evidence preservation Removing task or dynamic preservation reduces compound success by 12.3 and 8.6 percentage points, respectively (Table~ tab:main_mechanism ). ActiveWAM also outperforms framewise inversion using the same Wan prior, which achieves 43.5 success. These results support the contribution of task guidance and temporal preservation to control under compound shifts. Learned observation control and collector controls Table~ tab:main_active_view 's 20\,pp pose gain compares locked-camera to learned control, establishing the value of executable observation. Under an independently randomized collector, compound success remains 53 (42 raw); bounded external perturbations retain 51 . In 23 of successful compound episodes, the policy maintains a stable view for at least 0.5\,s while manipulation continues. The learned controller records 1.70\,rad of head travel per episode and 65 pose success, compared with 2.50\,rad and 61 for relation look-at with stay, and 4.10\,rad and 57.3 for object tracking (Table~ tab:main_active_view ). With matched RGB grounding, the learned controller reaches 62.7 pose success with 1.90\,rad of travel, compared with 61 and 2.50\,rad for relation look-at with stay. Controller diagnostics Under matched RGB grounding, the learned controller achieves 62.7 pose success compared with 57.3 for target centering (Table~ tab:behavior ). It also records higher co-visibility, lower head travel, and shorter timeout-capped reacquisition time, with values of 86.3 , 1.90\,rad, and 1.6\,s compared with 73.7 , 4.10\,rad, and 2.3\,s. The arms-busy result is evaluated on a separate TAVIS slice. The view oracle provides a reference result of 76.7 success. Prediction and paired-learning controls sec:prediction_control Table~ tab:main_attribution crosses video loss and inference mode. Video co-training improves matched joint graphs from 44.0 to 53.3 compound SR; separately trained action-only graphs reach 52.7 with video loss, 44.7 without. Thus video prediction is effective as a training signal but not required at test time. Decode-off diagnostics show zero action difference and 53 SR over ten evaluations. Equal-forward and pair-consistency removal underperform (Table~ tab:main_mechanism ). Composed Real-Robot Tasks sec:real_results sec:efficiency We deploy ActiveWAM on an AirbotPlay fixed-base dual-arm platform with a fixed focal Realsense D455 RGB camera on an IQR pan/tilt 2-DOF head. Each of three task segments composes two separately trained policies: (i) slicing—place cucumber horizontally, retrieve knife, then slice; (ii) egg frying—pour oil, crack egg while the left arm grasps the pan handle, then retrieve spatula and stir; (iii) mixing—pour cucumber and cooked egg, then retrieve spatula and stir-fry. Egg stirring retains the pan-handle grasp; stage switching is prescribed. Human inter-segment actions enter neither evaluation nor montage. Table~ tab:main_real reports Stage~1 and total-task success for the same 20 complete trials per task and method, yielding 60 trials per method and 300 trials across the five methods. ActiveWAM achieves 66.7 /50.0 Stage~1/total-task success, versus 60.0 /36.7 without inversion and 48.3 /23.3 for Fast-WAM. Deployment Efficiency and Failure Analysis sec:deployment On an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, action inference takes approximately 165\,ms. Action chunking yields an effective rate near 15\,Hz, while interpolation maintains 25\,Hz commands. ActiveWAM completes the full task in 30 of 60 physical trials. We review all 30 failed trials and assign each to one primary category: manipulation errors (12 trials, 40.0 ), premature termination (10 trials, 33.3 ), targets outside the pan/tilt camera's reachable field of view (5 trials, 16.7 ), and hardware issues (3 trials, 10.0 ). These percentages are calculated over the 30 failed trials. The categories describe the failure modes without establishing underlying causes.

title: World Motion Models: Flexible Sequence Modeling of SE(3) Trajectories
summary: Equipping artificial agents with spatial intelligence requires a comprehensive generative prior over the dynamic 3D world. We propose World Motion Models (WMMs) that capture "what was, is, and will be where across time" via sparse SE(3) pose trajectories. WMMs are built on the observation that elements of dynamic scenes can be well approximated by a set of rigid SE(3) trajectories, a minimal yet expressive primitive for 4D modeling. This representation unifies articulated objects, human bodies, hand-object interactions, piecewise-rigid scene dynamics, camera motion, and even robot states and actions into a single shared space. Given this representation, we cast the joint distribution of these entities as a flexible sequence modeling problem, utilizing flow-matching with per-token noise levels. Coupled with a context token mechanism for non-sequential conditioning, this formulation supports any-to-any marginal conditioning across an arbitrary number of entities and time steps. Tasks such as future prediction, motion infilling, model-predictive control, inverse kinematics, cross-embodiment retargeting, and policy learning all reduce to the application of different masks over the same network. Experiments on 6 diverse applications of 3D vision and robotics demonstrate the versatility and flexibility of WMMs with strong performance.

Introduction sec:intro The world that surrounds us is inherently three-dimensional and highly dynamic—a 4D space where perception and interaction are fundamentally tied to movement. Physical actions are achieved by moving limbs or end-effectors, generating forces that translate into the motion of objects, while other agents dynamically navigate and act within this same environment. As humans, we naturally develop a strong prior over these moving entities: we intuitively anticipate how others will move, plan the physical motions required to achieve a desired goal, and foresee the physical consequences of our own actions. To act and reason in the physical world, intelligent systems benefit from the same capability: a generative prior over the 4D world that captures the evolution of ``what'' and ``where'' across time. In this work, we present a unified generative model which provides a general prior over the dynamic 3D world. Our approach is highly flexible with minimal assumptions and handles unstructured scenes and arbitrary object categories. By supporting various prompting modes, a single model enables diverse inference tasks ranging from world modeling (e.g., action-conditioned/free future prediction) to complex planning (e.g., motion infilling, inverse dynamics). To build such a prior, we first need a unified representation that expresses the dynamic world in a physically grounded manner. Our insight is that complex, dense motion of the physical world can be compactly approximated by a sparse set of moving coordinate frames --- specifically trajectories. Most entities of interest naturally reduce to this format: the dense flow of thousands of mesh vertices on a human or robot collapses into tens of joint trajectories~ loper2015smpl,huang2026pointworld ; cameras and rigid objects track as single moving frames; and even non-rigid scene dynamics can be represented as interpolations of a small motion basis~ wang2024som,kratimenos2024dynmf,lei2024mosca . We therefore adopt the trajectory as our basic language for what is where across time. These trajectories subsume prior point trajectories in but can be far sparser, replacing, for instance, the flow of thousands of mesh vertices with the tens of joint poses of a SMPL human~ loper2015smpl or a robot~ huang2026pointworld . We further impose no category-specific structure: every entity is treated equally as a pose proxy, generalizing class-bound representations (SMPL~ loper2015smpl , MANO~ romero2017mano , URDFs) to any unstructured scene. It is also orthogonal to video-based world modeling~ blattmann2023svd,yang2024cogvideox,nvidia2025cosmos,assran2025vjepa2,zhou2024dinowm , which captures dynamics implicitly through color changes on a screen, entangling the underlying 3D motion with appearance, lighting, and viewpoint changes. In short, the trajectory provides a highly compact, physically grounded 3D abstraction for modeling arbitrary motion. The question now becomes: how do we learn a generative prior over these trajectories? Since motion naturally unfolds over time, this is inherently a sequence modeling problem. Traditionally, this is treated as a strictly causal task: a standard world model or dynamics model predicts future states conditioned on past history and actions. However, humans can perform non-causal inference as well, such as determining the actions required to achieve a specific goal (inverse dynamics) or planning intermediate motions between waypoints. The inference type varies widely across applications. To support these diverse inference schemes, we propose ( ), flow-matching generative models with per-token noise levels. Inspired by Diffusion Forcing~ chen2024diffusionforcing and discrete diffusion~ nie2025large,arriola2025blockdiffusion , treat each 6D pose at a given time step as an independent token, assign each its own noise level, and denoise the entire token field in a single shared forward pass. Once trained, a admits inference over arbitrary numbers of entities and time steps simply by dictating which tokens are clean (the condition) and which are noised (the prediction). Given past tokens, it acts as a future predictor ; applied to action tokens, it becomes a feed-forward policy ; and when both past states and actions are provided, it acts as an action-conditioned dynamics model supporting model-predictive control. Ultimately, realize any . By simply changing what is known, the exact same network transitions seamlessly between serving as a policy, an action prior, and a world model. While standard trajectory modeling assumes a strictly consecutive temporal horizon, many practical tasks require reasoning beyond it. For example, planning a complex interaction often relies on an abstract goal state situated arbitrarily far in the future. Similarly, tasks like cross-embodiment retargeting require inferring correspondences between trajectories, such as those of a human and a robot. Providing a few paired demonstration frames from outside the current episode serves as an in-context template that tells the model ``what is what.'' To support these non-consecutive anchors, we enhance the flexibility of by introducing a set of context tokens. Rather than being bound to the continuous physical timeline of the current episode, they are assigned to a decoupled context timeline with its own learnable positional embeddings. Mechanically, these context tokens are treated identically to real trajectory tokens, meaning they can seamlessly condition the model or be generated themselves. Together, this general formulation and our flexible sequence modeling enable to demonstrate broad versatility across applications, including robot policies and model-predictive control (MPC), scene future prediction, human-object interaction generation, and multi-embodiment humanoid retargeting (Sec.~ sec:exp:lt ), all with SOTA performance. Contributions. We propose a general formulation that uses the sparse trajectory as a unified representation for 4D world modeling. To learn a flexible generative prior over this space, we introduce , flexible flow-matching models with per-token noise levels. By supporting any-to-any marginal conditioning alongside a context token mechanism, deliver strong performance across diverse 3D vision and robotics tasks. sec:method Representation: A Language for Motion Modeling sec:method:representation aim to answer what was, is, and will be where across time. title: FlashDexRetarget: Accelerating Dexterous Manipulation Data Generation through Multi-Motion Retargeting
summary: Human hand-object demonstrations offer a reusable source of dexterous robot manipulation data, but transferring them across embodiments requires physically feasible retargeting. Existing physics-based approaches face limitations in retargeting success, motion-specific training efficiency, or both. To address these limitations, we introduce FlashDexRetarget, an RL-based framework for high-success, efficient dexterous motion retargeting. To make the demonstrated interaction easier to learn, we combine object point-cloud observations, hand-object distance features, and future trajectory encodings with complementary rewards that supervise object motion and reference hand-object relationships. To further accelerate learning, we employ separate left- and right-hand actor critic networks and adapt the off-policy algorithm, FlashSAC to dexterous motion tracking. On a benchmark of 50 motions spanning single-object and two-object interactions, FlashDexRetarget achieves a 90% success rate, approximately 2.5x that of the evaluated sampling-based baselines, while requiring up to 100x less training compute than the evaluated RL-based baselines. Evaluations on both XHand and Sharpa Wave Hand show consistent gains, and component-wise ablations examine the contributions of our design choices. Beyond the 50-motion benchmark, experiments with 200, 500, and 1,000 motions demonstrate that our method remains stable at larger scales and produces successful retargeted motions more efficiently as the training set grows. Qualitative replay results using real-world-captured demonstrations further illustrate the applicability of our framework to recorded human manipulation. Videos and code are available at https://davian-robotics.github.io/FlashDexRetarget/
full_text: [] #1 FlashDexRetarget at a glance. FlashDexRetarget converts collections of human hand-object demonstrations into physically grounded robot trajectories through multi-reference RL-based retargeting. Left and right hand policies are jointly trained across reference motions, avoiding repeated optimization for individual demonstrations, and successful rollouts are stored as robot data. The right plot shows cumulative conversion success rate versus total GPU hours on a logarithmic scale. CHORD results are obtained with its released implementation, which is trained with PPO~ schulman2017ppo . fig:main_figure ] Equal contribution. Corresponding author. Evaluations on both XHand and Sharpa Wave Hand show consistent gains, and component-wise ablations examine the contributions of our design choices. Videos and code are available at davian-robotics.github.io/FlashDexRetarget . Introduction Learning dexterous manipulation requires large amounts of robot interaction data. Human hand-object demonstrations~ liu2024taco,zhan2024oakink2,banerjee2025hot3d provide a promising source of such data, as diverse manipulation behaviors can be collected at scale without directly operating a robot. To use these demonstrations for robot learning, however, human motions must be translated into actions executable by a target robot hand. Physics-based retargeting addresses this issue by adapting human demonstrations to the morphology and actuation of the robot in simulation, while leveraging physical contact to reproduce the demonstrated object motion. To make large human motion datasets practical sources of robot data, retargeting must achieve high success at low compute cost. Existing physics-based retargeting methods adopt a single-reference formulation, optimizing each demonstration independently. Sampling-based methods~ paliwal2026dexterous,pan2025spider search directly over action sequences through simulated rollouts, but high-dimensional actions and long contact sequences make this search challenging under a finite simulation budget. RL-based methods~ zhu2026chord,li2025maniptrans,mandi2025dexmachina instead learn closed-loop policies to track the demonstrated hand-object interaction, but train a separate policy for each reference. Despite their difference in optimization strategies, both approaches retarget each demonstration independently, causing computational cost to grow linearly with the number of demonstrations. To avoid this repeated optimization, we study multi-reference tracking, where a single reference-conditioned policy is trained jointly across many demonstrations. By sharing learning across references, this formulation has the potential to amortize training cost over an entire dataset while retaining accurate tracking. Multi-reference tracking has been effective for humanoid whole-body motion~ luo2026sonic , but dexterous manipulation introduces additional challenges. First, object shapes and hand-object configurations vary across demonstrations, requiring the policy to distinguish interaction geometries. Second, reconstructed human demonstrations contain contact errors, making exact contact matching unreliable. Third, multi-reference training broadens the state distribution, increasing the need for model capacity and effective experience reuse. Finally, for bimanual motions, the two hands To address these challenges, we introduce FlashDexRetarget, an RL framework for multi-reference dexterous retargeting. First, we condition the policy on object geometry and future reference frames to distinguish diverse interactions across references. Second, we replace exact contact matching with distance-based interaction rewards to provide dense hand-object supervision despite imperfect contact reconstruction. Third, we adopt the off-policy learner FlashSAC~ kim2026flashsac and increase its replay and critic capacity to support learning across a broader multi-reference distribution. Finally, we use separate left- and right-hand actor critic networks to handle the and learning signals of the two hands. We evaluate FlashDexRetarget on 50 hand-object motions from TACO, OakInk2, and HOT3D~ liu2024taco,zhan2024oakink2,banerjee2025hot3d using XHand and Sharpa Wave Hand as target embodiments. Against sampling-based and RL-based baselines, we measure the fraction of successfully retargeted demonstrations as a function of total training compute. A single FlashDexRetarget policy retargets 90 of the benchmark using about 30 GPU-hours, compared with about 46 success at about 3,000 GPU-hours for CHORD~ zhu2026chord . This corresponds to approximately lower training compute and a improvement in retargeting success. Ablations examine how hand-object interaction objectives, off-policy training and capacity scaling, and left and right hand networks contribute to these gains in the multi-reference setting. We further show that the number of successfully retargeted trajectories continues to grow as the dataset scales. We also validate the retargeted trajectories through real-world replay. Our main contributions are: We introduce FlashDexRetarget, an RL framework that jointly retargets human hand-object demonstrations through multi-reference tracking with a single policy. We combine object point-cloud observations, hand-object interaction objectives, off-policy learning with larger replay and model capacities, and left and right hand actor-critic networks for joint dexterous tracking. We evaluate on 50 motions and two robot embodiments, achieving approximately lower training compute and percentage points higher success than CHORD, Related Work Human Hand-Object Interaction Data Human hand-object datasets cover diverse objects and manipulation behaviors. DexYCB provides annotated hand-object poses~ chao2021dexycb , while GRAB and OakInk capture grasping configurations and interaction geometry~ taheri2020grab,yang2022oakink . HOI4D and HOT3D extend this coverage to egocentric interactions~ liu2022hoi4d,banerjee2025hot3d , and TACO, OakInk2, and ARCTIC capture coordinated bimanual manipulation~ liu2024taco,zhan2024oakink2,fan2023arctic . GigaHands offers large-scale recordings of activities such as pouring, assembling objects, and playing cards~ fu2025gigahands . These datasets provide diverse manipulation experience for robot learning. However, these recordings capture human hands, so a robot cannot execute them directly, and kinematic retargeting is the common first step to close the embodiment gap. UniDex~ zhang2026unidex converts human hand-object trajectories into robot trajectories by solving fingertip inverse kinematics and adjusting the hand base by hand so that the retargeted fingers still appear to touch the object. VideoManip~ chen2026dexterous retargets human hand-object trajectories through keypoint matching and repairs the resulting contacts with contact optimization. In both, contact is imposed geometrically after the fact rather than produced by the robot hand acting on the object, so it is not guaranteed that executing the trajectory reproduces the demonstrated object motion. Retargeting must therefore be physics-based, Dexterous Retargeting from Human Demonstrations Kinematic and planning-based pipelines adapt human demonstrations to robot motions~ qin2023anyteleop,lakshmipathy2025kinematic,mu2026deximit,xin2026analyzing,Handa-2020-126758 , while physics-based optimization additionally accounts for hand-object contact dynamics in simulation~ liu2024parameterized,yang2025physicsgen . Within this physics-based setting, sampling-based methods search over simulated control rollouts~ deboer2005cem,williams2017mppi,howell2022predictivesampling to support dexterous planning~ li2025drop and demonstration refinement~ si2025exostart . For demonstration retargeting, SPIDER~ pan2025spider introduces temporary virtual forces between robot fingers and the object to guide annealed sampling toward trajectories that reproduce the demonstrated contacts. Building on this approach, Do as I Do~ paliwal2026dexterous incorporates hand-object reconstruction and physics-based refinement to retarget video demonstrations. Although these methods avoid training a tracking policy, they require a separate trajectory search for each reference, with effectiveness dependent on initialization and reference quality. Rather than searching trajectories directly, RL-based methods learn dexterous manipulation policies from human motion references and task objectives~ qin2022dexmv,chen2025objdex,li2025maniptrans,mandi2025dexmachina,lum2025human2sim2robot,yuan2025hermes,zhu2026chord,rajeswaran2017learning,feng2026minimalist . ManipTrans~ li2025maniptrans learns residual corrections to a pretrained hand-motion imitator, while DexMachina~ mandi2025dexmachina progressively reduces object assistance during training. CHORD~ zhu2026chord instead uses contact-wrench guidance to align human and robot object-motion capabilities. Although these methods replace trajectory search with policy learning, they still require separate training or adaptation for each demonstration. In contrast, FlashDexRetarget amortizes this cost by jointly learning hand-object tracking across demonstrations. Method Our goal is to efficiently generate a large number of physically grounded robot trajectories from an extensive collection of human hand--object demonstrations. Given a dataset of reference hand--object trajectories, where indexes the reference demonstration, contains the recorded human hand states and object poses at time , and denotes the trajectory length, Unlike single-reference retargeting, where a separate policy is optimized for each demonstration, we jointly train a reference-conditioned policy over the entire collection . During training, reference trajectories are sampled from and assigned to parallel simulation environments. At each step, the policy receives the current simulated state together with the next reference state: A policy predicts a robot action to track the reference object motion and hand--object interaction. The policy is optimized using tracking rewards defined from the resulting robot and object states. By sharing policy learning across demonstrations, our formulation enables efficient conversion of large reference collections. title: Affine-Aligned Atlas for Canonical Gaussian Construction in Video Representation
summary: Gaussian splatting has recently emerged as an efficient representation for images and videos due to its explicit structure and fast rendering capability. Existing Gaussian-based video representations often decompose a video into canonical Gaussians and temporal deformation. However, when a video contains large global motion such as camera movement, the canonical representation may become misaligned with individual frames, increasing the burden on the temporal deformation model. In this paper, we propose an affine-atlas canonical Gaussian representation, which constructs canonical Gaussians in a larger affine-aligned atlas space. Frame-wise affine transforms absorb global motion before canonical Gaussian construction, reducing the gap between the canonical representation and target frames. Since the proposed method only modifies the canonical construction stage, it can be integrated into existing canonical-Gaussian-based methods with negligible additional parameter cost. Experiments show that our method improves reconstruction quality especially for sequences with large camera motion.
full_text: Affine-Aligned Atlas for Canonical Gaussian Construction in Video Representation Gaussian splatting has recently emerged as an efficient representation for images and videos due to its explicit structure and fast rendering capability. Existing Gaussian-based video representations often decompose a video into canonical Gaussians and temporal deformation. However, when a video contains large global motion such as camera movement, the canonical representation may become misaligned with individual frames, increasing the burden on the temporal deformation model. In this paper, we propose an affine-atlas canonical Gaussian representation, which constructs canonical Gaussians in a larger affine-aligned atlas space. Frame-wise affine transforms absorb global motion before canonical Gaussian construction, reducing the gap between the canonical representation and target frames. Since the proposed method only modifies the canonical construction stage, it can be integrated into existing canonical-Gaussian-based methods with negligible additional parameter cost. Experiments show that our method improves reconstruction quality especially for sequences with large camera motion. Video representation, Gaussian splatting, canonical Gaussian, affine transform Introduction Video representation aims to express video data in a compact form while preserving reconstruction quality. Neural video representations encode videos into network parameters~ chen2021nerv,li2022nerv,chen2023hnerv, zhang2024boosting, yan2024ds, hayami2025sr , but their decoding process requires repeated neural network inference. Recently, Gaussian splatting has attracted attention as an explicit and efficient representation due to its fast rasterization capability~ kerbl20233d . This idea has also been extended to image and video representation~ zhang2024gaussianimage,zhang2025image, tai2025eigengs, takabe2026contour, sun2024splatter, bond2025gaussianvideo, liu2025d2gv, lee2025gaussianvideo, pang2025gsvr, lin2026stgv . Compared with purely neural representations, Gaussian-based methods have explicit parameters and can be rendered efficiently, making them suitable for high-speed video decoding. Many recent Gaussian-based video representation methods adopt a canonical-Gaussian-based formulation, where canonical Gaussians are constructed for a short temporal segment, i.e., a group of pictures (GOP), and a temporal model predicts frame-dependent deformation. This design is effective because it separates shared spatial structure from temporal variation, reducing redundant per-frame Gaussian parameters. Therefore, the quality of the canonical Gaussians plays a central role in both reconstruction accuracy and representation efficiency. However, when a video contains camera motion or large rigid motion, frames in the same GOP may not be well aligned. The canonical Gaussians must then represent multiple shifted appearances in a single coordinate space, and the temporal deformation model must compensate for a large gap between the canonical representation and each target frame. This can reduce representation efficiency and make temporal modeling more difficult. To address this issue, we propose an affine-atlas canonical Gaussian representation. Instead of constructing canonical Gaussians directly in the original frame coordinate space, we introduce a larger atlas space and align GOP frames using frame-wise affine transforms. By absorbing global motion during canonical Gaussian construction, the proposed method reduces the discrepancy between the rendered canonical representation and the target frames. The proposed method only modifies the canonical construction stage and can therefore be integrated into existing canonical-Gaussian-based methods such as D2GV~ liu2025d2gv , GSVR~ pang2025gsvr , and STGV~ lin2026stgv . In summary, our method improves canonical construction for motion-intensive sequences with negligible additional parameter cost. Related Work Neural Video Representation Neural video representation methods encode videos into neural network parameters and reconstruct frames through network inference~ chen2021nerv,li2022nerv,chen2023hnerv, zhang2024boosting, yan2024ds, hayami2025sr . These methods demonstrate that videos can be represented compactly by exploiting spatial and temporal redundancy. However, decoding requires repeated neural network inference for each frame, which can become a bottleneck when high decoding speed is required. In contrast, Gaussian-based representations use explicit primitives and rasterization, which can provide faster rendering. Gaussian Splatting for Images and Videos Gaussian splatting represents visual content using Gaussian primitives and enables efficient rasterization~ kerbl20233d . This idea has been extended to compact 2D image representation~ zhang2024gaussianimage,zhang2025image, tai2025eigengs, takabe2026contour , video representation~ sun2024splatter, bond2025gaussianvideo, liu2025d2gv, lee2025gaussianvideo, pang2025gsvr, lin2026stgv and 4D representation~ wu20244d, yang2024deformable, yang2024real, katsumata2024compact, li2024spacetime, luiten2024dynamic, chen2026pcgs . As illustrated in Fig.~ fig:categories , Gaussian-based video representation methods can be categorized into three types according to how they model temporal variation. The first category explicitly parameterizes temporal changes of Gaussian attributes~ sun2024splatter, bond2025gaussianvideo, katsumata2024compact , which directly controls Gaussian motion but may require frame-dependent parameters or temporal coefficients. The second category represents videos using spatio-temporal Gaussian structures~ smolak2025vegas,shah2026gaussian , which directly model temporal continuity but can make representation and optimization more complex. The third category uses canonical Gaussians and temporal deformation~ liu2025d2gv, pang2025gsvr, lin2026stgv, lee2025gaussianvideo , where shared spatial structure is represented by canonical Gaussians and temporal variation is modeled by a deformation field or network. This design is particularly attractive for video representation and compression because it separates shared spatial content from temporal variation. Canonical-Gaussian-Based Video Representation Among Gaussian-based video representations, canonical-Gaussian-based methods are closely related to our work. D2GV~ liu2025d2gv first fits 2D Gaussians to all frames in a GOP as a single canonical image and then learns temporal deformation using an MLP. GSVR~ pang2025gsvr follows a similar strategy but uses a hybrid deformation field consisting of triplane grids and polynomial motion. STGV~ lin2026stgv introduces spatio-temporal hash encoding for efficient temporal modeling. These methods demonstrate the effectiveness of the canonical Gaussian plus deformation framework. However, when frames in a GOP are not well aligned due to global motion, the canonical space can become suboptimal, increasing the burden on temporal deformation. Therefore, how to construct canonical Gaussians is a key factor for achieving efficient and accurate video representation. This motivates our affine-atlas formulation, which improves the canonical construction stage by absorbing global motion before temporal deformation. Proposed Method Overview We propose an affine-atlas canonical Gaussian representation for efficient video representation. As shown in Fig.~ fig:overview , the proposed method constructs canonical Gaussians in a larger atlas space instead of directly optimizing them in the original frame coordinate space. Each frame in a GOP is associated with a frame-wise 6-parameter affine transform, and the frames are aligned in the atlas space before canonical Gaussian construction. This design allows global motion, such as translation, rotation, and scaling, to be absorbed before canonical Gaussian construction. After this construction stage, each baseline temporal deformation model is applied without modification. Affine-Atlas Canonical Space Let a GOP contain frames . Conventional canonical-Gaussian-based methods construct a canonical Gaussian set directly from these frames or a single key frame in the original frame coordinate space. In contrast, we define a larger atlas space that covers the affine-aligned regions of all frames in the GOP. Each frame is associated with an affine transform matrix , which maps coordinates in the atlas space to coordinates in the frame space. These affine transforms are precomputed, fixed during optimization, and used to project atlas Gaussian positions into each target frame coordinate system. The canonical Gaussian set in the atlas space is represented as where denotes the center position of Gaussians in the atlas space, denotes its covariance matrix, denotes color, and is the number of Gaussians. For each frame , we define a frame-wise canonical Gaussian set projected from the atlas as The projected position is computed by the precomputed affine transform where \( _t = [ _t _t]\) maps the atlas coordinates to the frame coordinates. In the implementation, the affine transform is applied only to Gaussian positions, while the covariance and color are shared from the atlas Gaussian set. By using this transform, the same atlas Gaussian can more consistently explain corresponding regions across multiple frames under global motion. Canonical Gaussian Construction Given the precomputed affine transforms, the objective of canonical Gaussian construction is to optimize the atlas Gaussian parameters so that the rendered images match the target GOP frames after the affine transform. Let denote the Gaussian rasterizer. For frame , the rendered frame is obtained as The reconstruction loss is defined as where is an image reconstruction loss such as an L2 loss. Through this optimization, the atlas Gaussians are encouraged to represent the shared content of the GOP in an aligned coordinate system. During the following temporal modeling stage, is further deformed by the baseline deformation model before final rendering. Compared with conventional canonical construction, the proposed formulation reduces the gap between the canonical representation and each target frame. Since global motion is handled by affine transforms, the subsequent temporal deformation model can focus more on residual local motion and appearance changes. Experiments Experimental Setup We conduct experiments on Big Buck Bunny~ roosendaal2008big and the UVG dataset~ mercat2020uvg . For Big Buck Bunny, we use 132 frames with a resolution of . For the UVG dataset, we use a spatial resolution of and temporally subsample each sequence by a factor of five. Each video sequence is divided into GOPs of 10 frames, and each GOP is reconstructed independently. This setting follows the common video representation pipeline, where canonical Gaussians and temporal deformation are optimized for each GOP. We evaluate the reconstruction quality using PSNR and MS-SSIM. We compare each baseline method with its affine-atlas variant: D2GV, GSVR, and STGV are evaluated with and without the proposed canonical Gaussian construction. In all variants, only the canonical construction stage is replaced, while the temporal modeling component of each method is kept unchanged. For the affine-atlas variants, frame-wise affine transforms are precomputed using ORB feature matching. We estimate a two-dimensional affine transform between adjacent frames and compose them to obtain frame-wise transforms within each GOP. The estimated affine matrices are fixed during training and are not optimized as learnable parameters. We also use the average translation magnitude of the adjacent-frame affine transforms as the global motion magnitude for sorting UVG sequences in Table~ tab:uvg_results . title: ChunkVLA-AM: Parallel Action Chunking for Vision-Language-Action Robot Control in Additive Manufacturing
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language understanding, and action generation, offering new opportunities for automation in additive manufacturing (AM). However, deployment in AM remains challenging because adapting these models to unseen robot embodiments is costly, and performance can degrade under environment changes. In this work, we present a framework for deploying OpenVLA-OFT on a FAIRINO FR3 robot in a fixed AM workcell. A data pipeline converts monocular real-world demonstrations into OpenVLA-compatible TFDS/RLDS datasets to support adaptation to the FR3 embodiment. At runtime, each inference request predicts an eight-step chunk of 7-D actions. The FR3 executes each chunk open loop before capturing a new observation, providing closed-loop feedback between chunks. The system uses a cloud-edge architecture in which the FR3 client streams observations to a remote inference server through a FastAPI interface. In 42 physical A-to-B object-transfer trials, evenly split between red and blue targets, the system succeeded in 39 (92.9%). All three failures occurred during final placement, when insufficient release-height control caused the object to topple. An illumination sweep identified a low-error luminance range of 85-125 on a 0-255 scale, with the lowest mean spatial error at 95.
full_text: ChunkVLA-AM: Parallel Action Chunking for Vision-Language-Action Robot Control in Additive Manufacturing Zhugang Liu \\ zhugang.liu01@utrgv.edu Kaichuang Zhang \\ kaichuangzhang@usf.edu Jinman Zhang \\ jinman.zhang01@utrgv.edu Pu Sun \\ psun9932@sdsu.edu Martha Asare \\ martha.asare01@utrgv.edu Jose Hernandez \\ jose.hernandez112@utrgv.edu Maxim Ermolinsky \\ maxim.ermolinsky01@utrgv.edu Efren Saenz \\ efren.saenz01@utrgv.edu Qi Lu \\ qi.lu@utrgv.edu Jinghao Yang \\ jinghao.yang@utrgv.edu Department of Computer Science, The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley \\ Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, The University of Texas Rio Grande Valley \\ Department of Electrical Engineering, University of South Florida \\ Department of Computer Science, San Diego State University \\ Corresponding Author Vision–language–action (VLA) models unify visual perception, language understanding, and action generation, offering new opportunities for automation in additive manufacturing (AM). However, deployment in AM remains challenging because adapting these models to unseen robot embodiments is costly, and performance can degrade under environment changes. In this work, we present a framework for deploying OpenVLA-OFT on a FAIRINO FR3 robot in a fixed AM workcell. A data pipeline converts monocular real-world demonstrations into OpenVLA-compatible TFDS/RLDS datasets to support adaptation to the FR3 embodiment. At runtime, each inference request predicts an eight-step chunk of 7-D actions. The FR3 executes each chunk open loop before capturing a new observation, providing closed-loop feedback between chunks. The system uses a cloud–edge architecture in which the FR3 client streams observations to a remote inference server through a FastAPI interface. In 42 physical A-to-B object-transfer trials, evenly split between red and blue targets, the system succeeded in 39 (92.9 ). All three failures occurred during final placement, when insufficient release-height control caused the object to topple. An illumination sweep identified a low-error luminance range of 85–125 on a 0–255 scale, with the lowest mean spatial error at 95. . vision-language-action model, additive manufacturing, robot manipulation, action chunking, OpenVLA Introduction Additive manufacturing (AM) has become an important production paradigm for rapid prototyping, customized medical devices, aerospace components, and high-value industrial parts~ Gibson2021AM,Ngo2018AMReview,DebRoy2018MetalAM . Beyond deposition itself, practical AM workflows require inspection, part retrieval, build-plate handling, post-processing, and occasional intervention after process failures. These operations can expose human operators to process-specific risks: fused deposition modeling (FDM) may emit ultrafine particles and volatile organic compounds during heated thermoplastic extrusion~ Stephens2013UFP,Azimi2016FDMEmissions , while selective laser melting (SLM) involves fine metallic powders and particulate-matter hazards~ Chen2020MetalAMHazards . Robotic automation is therefore attractive for AM workcells because it can improve repeatability and reduce human exposure during inspection, transfer, and failure response. However, conventional rule-based robot programs are difficult to reuse across different printers, robot platforms, camera configurations, lighting conditions, object poses, and defect types such as FDM warping, inter-layer delamination, SLM porosity, lack-of-fusion holes, and cracks~ Zhang2006FDMFEM,Jin2020InterlayerAI,Zhang2017SLMDefects . Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a possible route toward more flexible AM robotic systems. By mapping visual observations and natural-language task descriptions directly to robot actions, VLA policies can represent tasks such as ``retrieve the printed part,'' ``inspect the warped edge,'' or ``move the build-plate sample to the cooling area'' without requiring a separate perception pipeline and a handcrafted state machine. Recent systems including RT-1, RT-2, Open X-Embodiment, and OpenVLA have shown that large-scale robot datasets, vision-language backbones, and action-token prediction can support general manipulation and transfer across tasks and embodiments~ Brohan2022RT1,Brohan2023RT2,OpenXEmbodiment2023,Kim2024OpenVLA . This capability is relevant to AM because the robot must interpret both the visual manufacturing context and the language instruction while generating manipulation commands within a constrained workspace. Despite this potential, transferring a VLA model to an AM workcell is not a straightforward model-deployment problem. The first difficulty is migrating demonstrations and action interfaces across robot platforms. Robot datasets often differ in image resolution, observation structure, sampling rate, episode organization, coordinate frames, state definitions, and gripper conventions. Their action spaces may also represent joint positions, joint velocities, absolute Cartesian poses, or relative end-effector motion. Even when two platforms expose action vectors of the same dimension, the individual elements may have different physical meanings, units, ranges, or normalization rules. RLDS and TFDS provide a common structure for organizing episodic robot data, but they do not by themselves resolve these embodiment-specific differences~ Guadarrama2021RLDS,TFDS . As a result, transferring an existing VLA pipeline to a platform such as the FAIRINO FR3 requires more than renaming dataset fields. Coordinate transformations, action semantics, gripper commands, and normalization statistics must all be defined consistently before the model can be trained and safely deployed. The second difficulty is robustness to changes between the demonstration environment and the deployed AM workcell. Lighting intensity, illumination direction, camera exposure, background clutter, camera viewpoint, and object pose may vary between data collection and execution. Reflective build plates, dark polymer parts, shadows cast by the robot, and changes in printer illumination can further alter the visual appearance of the part and the gripper. These variations are especially relevant when the model is adapted using demonstrations collected under a fixed camera and lighting configuration. Because a VLA policy predicts actions directly from image observations, it may associate the required motion with incidental visual features of the training environment instead of the task geometry. A policy that succeeds under the original lighting condition may therefore become less reliable when the workcell appearance changes, even though the physical task remains the same. In this work, we present ChunkVLA-AM, a reproducible OpenVLA-OFT-based deployment pipeline for FR3-based AM post-print retrieval. To make embodiment adaptation explicit, we construct a conversion pipeline that transforms monocular FR3 demonstrations, Cartesian end-effector states, binary gripper commands, language instructions, and episode metadata into OpenVLA-compatible TFDS/RLDS episodes. The pipeline defines the coordinate frames, action semantics, and normalization procedure required by the target FR3 system, while LoRA is used to avoid full-parameter fine-tuning. For robot control, we adopt a horizon- action-chunk interface and use in the reported physical tests, allowing the model to predict short-horizon motion sequences in a single request. The FR3 client then applies action denormalization, workspace clipping, unsafe-action rejection, and chunk-wise replanning after execution of the returned actions. This implementation focuses on the system-level adaptation and deployment required to use an action-chunked VLA policy in a fixed AM workcell and to evaluate its behavior under changes in lighting and object pose. Related Work sec:related Vision-Language-Action Models for Robot Control Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged from the broader trend of connecting language, perception, and embodied decision making. Early generalist and language-conditioned robot systems, including Gato, SayCan, PaLM-E, and VIMA, showed that multimodal representations can support instruction following, planning, and interactive manipulation across diverse tasks~ Reed2022Gato,Ahn2022SayCan,Driess2023PaLME,Jiang2022VIMA . More recent VLA policies such as RT-1, RT-2, Open X-Embodiment, and OpenVLA further demonstrate that large-scale robot datasets and vision-language backbones can be used to predict robot actions directly from images and natural-language instructions~ Brohan2022RT1,Brohan2023RT2,OpenXEmbodiment2023,Kim2024OpenVLA . These studies provide the main methodological foundation for applying VLA models beyond household or tabletop manipulation. However, their evaluation settings are still largely centered on general manipulation benchmarks, leaving manufacturing-oriented scenarios comparatively underexplored. Robotic Automation in Additive Manufacturing Additive manufacturing (AM) has been widely studied as a flexible production technology for customized, lightweight, and high-value components~ Gibson2021AM,Ngo2018AMReview,DebRoy2018MetalAM . Robotic systems have also been introduced into AM workflows for material handling, inspection, deposition assistance, post-processing, and large-scale or wire-arc manufacturing~ Ding2015WireArcAM . Compared with conventional automation, AM workcells pose distinctive perception and decision-making challenges because part geometry, surface appearance, thermal history, defect morphology, and process state can vary significantly across builds. Defects such as warping, delamination, porosity, lack of fusion, and cracking further require robots to reason over visual manufacturing evidence instead of simply replaying fixed trajectories~ Zhang2006FDMFEM,Jin2020InterlayerAI,Zhang2017SLMDefects . These characteristics make AM a natural application domain for VLA models: language can specify task intent, visual input can capture part and process context, and action prediction can support flexible intervention. Challenges of Applying VLA Models to AM Although VLA models are promising for AM, existing literature suggests two major barriers to practical use. The first is data and adaptation cost. AM tasks are weakly represented in large robot-learning datasets, while effective VLA adaptation requires demonstrations that align visual observations, language instructions, action labels, and episode structure in reusable formats such as TFDS/RLDS~ Guadarrama2021RLDS,TFDS . Full fine-tuning of large VLA models can be expensive and data-hungry, motivating parameter-efficient adaptation methods such as LoRA~ Hu2022LoRA . The second challenge is achieving temporally coherent motion. Single-step autoregressive prediction can accumulate covariate shift and produce open-loop drift during precise manipulation. Prior work on action chunking and horizon-based visuomotor policies shows that predicting multiple future actions as a structured sequence improves motion consistency~ Zhao2023ACT,Chi2023DiffusionPolicy . In AM settings, such temporal coherence must be balanced against responsiveness and safety, because robot motions often occur near printed parts, build plates, tools, or process-sensitive regions. Therefore, the VLA--AM research gap is not only whether VLA models can represent AM tasks, but also how they can be adapted and executed with sufficient temporal stability for precise manufacturing intervention.
