title: GenCOPE: Syn2Real Generalized Category-Level Object Pose Estimation for Robotic Picking
summary: Category-level object pose estimation (COPE), capable of generalizing to intra-class unknown objects, has become a core technique for robotic 3D scene understanding. However, existing COPE methods still require labor-intensive recollection of real-world training data for novel object categories, which limits their scalability in practical applications. This paper aims to achieve synthetic-to-real (Syn2Real) generalized COPE, where a model is trained solely on rendered synthetic data and directly generalized to real-world deployments. The central challenge lies in the significant domain gap between synthetic and real-world data, particularly in texture appearance. To address this, we aim to enhance domain generalization by learning domain-invariant representations that capture semantic commonalities among objects within the same category. We introduce 2D and 3D semantic consistency constraints to reduce the sensitivity of feature encoders to domain-specific features. In addition, we propose an end-to-end pose regression framework that performs 2D-3D cross consistency learning, leveraging dense cross-modality fusion to further refine pose estimation. Since simplicity and effectiveness are essential for real-world robotic deployment, our model operates exclusively on global features, yielding a highly lightweight and efficient architecture. Extensive experiments on the REAL275 and Wild6D benchmarks, as well as real-world robotic manipulation scenes, show superior Syn2Real generalization performance of our paradigm. Code and demos are released at https://paperreview99.github.io/GenCOPE/.
full_text: Category-level object pose estimation (COPE), capable of generalizing to intra-class unknown objects, has become a core technique for robotic 3D scene understanding. However, existing COPE methods still require labor-intensive recollection of real-world training data for novel object categories, which limits their scalability in practical applications. This paper aims to achieve synthetic-to-real (Syn2Real) generalized COPE, where a model is trained solely on rendered synthetic data and directly generalized to real-world deployments. The central challenge lies in the significant domain gap between synthetic and real-world data, particularly in texture appearance. To address this, we aim to enhance domain generalization by learning domain-invariant representations that capture semantic commonalities among objects within the same category. We introduce 2D and 3D semantic consistency constraints to reduce the sensitivity of feature encoders to domain-specific features. In addition, we propose an end-to-end pose regression framework that performs 2D-3D cross consistency learning, leveraging dense cross-modality fusion to further refine pose estimation. Since simplicity and effectiveness are essential for real-world robotic deployment, our model operates exclusively on global features, yielding a highly lightweight and efficient architecture. Extensive experiments on the REAL275 and Wild6D benchmarks, as well as real-world robotic manipulation scenes, show superior Syn2Real generalization performance of our paradigm. Introduction Nine-degrees-of-freedom (9DoF) object pose estimation, which aims to estimate the 3DoF translation, 3DoF rotation, and 3DoF size of an object in the camera coordinate system liu2026survey, NOCS, query6dof, GeoReF , is a fundamental problem in robotic 3D scene understanding and manipulation PhoCaL, HouseCat6D, LanCOPE, zhang2024omni6dpose, huang2025givepose, liu2026sinref6d . Early studies primarily focused on instance-level pose estimation DenseFusion, PVN3D, FFB6D, GDR-Net, yang2026occlusion , where models are restricted to objects seen during training. Alternatively, category-level object pose estimation (COPE) has emerged as a promising direction Synthesis, CR-Net, OLD-Net, BundleTrack, CATRE, AG-Pose, monodiff9d , as it enables generalization to intra-class unknown objects without relying on explicit prior information such as CAD models or reference views. Despite the impressive generalization capability of category-level approaches across unknown instances within the same category, existing methods still require labor-intensive collection and annotation of real-world training data for each novel object category mkpose, yang2026genhoi, ren2026compose, lin2026mempose . This requirement significantly hinders scalability and limits their practicality in large-scale robotic applications zhao2020sess, zhao2021few, yang2025rgb, geng2026disentangled . In contrast, recent advances in rendering technology have made large-scale synthetic data readily available, with accurate pose annotations obtained at negligible cost. Motivated by this observation, this paper aims to achieve Syn2Real domain-generalized COPE, referred to as GenCOPE, where models trained purely on synthetic data can be directly deployed in real world. The central challenge in GenCOPE lies in the significant domain gap between synthetic and real-world data. Through an analysis of the rendered synthetic data used for object pose estimation NOCS , we observe that the most pronounced discrepancy arises from texture appearance, as illustrated in Fig. Fig1 . However, existing methods primarily rely on feature extractors pspnet, ViT that emphasize fine-grained image features DPDN, IST-Net, miao2026langmap , which inherently encode substantial texture information while failing to explicitly capture domain-invariant properties shared between synthetic and real-world data. Consequently, the learned representations become overly sensitive to texture variations, making them suboptimal for robust Syn2Real domain-generalized pose estimation. To address the aforementioned challenge, we argue that although intra-class unknown objects exhibit substantial texture discrepancies between synthetic and real-world domains, their 2D and 3D semantic structures remain largely consistent. For instance, at the 2D level, objects such as bottles typically consist of semantic parts including a cap, a neck, and a base container. Similarly, at the 3D level, their geometric composition can be abstracted as a small neck cylinder, a transitional cone, and a large bottom cylinder. Based on this observation, we posit that explicitly incorporating semantic knowledge as constraints during 2D and 3D feature encoding can encourage encoders to focus on domain-invariant semantic cues, thereby suppressing the adverse effects of domain-specific features. An overview of the proposed GenCOPE is illustrated in Fig. Fig1 . Given a segmented RGB image and its corresponding point cloud (obtained via depth map back-projection) as inputs, we first perform feature embedding using the proposed 2D/3D semantic consistency encoders, followed by a 2D-3D cross consistency learning module and an end-to-end pose decouple decoder. During training, semantic consistency is enforced by leveraging semantic supervision derived from a pretrained large language model team2023gemini and the CLIP text encoder clip , which aligns the 2D and 3D feature representations in a shared semantic space. The resulting semantically consistent features are then fused through a 2D-3D cross transformer-based module to perform cross-consistency learning yang2022deepinteraction . Finally, the fused features are concatenated and fed into a pose decouple decoder to regress the full 9DoF object pose. To prevent feature extractors from overemphasizing fine-grained texture-dependent features while maintaining computational efficiency, we adopt the most lightweight backbones based on ResNet18 ResNet and PointNet PointNet as the 2D and 3D encoders, respectively, and operate exclusively on global features throughout the pipeline. This design is deliberately adopted to jointly enhance domain generalization robustness while meeting the real-time requirements of practical robotic manipulation scenarios. Overall, our main contributions are as follows: (1) We propose a simple yet effective framework for Syn2Real domain-generalized COPE, explicitly designed for real-world robotic deployment. The framework operates purely on global features from most lightweight backbones, avoiding dense local texture correspondences, making it highly efficient under resource-constrained settings. (2) We introduce semantic consistency encoders in both 2D and 3D spaces to learn semantic-invariant features shared across intra-class objects, alleviating the severe gap between synthetic and real-world domains. (3) We propose an end-to-end pose estimation pipeline based on 2D-3D cross consistency learning, featuring a cross-modal fusion network and a pose decouple decoder, enabling mutual reinforcement across modalities for more accurate and robust pose estimation. Related Work -Supervised COPE Methods. NOCS NOCS introduces a normalized object coordinate space formulation and establishes two widely adopted benchmarks that advance the research of COPE methods. To address substantial shape variability among intra-class objects, SPD SPD first leverages category-level CAD model libraries to extract shape priors offline and subsequently reconstructs NOCS representations through shape prior deformation for pose estimation. This paradigm has inspired a series of follow-up approaches that explicitly incorporate shape priors SGPA, centersnap, RBP-Pose, SSP-Pose . Despite their effectiveness in modeling intra-class shape variability, prior-based approaches rely on manually constructed category-level CAD model libraries, which incur substantial human effort. The limitation aforementioned has motivated the development of prior-free alternatives DualPoseNet, FS-Net, GPV-Pose, IST-Net, AG-Pose, GenPose, clipose, SpotPose, cleanpose . FS-Net FS-Net proposes a 3D graph convolution-based network and performs decoupled pose regression. GPV-Pose GPV-Pose enhances the learning of pose-sensitive features via geometry-guided point-wise voting. Beyond these depth-only approaches, several RGB-D methods IST-Net, VI-Net jointly leverage appearance and geometric cues. SecondPose SecondPose introduces DINOv2 DINOv2 to provide SE(3)-consistent semantic features for pose estimation. GCE-Pose GCE-Pose enhances COPE under partial visibility by reconstructing category-level global context via semantic shape reconstruction and fusing it with local RGB-D observations. CleanPose cleanpose mitigates data bias by integrating causal inference with front-door adjustment and residual-based knowledge distillation from 3D foundation models. Although these fully-supervised methods achieve competitive performance, their dependence on extensive real-world data annotation makes them difficult to scale to novel object categories. -Efficient COPE Methods. To alleviate the scalability bottleneck caused by extensive real-world data annotation, recent studies have explored label-efficient COPE CPPF, SAR-Net, Wild6D, SSC6D, DPDN, UDA-COPE, TTA-COPE, MH6D, diffusionnocs, Diff9D . CPPF CPPF introduces a category-level point pair feature voting formulation that enables pose estimation in the wild without dense supervision. SAR-Net SAR-Net investigates object shape alignment by directly matching the observed point cloud with shape prior, reducing the reliance on real-world training data. DPDN DPDN designs a domain-generalized learning framework based on parallel deep prior deformation. UDA-COPE UDA-COPE leverages a teacher-student self-supervised learning scheme to achieve domain adaptation. Further, TTA-COPE TTA-COPE proposes a test-time adaptation strategy that first learns from labeled synthetic data and then adapts the pretrained model online to real-world data during inference. More recently, DiffusionNOCS diffusionnocs adopts diffusion models to predict dense canonical maps for pose estimation, demonstrating strong robustness to symmetry and effective Syn2Real generalization. Diff9D Diff9D directly formulates COPE as a diffusion-based generative process, enabling Syn2Real generalization without requiring 3D shape priors. Although existing methods perform well, they do not explicitly model the consistent properties shared between synthetic and real-world data. In contrast, this paper analyzes the domain-invariant characteristics across synthetic and real domains and explicitly incorporates semantic knowledge as constraints during both 2D and 3D feature encoding. This design encourages encoders to focus on domain-invariant semantic cues, alleviating the adverse impact of domain-specific information. title: EvenSplat: Coupled 2D-3D Decomposition for Gaussian Splatting under Exposure and Illumination Variation
summary: A surface photographed under even light presents nearly the same appearance from every angle; the same surface under uneven light does not. Exposure changes between views, illumination varies within a single image, and locally strong light sources leave one region bright and its neighbor in shadow. Multi-view reconstruction methods such as 3D Gaussian Splatting treat these lighting artifacts as if they were properties of the scene, entangling capture-specific illumination with the geometry and color they recover. We present EvenSplat, a framework that separates the two. EvenSplat couples an image-space illumination decomposition with an illumination field carried by the Gaussians, so that the same explanation of the lighting is shared between the two-dimensional and three-dimensional views of the scene; a camera-response network and a local exposure-compensation module absorb the global and residual differences that remain across training images. Through extensive experiments across multiple datasets and diverse forms of uneven illumination (cross-view exposure, spatial illumination variation, and high-contrast lighting) on both real-world captured and simulated benchmarks, EvenSplat generally outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly under high-contrast illumination.
full_text: A surface photographed under even light presents nearly the same appearance from every angle; the same surface under uneven light does not. Exposure changes between views, illumination varies within a single image, and locally strong light sources leave one region bright and its neighbor in shadow. Multi-view reconstruction methods such as 3D Gaussian Splatting treat these lighting artifacts as if they were properties of the scene, entangling capture-specific illumination with the geometry and color they recover. We present EvenSplat, a framework that separates the two. EvenSplat couples an image-space illumination decomposition with an illumination field carried by the Gaussians, so that the same explanation of the lighting is shared between the two-dimensional and three-dimensional views of the scene; a camera-response network and a local exposure-compensation module absorb the global and residual differences that remain across training images. Through extensive experiments across multiple datasets and diverse forms of uneven illumination (cross-view exposure, spatial illumination variation, and high-contrast lighting) on both real-world captured and simulated benchmarks, EvenSplat generally outperforms state-of-the-art methods, particularly under high-contrast illumination. Introduction sec:intro Photographs of the same scene are rarely taken under the same light. A camera's exposure adapts from shot to shot~ shim2014autoexposure , a flash or a window lights one side of an object more than the other~ debevec1997hdr , and a bright sky or lamp splits a single frame into washed-out and shadowed regions~ petschnigg2004flash . For a human these differences are unremarkable; for a system that reconstructs a scene from many such photographs, they are a problem. Each image reports a different brightness and color for the same physical surface, and the reconstruction is left to reconcile observations that no longer agree. Novel View Synthesis (NVS) methods such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF)~ DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2003-08934 and 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)~ kerbl20233dgaussiansplattingrealtime reconstruct such scenes with high fidelity, but they assume photometric consistency across views. When the inputs disagree, fitting them faithfully entangles the lighting of each capture with the geometry and color of the scene, so the recovered model carries the artifacts of how it was photographed rather than what was photographed. These inconsistencies take three characteristic forms: Cross-View Exposure Variation (CEV), as when a camera re-meters between shots; Spatial Illumination Variation (SIV) within a single view, as under a flash or a side window; and High-Contrast Illumination (HCI) with strong bright–dark imbalance, as under a harsh local light source. The first is a property of the camera, the latter two of the scene, but all three break the photometric agreement that reconstruction relies on (Fig.~ fig:teaser ). To evaluate these conditions beyond digital image perturbations, we assembled a nine-scene real-world dataset with exposure-bracketed and flash-illuminated captures. It covers the three settings with three CEV, four SIV, and two HCI scenes, together with evenly illuminated reference captures for appearance evaluation. This dataset forms a central part of our evaluation, complemented by controlled simulated benchmarks and a directional-lighting robustness experiment. We introduce EvenSplat, a coupled 2D--3D appearance decomposition framework inspired by the reflect- ance--illumination factorization of Retinex theory~ land1977retinex . Its central design is to use an image-space decomposition optimized together with the Gaussian representation. A multi-scale network predicts per-image illumination and derives a base-appearance estimate, while a Gaussian-level illumination field predicts illumination coefficients conditioned on position, surface normal, and viewing direction. Aligning the image-space and rendered illumination maps connects the two branches. Our contributions are: (1) A coupled 2D--3D decomposition framework that transfers online image-space illumination guidance to a Gaussian-level illumination field for reconstruction from exposure- and illumination-inconsistent inputs. (2) An image-specific correction combining global camera response and illumination-guided local exposure compensation for residual variation in training views. (3) A nine-scene real-world captured dataset spanning cross-view exposure variation, spatial illumination variation, and high-contrast illumination, with reference captures for evaluating appearance reconstruction. Related Work sec:related NVS in Challenging Lighting Conditions Recent ``in-the-wild'' NVS methods explicitly model appearance variations that violate the photometric consistency assumed by standard NeRF and 3DGS. NeRF-W~ martinbrualla2020nerfw introduced per-image appearance embeddings for unconstrained photo collections. GS-W, SWAG, and WildGaussians zhang2024gs-w,dahmani2024swag,kulhanek2024wildgaussians transfer this idea to Gaussian scenes, while WildSplat and WilLaGS zhang2026wildsplat,bai2026willags address unposed or strongly appearance-varying inputs. A complementary line targets low-light image formation and exposure. RawNeRF~ mildenhall2022rawnerf and HDR-NeRF~ huang2022hdr model HDR image formation, while HDR-GS~ hdr_gs and PhysHDR-GS~ zeng2026physhdrgs adapt this objective to Gaussian representations. Lighting-up NeRF~ wang2023lighting , Aleth-NeRF~ cui2023aleth , and Gaussian-DK~ ye2024gaussiandk instead target dark observations. LITA-GS~ zhou2025litags introduces illumination-invariant physical priors, while LL-Gaussian sun2025llgaussian separates reflectance, illumination, and transient residuals. Luminance-GS~ cui_luminance_gs , PPISP~ deutsch2026ppisp , and P2GS~ shimomura2026p2gs focus on exposure, camera processing, and tone-mapping variation. Other methods address view harmonization or explicitly changing illumination. CHROMA~ shin2026chroma harmonizes multi-view inputs using predicted bilateral grids. DarkGS and SunFaded zhang2024darkgs,chang2026sunfaded model camera-mounted moving lights, whereas L2DGS and Disco-GS~ kumar2026l2dgs,kumar2026discogs address dynamic or colored lighting. A related but distinct line performs inverse rendering for relighting. GS-IR, Relightable 3D Gaussians, and GI-GS liang2024gsir,gao2024relightable3dgs,chen2025gigs recover normals, materials, visibility, and illumination for relighting. Subsequent methods extend this factorization to spatially varying materials, indirect illumination, and unconstrained lights~ sun2025svgir,du2025gsid,zhang2025surgs . Even these advances remain brittle in extreme spatially uneven lighting, for instance, scenes with severe cross-view exposure discontinuities, mixed HDR regions, and strong, locally varying light sources across large indoor spaces. In such cases, appearance changes overwhelm per-image embeddings or local feature transfers and drive spurious densification or residual tone inconsistency. EvenSplat considers CEV, SIV, and HCI in one formulation without requiring calibrated light geometry. Instead of aiming to recover a full BRDF or a physically calibrated light, EvenSplat learns an illumination-consistent base appearance for novel-view synthesis by coupling image-space decomposition with a shared Gaussian illumination field while retaining the efficient, explicit rendering structure of 3DGS. Image-Space Illumination Decomposition Retinex theory Land1971LightnessAR separates observed appearance into reflectance and illumination. RetinexNet, KinD, and URetinex-Net~ wei2018deep,zhang2019kindling,wu2022uretinex replace handcrafted decomposition priors with learned illumination estimation for low-light enhancement. Later work broadens the restoration model: Retinexformer~ cai2023retinexformer uses illumination-guided attention; RetinexMamba and ECMamba~ bai2024retinexmamba,dong2024ecmamba employ state-space architectures; and Fourier, video, and diffusion formulations address mixed exposure and general illumination degradation huang2022deepfourier,liu2024vecnet,he2025retidiff . Beyond Retinex, intrinsic image decomposition methods separate surface appearance from shading rather than directly producing an enhanced photograph. Recent work extends the classical albedo--shading formulation toward more complex illumination and richer intrinsic properties careagaColorful,Dirik_2026_CVPR . Related multi-view inverse-rendering work further models material, spatial illumination, and camera response from captured images Lin_2025_CVPR . These decomposition-based formulations motivate our image-space branch, which separates illumination from base appearance and uses the resulting decomposition to guide the learning of a shared 3D Gaussian illumination representation. EvenSplat sec:method EvenSplat learns a shared Gaussian base-appearance representation from views with inconsistent exposure and spatially uneven illumination. As shown in Fig.~ fig:retinex3d-pipeline , an online image-space decomposition guides a Gaussian-level illumination field, while global and local image-specific corrections absorb residual capture variation during training. The resulting scene representation supports base-appearance rendering from unseen viewpoints without fitting a test image. Gaussian Appearance and Illumination subsec:retinex3d Starting from a structure-from-motion point cloud~ schoenberger2016sfm , we use the standard 3DGS geometry, opacity, and spherical-harmonic color parameters~ kerbl20233dgaussiansplattingrealtime . We interpret the SH color as Gaussian base color, while a shared neural field predicts multiplicative illumination from Gaussian position, normal, and viewing direction: Using the same front-to-back compositing weights , we rasterize the illumination-modulated observation and its illumination map for view : Illumination therefore acts before compositing and is shared across views. Because the decomposition is learned in sRGB without radiometric calibration and SH base color can remain view-dependent, we describe as Gaussian base color, not physical albedo. Image-specific adaptation (Sec.~ subsec:rlem ) and cross-domain supervision (Sec.~ subsec:coupling ) constrain this ambiguity without guaranteeing a unique intrinsic decomposition. Compositing and interpretation details are given in Appendix~ app:rendering_details . Image-Specific Appearance Corrections subsec:rlem The shared illumination field cannot represent every capture-specific photometric residual. A camera response network (CRN) predicts a spatially uniform per-image gain within the training image-formation path. During training, the CRN compensates for exposure and color-response variations consistently to the rendered observation and illumination map: Illumination-guided local exposure compensation (ILEC) models remaining spatial residuals with a low-resolution log-gain map . Bilinear upsampling and a gradual activation ramp yield the adapted observation and illumination map: The low-resolution parameterization limits texture memorization, while illumination-guided magnitude, shrinkage, and promotion terms regularize the map (Appendix~ app:local_losses ). CRN and ILEC absorb image-specific photometric variation during training rather than becoming part of the transferable scene representation. They affect training but cancel from the base-appearance ratio because they multiply both paths. At novel views, their image-specific gains are set to the identity. title: Fewer Tokens, Better Action: GPT-6 Astra Robot Agents with 14% Higher Success Rate but 65% Fewer Tokens
summary: Vision language model (VLM) agents can control robots through visual feedback and action primitives, but repeated model invocations and redundant observations incur substantial token overhead. We introduce PyRUA-Lean, an interactive code-execution framework that couples feedback-driven primitive composition with selective observation: the agent composes classical robot primitives and learned vision-language-action (VLA) policies into Python cells that perform conditional checks and local retries, returning only explicitly requested images and state feedback for replanning. Across 700 simulated task instances from LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboCasa365, we compare PyRUA-Lean with a tool-calling baseline using the same GPT-6 Astra planner and underlying robot primitives. Under equal LLM-call budgets, PyRUA-Lean increases overall success from 63.1% to 71.7%. On instances solved by both agents, it uses 49% fewer LLM calls and 65% fewer input tokens.
full_text: PyRUA-Lean matches or exceeds tool calling’s success rate on each sub-suite and costs less on every benchmark. (a) Success rate on all 700 instances, tagged by task property (semantic: perturbed layouts, objects, goals); RoboTwin 2.0 split by skill from task names. (b, c) Input tokens and GPT-6 Astra list-price dollars per solved episode, on instances both agents solved; Avg: mean over all of them. RC365: RoboCasa365. fig:overview Introduction sec:intro Vision-language models (VLMs) can perform robot manipulation by interpreting visual observations and robot state, then invoking motion, perception, and grasping primitives, including vision-language-action (VLA) policies~ ahn2022saycan,huang2022inner,zhang2026harness,su2026astra . Their efficiency depends partly on how these primitives are exposed to the planner. In a tool-calling interface, an operation that depends on a previous tool's result generally requires another VLM invocation. Intermediate results also accumulate in the conversation and are processed in subsequent calls; in systems such as RPent~ zhang2026harness , motion primitives automatically return multiple camera images at the end of each step of execution. Tasks requiring repeated localization, motion, and recovery can therefore incur substantial inference overhead, even when individual primitives are reliable. Executable code provides a way to reduce this overhead. A program can compose primitives, inspect their outputs, and execute conditional branches or retries before returning control to the VLM. Code-based robot control is well established: Code as Policies and ProgPrompt generate robot programs from language instructions~ liang2023code,singh2023progprompt , while more recent systems incorporate execution feedback or refine programs across trials~ fu2026capx,lu2026aspire . Outside robotics, code-based agent interfaces have also shown benefits in task completion and context efficiency~ wang2024codeact,anthropic2025mcp,varda2025codemode . These findings motivate our central question: how can a VLM agent compose robot primitives to reliably complete tasks while reducing token consumption through selective observation and context management? We introduce PyRUA-Lean (Python for Lean Robot-Use Agents), an interactive code-execution interface for feedback-driven primitive composition and selective observation. The agent generates Python programs that compose robot primitives, check intermediate outcomes, and condition subsequent actions on execution feedback. Intermediate results remain available in a persistent program state, while only explicitly printed outputs and requested camera images are returned to the VLM. This allows the agent to handle intermediate execution steps without repeated model invocations and to control which observations enter its context. PyRUA-Lean builds on RPent's robot stacks and primitive implementations~ zhang2026harness . We compare it with RPent's tool-calling agent under the same GPT-6 Astra planner, frozen VLA policies, evaluation task instances, and LLM-call budgets. Both agents operate without cross-episode memory. The comparison evaluates the interfaces as a whole, including their support for control flow, persistent program state, and observation delivery. Experiments cover 700 simulated task instances from LIBERO-PRO, RoboTwin 2.0, and RoboCasa365. Our contributions can be summarized as: An interactive interface for robot primitive composition. We introduce PyRUA-Lean, a Python execution interface built on RPent's robot stack. It supports feedback-driven primitive composition, persistent program state, and selective observation delivery. Comprehensive evaluation on three robot benchmarks. Across 700 simulated instances, PyRUA-Lean improves overall success by approximately 14 relative to tool calling. On jointly solved instances, it uses 49 fewer VLM calls and 65 fewer input tokens. Analysis of efficiency gains and limitations. Traces and ablations identify fewer LLM calls as the main source of token savings, which persist without VLA policies or operating guides but diminish on VLA-dominated tasks, and illustrate geometric computation and scripted recovery. Related Work sec:related VLM-based robot control. Language models have been used to select robot skills, interpret execution feedback, and generate motion commands. SayCan grounds skill selection in language instructions and learned affordances~ ahn2022saycan , while Inner Monologue incorporates environment feedback into planning~ huang2022inner . More recent systems support finer-grained control: Show-Harness exposes discrete semantic actions to a VLM~ chen2026showharness , and GPT-6 Astra has been evaluated as an embodied policy that generates or corrects robot actions~ su2026astra . VLA models provide learned visuomotor capabilities for language-conditioned control~ brohan2023rt2,kim2024openvla,black2025pi0,intelligence2025pi05 . Harness VLA integrates frozen VLA policies with analytic primitives through RPent, a memory-guided agent framework~ zhang2026harness . PyRUA-Lean builds on RPent's robot stacks and primitive implementations, exposing these capabilities through an interactive Python interface. We compare this interface with RPent's tool-calling interface using the same planner and underlying primitives, with cross-episode memory disabled in both agents. Code-based robot control. Code as Policies and ProgPrompt generate executable robot programs from language instructions~ liang2023code,singh2023progprompt , while VoxPoser generates code that constructs spatial value maps for motion planning~ huang2023voxposer . Subsequent work explores execution feedback and program adaptation. CaP-X benchmarks coding agents across primitive abstraction levels and single- or multi-turn interaction modes~ fu2026capx , and VLCP periodically regenerates a control function from updated observations within an episode~ naouali2026vlcp . Other systems accumulate reusable capabilities across trials: Voyager develops a code-based skill library in Minecraft~ wang2023voyager , ASPIRE refines robot programs and consolidates experience into reusable skills~ lu2026aspire , and RoboRSI converts established tool-use workflows into executable routines as part of a robot self-improvement system~ noematrix2026roborsi . These studies establish program synthesis, feedback-driven execution, and skill reuse as complementary approaches to embodied control. Our focus is the success and inference cost of interactive code execution relative to tool calling over the same robot primitives, including VLA policies. We evaluate this comparison without cross-episode skill accumulation, while allowing state and code reuse within each episode. Code-based interfaces for efficient agents. Research on general-purpose agents provides a broader motivation for this comparison. ReAct interleaves reasoning with environment interaction~ yao2023react , and Toolformer studies the use of external APIs by language models~ schick2023toolformer . CodeAct shows that executable Python can improve agent performance relative to text or JSON action interfaces~ wang2024codeact , while SWE-agent demonstrates the importance of interface design for software-engineering agents~ yang2024sweagent . More recent systems use code to compose tool calls and process intermediate results outside the model context, reducing the information returned to the VLM~ anthropic2025mcp,varda2025codemode . PyRUA-Lean applies these interface principles to robot manipulation, where observations are visual and primitive execution may fail. We measure task success together with LLM-call usage, input-token consumption, and inference cost, and analyze how programmatic composition and observation passing contribute to the gains. PyRUA-Lean: Primitive Composition with Selective Observation sec:method PyRUA-Lean is an interactive code-execution interface for VLM-based robot agents. It supports two complementary mechanisms: composing robot primitives into programs that respond to execution feedback, and controlling which intermediate results and visual observations enter the VLM context. The interface builds on RPent's robot stacks and primitive implementations~ zhang2026harness , including classical motion and perception primitives and learned VLA policies. Robot Interface and Execution Model sec:execution_model The robot is exposed as a Python object, robo, whose methods invoke primitives and return structured results, such as object positions and motion outcomes. The agent receives an API reference (Table~ tab:interface lists the primitives) and interacts with the robot through a python(code) tool. At each interaction, the VLM generates a code cell, the runtime executes it, and the returned feedback informs the next code cell. A persistent Python namespace retains variables and helper functions across cells within an episode. Our evaluation uses no cross-episode memory. An uncaught exception terminates the current cell and returns its traceback to the VLM. Variables assigned before the exception remain in the persistent namespace, allowing the agent to revise the failed operation in a subsequent cell. Before each primitive that acts on the robot, the runtime terminates the cell if the task has already succeeded. An external watchdog enforces the two-hour episode limit by interrupting any active primitive and stopping the planner. We impose no separate per-cell execution limit; in our setup, the Codex CLI returns a tool-call timeout after 300~s without cancelling the cell, and subsequent cells are queued. Feedback-Driven Primitive Composition sec:primitive_composition Each cell can compose multiple primitives and condition subsequent operations on their outcomes. For example, a program may approach an object, attempt a grasp only if the approach succeeds, and retry or stop based on the resulting state. These checks and branches execute within the cell without additional LLM invocations. At the end of the cell, the returned feedback allows the LLM to revise subsequent actions, combining program-level feedback with LLM-level replanning. Beyond composing primitive calls, programs can compose task-specific computations and control routines from existing observations and primitives, as illustrated by the geometric computation in Figure~ fig:method (c). For example, the agent computes the bowl's base height from a world-coordinate map to determine a placement target that no individual primitive directly returns. It can also define helper functions for repeated operations, such as a guarded descent. Computed values and helper functions remain available to later cells through the persistent namespace. Selective Observation and Context Management sec:context_management Primitive results remain available in the runtime without being individually added to the LLM conversation. The agent specifies which feedback to return through explicit output statements and camera requests such as robo.show. Requested images and state messages are recorded at the points specified in the code and returned together at the end of the cell. In the episode summarized in Appendix~ app:calls , cell 5 requests a camera image after transporting the bowl. The placement cell shown in Figure~ fig:method (c) requests an image only if the task remains unfinished and therefore returns no images after successful placement. Programmatic composition reduces the LLM invocations needed for dependent operations, while selective feedback limits the outputs and images added to subsequent prompts. Persistent program state retains intermediate data outside the conversation. These mechanisms control new context rather than removing existing history: both agents run in the Codex CLI~ openai2025codexcli , which keeps the full conversation and compacts it, summarizing earlier turns, only when it approaches 272K tokens. title: From Reasoning Failures to Composable Video Spatial Intelligence
summary: Spatial reasoning benchmarks evaluate vision-language models across diverse tasks, but task-level scores do not reveal which underlying capabilities account for success or failure. Each task requires recovering spatial evidence, representing geometry, and reasoning over it. We disentangle these capabilities by comparing predicted and ground-truth spatial context under a shared schema and coordinate contract. This comparison reveals four recurring sources of error: inaccurate perception, missing information in the spatial context, selection of the wrong measurement, and errors in reference frames or in tracking position and orientation. Guided by this diagnosis, we develop CROSS, a training-free library of typed geometric operators and spatial skills that function over available evidence to support reliable video spatial reasoning. The resulting library supplies verified context to non-coding VLMs or callable skills to a SpatialClaw agent. We evaluate \methodname{} on five benchmarks. \methodname{} raises the average score from 55.9\% to 60.2\% on ReVSI and improves the SpatialClaw result from 62.8\% to 66.3\% on DSI-Bench. These gains demonstrate that explicit handling of spatial conventions can repair systematic reasoning failures without additional training.
full_text: Experiments sec:experiments We first diagnose failures under controlled evidence and test their repair on and . We then compare with prior work on ReVSI, VSI-Bench, and STI-Bench and test transfer to DSI-Bench. Per-subtask effects, ablations, and limitations appear in Appendices~ sec:ablations and~ sec:limitations . Diagnostic experiments sec:diagnostic_results Scope. We conduct controlled diagnosis on two compact benchmark subsets using the evidence and target validity checks in Appendix~ sec:diagnostic_validity . Our evaluation uses 823 questions from ReVSI's released tiny split zhang2026revsi . For dynamic spatial reasoning, we construct , a 775-question diagnostic subset of sun2026restisourcegroundedauditrepair covering six tasks involving camera pose, motion, time-indexed quantities, and metric measurement. The diagnostic runs use dataset-specific frame budgets of 32 for and 30 for , held fixed across matched conditions. Table~ tab:diagnostic reports the results; subset construction and exclusion details are provided in Appendix~ sec:diagnostic_scope_appendix . Models and metrics. All context-based diagnostic experiments use Qwen3-VL-32B-Thinking with a shared decoding configuration; the code-writing arms evaluate SpatialClaw. The four numerical tasks use the benchmark's mean relative accuracy (MRA); its categorical tasks and all tasks use multiple-choice accuracy. We report both in percent and differences in percentage points. Predicted context exposes different perception regimes. On , predicted context lowers the average from 55.9 to 50.0 , chiefly on counting, absolute distance, and object size; on , it raises the average from 21.3 to 34.3 and improves five of six subtasks. This contrast suggests that the current predictor recovers trajectory structure more reliably than object identity and object-level metric geometry. Does GT context suffice for reasoning? GT context largely resolves tasks that require access to accurate entities or camera geometry, but leaves errors in operation choice, frame conventions, and evidence sufficiency. Counting rises from 58.2 to 93.1 and object size from 67.9 to 100.0 ; relative distance reaches 91.0 , whereas absolute distance remains at 58.4 because the model often substitutes center-to-center distance for the closest surface gap. Frame-sensitive tasks remain harder: relative direction reaches 52.8 , with left--right reversals and misinterpretations of ``facing away,'' which requires reversing the anchor-to-reference vector by . Route planning falls from 36.8 to 29.8 , with left--right swaps accounting for 43 of 64 incorrect turn tokens. This recurring signature does not by itself establish a failure to update heading. Pose estimation reaches only 66.2 , with errors matching omitted or incorrect ego-to-world transformations. By contrast, speed and egocentric orientation reach 97.4 and 97.1 . The combined displacement-and-path-length row in Table~ tab:diagnostic hides a further distinction: endpoint displacement reaches 99.2 accuracy, but path length reaches only 19.7 , because sparse poses retain the endpoints without preserving the motion between them. Room size has an analogous representation limit: multiplying the dimensions of a scene envelope, such as an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB), gives the area of an enclosing rectangle rather than the queried floor polygon. This rectangle can coincide with an axis-aligned rectangular room, but counts the missing corner of an L-shaped room and can span multiple rooms. Thus, accurate context can still be insufficient, even when the arithmetic is correct. Effectiveness of on diagnosed failures GT context. improves reasoning over the same GT context, as shown by the paired scores and gain annotations in Table~ tab:diagnostic . On , it raises the average from 76.2 to 92.3 (+16.1), with the largest gains on absolute distance (+41.6) and relative direction (+47.2)--- the tasks most affected by the diagnosed wrong-measurement and frame errors. The gains are not uniform: object size, relative distance, and room size do not improve. On , the average rises from 77.3 to 84.7 (+7.4), led by pose estimation (+28.2). These results show that accurate evidence alone does not remove the need for convention-correct reasoning. Predicted evidence across inference interfaces. also improves inference when the spatial context is predicted rather than supplied by GT annotations. On , noisy predicted context lowers the average from 55.9 for direct inference to 50.0 , but adding raises it to 60.4 (+10.4 over predicted context), exceeding both baselines. On , predicted context raises the average from 21.3 to 34.3 , and further improves it to 43.9 (+9.6). The benefit extends beyond GT context to imperfect predicted evidence. For code-writing, we expand SpatialClaw's toolbox with tools rather than supplying an augmented context. This raises SpatialClaw's average from 40.7 to 45.9 (+5.2) on and from 39.4 to 43.5 (+4.1) on . The improvements in both interfaces support the reuse of the same reasoning operators through either context augmentation or agent tool calls. Correcting the same question through both interfaces. Figure~ fig:cross_baseline_corrections asks whether the cooktop is left, right, or behind when facing the TV from the nightstand. Left pair: empty masks produce invalid centroids and Angle: nan degrees, yet SpatialClaw returns C (right). The run recovers centroids and calls rel direction to obtain left, with a kitchen-counter proxy for the cooktop. Right pair: direct video reasoning confuses room-level and observer-relative directions; predicted context with supplies a bearing and yields A (left). The agent prompts and geometry differ, so this selected success does not isolate the operator's causal effect. Main evaluation on ReVSI, VSI-Bench, and STI-Bench ReVSI. ReVSI is our primary large-scale test because it covers the same failure taxonomy as the diagnostic subset while using the 64-frame setting. Table~ tab:full-revsi presents all seven subtask columns alongside prior work zhang2026revsi,dai2026sagent . improves the ReVSI average from 55.9 for direct inference and 52.2 for predicted context to 60.2 with Qwen3-VL-32B-Thinking fixed. Our score is numerically 1.4 points above S-Agent's reported 58.8 and 0.7 points below Gemini 3 Pro's 60.9 dai2026sagent,zhang2026revsi . For code-based inference with Gemma-4-31B-FP8 team2026gemma , adding raises SpatialClaw's average from 55.6 to 58.9 (+3.3). exceeds the spatially specialized models listed in Table~ tab:full-revsi , without adding a spatial fine-tuning stage. Cross-system protocol differences are discussed in Appendix~ sec:limitations . VSI-Bench and STI-Bench. Tables~ tab:vsibench and~ tab:stibench compare our training-free method with published systems on the released benchmarks yang2025thinking,zhang2026revsi,li2025stibench,ouyang2025spacer . We use 64 video frames for VSI-Bench and at most 30 uniformly sampled frames for STI-Bench. On VSI-Bench, raises the average over eight subtasks from 59.8 to 61.4 (+1.6). On STI-Bench, the average rises from 41.6 to 45.3 (+3.7), exceeding the listed Gemini 2.5 Pro (41.4 ) and SpaceR (38.7 ) scores. Cross-benchmark transfer on DSI-Bench sec:cross_benchmark_transfer Table~ tab:generalization tests transfer through the code-writing interface on the full DSI-Bench. Published rows, including SpatialClaw's results on a fixed-seed subset of 1,000 questions, are external context only zhang2025dsibench,wu2026polyv,cho2026spatialclaw . Our full-set SpatialClaw reproduction obtains 62.8 , close to the 62.9 reported on that subset. With the atomic operators frozen and composed into skills for DSI-Bench tasks, SpatialClaw reaches 66.3 , a 3.5-point gain over our reproduction. This result supports transfer of the operator basis through the code-writing interface; it does not establish transfer through context augmentation on DSI-Bench.
